**Surah al-Anfal has seventy-five verses and is Medinan.**

**In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.**

﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: "The spoils belong to God and the Messenger. So fear God, set right what is between you, and obey God and His Messenger, if you are believers."﴾ ﴿The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when God is mentioned, whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them, and who put their trust in their Lord.﴾ [al-Anfal: 2] ﴿Those who establish the prayer and spend of what We have provided them.﴾ [al-Anfal: 3] ﴿Those are the true believers. For them are ranks with their Lord, forgiveness, and generous provision.﴾ [al-Anfal: 4] ﴿Just as your Lord brought you forth from your house in truth, though a group of the believers were averse.﴾ [al-Anfal: 5] ﴿They argue with you concerning the truth after it has become manifest, as though they were being driven to death while looking on.﴾ [al-Anfal: 6] ﴿And when God promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours, and you wished that the unarmed one would be yours, while God wished to establish the truth by His words and to cut off the roots of the disbelievers.﴾ [al-Anfal: 7] ﴿That He might establish the truth and nullify falsehood, even though the criminals detested it.﴾ [al-Anfal: 8] ﴿When you sought help from your Lord, and He answered you: "I will reinforce you with a thousand angels, following one another."﴾ [al-Anfal: 9] ﴿God did not make it except as good news, and so that your hearts might be reassured by it. Victory comes only from God. Indeed God is Mighty, Wise.﴾ [al-Anfal: 10] ﴿When He caused slumber to overcome you as a security from Him, and sent down water on you from the sky to purify you by it, to remove from you the defilement of Satan, to strengthen your hearts, and to make your feet firm.﴾ [al-Anfal: 11] ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels: "I am with you, so strengthen those who believe. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved. So strike above the necks and strike every fingertip of them."﴾ [al-Anfal: 12]

(p-455) The *nafl* (surplus, extra) is an addition beyond what is obligatory, and the spoils of war were named after it, because they are an addition beyond the effort of protecting the territory. Labid said:

*Indeed, the piety of our Lord is the best nafl,*
*and by God's permission, my delay and my haste.*

That is, the best spoil. Another said:

*When the battle grows red, we are the ones who are rich,*
*and we abstain at the division of the spoils (anfal).*

*Wajal* means fear. *Shawka* — al-Mubarrad said: it means weapons. Its root is from *shawk*, a plant that has thorns; from it one says "a man *shaki* al-silah (armed with weapons)" when he has a sharp spear-head and blade. The original form is *sha²ik*, an active participle from *shawka*. He said:

*Before a lion, armed with weapons, hurled forward,*
*whose mane and claws have never been trimmed.*

Abu Ubayda said: *al-shaki* and *al-shaik* both mean the one possessing *shawka* (armed strength), and the weapon is described with it just as a man is. He said:

*And I put on, from His pleasure, on my path,*
*a weapon that frightens the brave, armed.*

It is said: "a man *shakin*, and a weapon *shakin* and *shakin*." The form *shakin* originally derives from *shawk*, like *kabsh safin* (a ram that is wooly), meaning *sawf* (wool). As for *shakin*, it is either with an elided letter or transposed; the explanation of this belongs to the science of grammar.

*Al-istighatha* is seeking help and support. It is said *ghawitha al-rajul* (the man was helped), and one says "O help me!" (*wa-ghawthah*). The noun is *al-ghawth*, *al-ghiwath*, and *al-ghawath*. It is also said: *al-istighatha* is seeking the relief of a friend at the time of need; and it is also said: it is seeking protection (*al-istijara*).

*Radifa* and *ardafa* have one meaning: he followed. One says *ardaftuhu iyyahu*, meaning: I followed him. The *unuq* (neck) is well known; its plural for a small number is *a'naq*, and for a large number is *'unuq*. *Al-banan* means the fingers; it is a collective noun whose singular is *banana*. They also said *al-banam* with a *m* in place of the *n*. Ru'ba said:

*O Sal, the one with the stammering speech,*
*and your hand dyed, the fingers* (*al-banam*).

﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: "The spoils belong to God and the Messenger. So fear God, set right what is between you, and obey God and His Messenger, if you are believers."﴾

This surah is entirely Medinan. Ibn Abbas said: except for seven verses, the first of which is: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plot against you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30] to the end of the verses. Muqatil said: except for one verse, which is: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plot against you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30], the verse, and it was revealed concerning an event that occurred in Mecca. It is possible that the verse was revealed in Medina concerning that. There is no disagreement that it was revealed on the day of Badr and concerning the matter of its spoils. The exegetes, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and others, have elaborated at length on determining what was the cause of revelation of these verses. Its summary is: the souls of the people of Badr became estranged, and there occurred in them what occurs in human souls of desiring preference and exclusivity. We do not name the one who performed well on that day. So the verses were revealed, and the Muslims were content and submitted, and God set right the state of affairs among them (p-456).

The exegetes differed concerning what is meant by *al-anfal*. Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatada, Ata, and Ibn Zayd said: it means the spoils in general. Ikrima and Mujahid said: this ruling was from God to quell the dispute, and then it was abrogated (*nusikha*, i.e., superseded by a later ruling, *naskh*) by His saying: ﴿And know that whatever you gain of any booty﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], the verse. Abu Zayd said: there is no abrogation; He only informed that the spoils belong to God insofar as they are His possession and provision, and to the Messenger insofar as he explains God's ruling; the present tense in it is so that submission to it occurs among the people, and the ruling of distribution occurs within that. Ibn Abbas also said: *al-anfal* in the verse is what the leader gives to whomever he wishes of a sword, a horse, or the like. Ali ibn Salih, Ibn Jinni, and al-Hasan said: *al-anfal* in the verse is the one-fifth (*khums*). Ibn Abbas and Ata also said: *al-anfal* in the verse is what strayed of the property of the polytheists to the Muslims, such as a runaway horse or a runaway slave, and it belongs to the Prophet (ﷺ), who does with it what he wills. Ibn Abbas also said: *al-anfal* in the verse is what was obtained of the property of the polytheists after the division of the spoils. These four opinions contradict what the reported occasions of revelation agree upon. The sound view is the first, which is what the reports converge upon. Al-Sha'bi said: *al-anfal* means the captives, and this is only one example of it. Ibn Atiyya and others have elaborated at length on the rulings concerning what the leader takes and the ruling on spoils (*salb*, the equipment taken from a slain enemy); the subject of that is found in the books of jurisprudence.

The pronoun of the subject in *yas'alunaka* does not refer back to anything mentioned before it; rather, the event of Badr clarifies it. So it refers to those among the Companions who attended it, and it is as though the questioners were known and specified on that day, so the pronoun returned to them. The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ). The question may be for demanding a meaning in the thing asked about, and then it is transitive with *'an* (about), as in the saying:

*Ask if you are ignorant of the people concerning us and concerning them.*

God the Exalted said: ﴿They ask you about the Hour﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾ [al-Baqara: 217]. Likewise here: ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾, meaning its ruling and to whom it belongs; that is why the answer came: ﴿Say: the spoils belong to God and the Messenger﴾. The question may also be for demanding property or the like, and then it is transitive to two objects. You say: "I asked Ziyad for property." Some exegetes took the question here in this sense, and claimed that *'an* is superfluous, and that the intended meaning is: "they ask you for the spoils." There is no necessity for this. It is more appropriate to interpret the reading of those who read without *'an* as intending it, because omitting a particle while it is intended in meaning is easier than adding it without meaning other than emphasis. This is the reading of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ali ibn al-Husayn and his two sons Zayd and Muhammad al-Baqir, and the son of the latter, Ja'far al-Sadiq, Ikrima, Ata, al-Dahhak, and Talha ibn Musarrif. It is also said: *'an* has the meaning of *min* (from), that is: "they ask you from the spoils." There is no necessity to give a particle the meaning of another particle.

Ibn Muhaysin read: *'alanfal*. He transferred the vowel of the hamza to the definite article *lam* and dropped the hamza, and he counted the opposing vowel as valid, so he assimilated (idgham), like: *wa-qad tabayyana lakum* (and it has become clear to you).

The meaning of ﴿Say: the spoils belong to God and the Messenger﴾ is that there is no share in them for any of the Emigrants or the Helpers, and it has not been delegated to anyone; rather it is delegated to God according to what He wills, and to the Messenger insofar as he conveys the rulings from God. He commanded them to be pious so that disputing would cease among them and they would become loving one another for God's sake. He commanded them to set right the state of affairs between them. This indicates that there was estrangement and distance among them, which might have led them to destroy the affection and well-being that existed between them. The discussion of *dhat* (state, essence) has already been given in His saying: ﴿with what is in the breasts﴾ [al-Anfal: 43]. *Al-bayn* here means separation and distancing. *Dhat* here is an adjective of an omitted object, meaning: "set right states that are (characterized by) your separation." Since the states were connected to the separation, the adjective of them was attributed to it, just as you say: "give me to drink of the one of your vessel," meaning: "the water of the owner of your vessel." Since the water was in the vessel, it was described with *dhu* and attributed to the vessel, and the meaning is: "give me to drink what is in the vessel of water."

Ibn Atiyya said: *dhat* in this place is used to mean the very thing and its reality. What is understood from *baynikum* is a meaning that encompasses all connection, unions, and affections; and *dhat dhalika* (that very state) is what is commanded to be set right, that is, its essence and reality. So God urged the setting right of those parts, and when those are attained, the setting right of what encompasses them is attained, which is the *bayn* (relationship) that they have. The word *dhat* is sometimes used to mean something inseparable from what it is attributed to, even if it is not its essence or reality. This is in His saying: ﴿knower of what is in the breasts﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 7] and ﴿the one with the thorn (shawka)﴾ [al-Anfal: 7]. It may be that *dhat al-bayn* is this. It may also be said that *dhat* has another meaning, though close to this, which is the saying: "I did such-and-such *dhat yawm*" (on a certain day). From it is the saying of the poet:

*The dog does not bark in it except once,*
*on a night of evening, nor do its snakes move.*

Al-Tabari reported from some of them that he said: *dhat baynikum* means "the state that is between you," just as *dhat al-'isha'* means "the hour in which there is evening." Al-Tabari endorsed this, but it is an opinion clearly refuted. Its summary: *al-bayn* is applied to separation and is also applied to connection. This is the view of al-Zajjaj here. He said: "Similar to it is ﴿Your bond has been severed﴾ [al-An'am: 94], and it may be a noun of place meaning "middle." *Dhat* may be attributed to each of these meanings. We have chosen that it means separation, because its use in that sense is more well known than its use for connection, and because the attribution of *dhat* to *bayn* in the sense of separation is more frequent than its attribution to *bayn* as a spatial adverb, since it is not very variable in usage; rather its usage is like that of *amam* (in front of) and *khalf* (behind), which is a moderate usage, not frequent.

God, the Exalted, first commanded piety, because it is the root of acts of obedience; then He commanded setting right what is between them, because that is the most important result of piety at that time when they were quarrelling. Then He commanded obedience to Him and to His Messenger regarding what He commanded them of piety and setting right and other things. The meaning of ﴿if you are believers﴾ [al-A'raf: 85] is: if you are those whose faith is complete. Al-Zamakhshari here was confused and inconsistent. He said: He made piety, setting right what is between them, and obedience to God the Exalted and to the Messenger (ﷺ) among the requirements and necessary consequences of faith, to inform them that the perfection of faith depends on fulfilling them. The meaning of ﴿if you are believers﴾ [al-A'raf: 85] is: if you are those whose faith is complete. Ibn Atiyya said: just as a man says: "If you are a man, then do such-and-such," meaning: if you are complete in manhood. He said: the response to the condition in His earlier saying ﴿and obey﴾ [al-Anfal: 46] — this is the view of Sibawayh; and the view of Abu al-Abbas is that the response is omitted and placed later, indicated by what precedes it, its estimate being: "if you are believers, obey." His view in this is that the response does not precede the condition. What he said contradicts the statements of the grammarians, for they say: the view of Sibawayh is that the response is omitted, and the view of Abu al-Abbas, Abu Zayd al-Ansari, and the Kufans is the permissibility of placing the response of the condition before it. This transmission is the correct one.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verse 2–6 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Only those are the believers whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely.﴾ It is recited "wajilat" (وجلت) with a fatha on the jim, which is a dialect form. Ibn Mas'ud read "fariqat" (فرقت), and Ubayy read "faza'at" (فزعت). These two readings should be taken as explanations (tafsir). Since the meaning of "in kuntum mu'minin" (﴿if you are believers﴾) [al-A'raf: 85] was present, He said: "innama al-mu'minun" (﴿only the believers﴾), meaning those whose faith is complete. Then He described them with a relative clause joined to three great stations: the station of fear, the station of increase in faith, and the station of reliance (tawakkul). His saying "idha dhukira Allah" (﴿when Allah is mentioned﴾) may mean that when His name is mentioned and pronounced, their hearts are startled by its mention, out of magnification, reverence and awe. This remembrance differs from the remembrance in His saying: ﴿Then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Zumar: 23], because the remembrance of Allah there is His kindness, mercy and reward. It is also possible that "dhikr Allah" is by omission of a modifier, meaning: the greatness of Allah, His power, and what He threatened those who disobey Him with, are mentioned. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Al-Suddi said: it refers to a man who intends to commit a sin, then remembers Allah and is restrained from it. In the hadith about the seven whom Allah will shade under His shade on the day when there is no shade but His: "A man whom a woman of beauty and high station invites, and he says: 'Indeed I fear Allah.'" The meaning of "zadat-hum iman" (﴿they increase them in faith﴾) is certainty and steadfastness, because the convergence and reinforcement of proofs is stronger for the tranquility signified and firmer for its footing. It was also said: the meaning is that if he had not heard a ruling from the rulings of the Qur'an revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he believed in it, his faith increased with respect to all that he had already believed in, since for each ruling there is a specific affirmation. For this reason Mujahid said: "increase in faith" is an expression for increase in knowledge and its rulings. It was also said: the increase of faith is a metaphor for increase in action. It is reported from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that faith has a sunnah, obligations and laws, and whoever completes them completes the faith. It was also said: this refers to the wrongdoer who is admonished and told: "Fear Allah," and he desists, and that increases him in faith. The apparent view is that His saying "wa 'ala Rabbihim yatawakkalun" (﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾) is part of the relative clause of "alladhina," as we said earlier. It was also said that it is a new independent clause. The arrangement of these stations is the best arrangement: He began with the station of fear, whether the fear of reverence and awe or the fear of punishment; second, with faith in the obligations revealed; third, with entrusting the matter to Allah, devoting oneself to Him, and disregarding everything else.

﴿Those who establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them﴾. It is best that "alladhina" (الَّذِينَ) be an attribute of the preceding "alladhina," so that it falls within the scope of the same subject. Thus it is a report about the believers with three things: the inward attribute, the bodily attribute, and the financial attribute. He used the plural for the actions of the hearts because they are more noble, and in the actions of the limbs He combined prayer and charity, because they are the two pillars of actions. Al-Hawfi and al-Tabrizi permitted that "alladhina" be a substitute (badal) for "alladhina," or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are those who... The apparent meaning of "wa mimma razaqnahum yunfiqun" (﴿and spend from what We have provided them﴾) is general, covering zakat, voluntary charity, maintaining kinship ties and other financial good deeds. A group of commentators restricted it to zakat because it is joined with prayer.

﴿Those are the believers in truth﴾. Ibn Atiyya said: "haqqan" (حقًّا) is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar), as Sibawayh explicitly stated; it is the non-transferred verbal noun, and its governing verb is "ahaqqa dhalika haqqan," end of quote. The meaning is that it is an emphasis on what the nominal sentence contains of predication, and that there is no metaphor in that predication. Al-Zamakhshari said: "haqqan" is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: ﴿Those are the believers﴾ with true faith, and it is an emphatic verbal noun for the sentence ﴿Those are the believers﴾, like his saying: "He is the servant of Allah, truly," meaning: "that is truly established." It is reported from al-Hasan that a man asked him: "Are you a believer?" He said: "Faith is of two kinds. If you are asking me about faith in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, Paradise and Hell, resurrection and reckoning, then I am a believer. But if you are asking me about His saying: ﴿Only the believers﴾, then by Allah I do not know whether I am among them." He who claimed that the sentence is complete at His saying ﴿Those are the believers﴾, and that "haqqan" is connected to what follows, meaning "for them truly are degrees," is far off, because the accusative of "haqqan" in this case would precede the completion of the nominal sentence, since it is an emphatic verbal noun for the content of the sentence, and so it is not permissible to place it first. Some have permitted it, but it is weak.

﴿For them are degrees with their Lord, and forgiveness and a generous provision﴾. Since three attributes were mentioned earlier, the heart-related, the bodily and the financial, three things were arranged upon them. The actions of the heart are matched with degrees, the bodily with forgiveness, and it is reported in a hadith that a man had approached a non-related woman in a way that a man does with his wife short of intercourse, and when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was informed of that, he asked him: "Did you pray with us?" He said: "Yes." He said to him: "Allah has forgiven you." The financial attribute is matched with "generous provision" (rizq karim). This type of correspondence is among the fine points of rhetoric (badi' 'ilm al-bayan). Ibn Atiyya and the majority said that the intended meaning is the levels and stations of Paradise and its ranks, according to their deeds. Al-Tabari reported from Mujahid that they are the degrees of worldly deeds. His saying "rizq karim" intends the foods and drinks of Paradise, and "karim" is an attribute that implies elevation of rank, as in the saying: "a noble garment" and "a noble lineage." Al-Zamakhshari said: degrees of honour and dignity, elevation of station and forgiveness, overlooking their misdeeds, and generous provision, meaning the good and lasting benefits of Paradise in a manner of exaltation, and this is the meaning of reward, end of quote. Ata' said: the degrees of Paradise they ascend by their deeds. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: seventy degrees, between every two degrees is the distance a galloping horse covers in seventy years. It was also said: they are levels and stations in Paradise, some above others. In a hadith: "The people of Paradise will see the people of the chambers as one sees a bright star." These three opinions indicate that the degrees are meant literally. It is reported from Mujahid that they are degrees of lofty deeds.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verses 2–6 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth, though a party of the believers were averse. They dispute with you concerning the truth after it had become clear, as if they were being driven to death while they looked on.﴾ The exegetes (mufassirun) differed greatly over His words: ﴿Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾, and they gave fifteen opinions on it. The first: the kaf (the "just as") is in the sense of the oath particle waw, and ma is in the sense of "the one who" (alladhi), referring to one who has knowledge, namely Allah, as it occurs in His words: ﴿and by Him who created the male and the female﴾ (al-Layl 3). The answer to the oath is ﴿they dispute with you﴾, and the intended meaning is: "By Allah, who brought you out of your house, they dispute with you concerning the truth." This was said by Abu 'Ubayda, who was weak in the science of grammar. al-Kirmani said: "This is an error." Ibn al-Anbari said: "The kaf is not one of the particles of oath." End of quote. In this view there is also the problem that the answer to the oath is in the affirmative present tense without the lam or the emphatic nun, and both are necessary in such a construction according to the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun, the grammarians of Basra), or the alternation of one of them with the other according to the Kufan grammarians (al-Kufiyyun, the grammarians of Kufa). As for its being devoid of both or of one of them, this is an opinion that contradicts what the Kufans and Basrans agreed upon (ijma', scholarly consensus).

The second opinion: the kaf is in the sense of idh ("when") and ma is extra (za'idah), the meaning being: "Remember when He brought you out." This is weak, because it has not been established that kaf means idh in the language of the Arabs, nor has it been established that ma is added after this except in the conditional sense, and likewise it is not added in the sense that is claimed for it.

The third opinion: the kaf is in the sense of 'ala ("upon") and ma is in the sense of alladhi, the meaning being: "Proceed upon that which your Lord brought you out of your house." This is weak, because it has not been established that kaf means 'ala, and because the relative pronoun requires a returning pronoun (a 'a'id), and this cannot be omitted in such a construction.

The fourth opinion: 'Ikrimah said: the meaning is: "Obey Allah and His Messenger if you are believers, just as your going out in obedience is good for you, just as your going out was good for them."

The fifth opinion: al-Kisa'i and others said: "Just as your Lord brought you out of your house, despite the aversion of a party among them, so they dispute with you concerning fighting the disbelievers of Makkah, and they wish for the unarmed party (ghayr dhat al-shawkah) after it has become clear to them that you are only doing what you were commanded, not what they desire." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The meaning according to this interpretation is: they dispute with you concerning the truth with a dispute that resembles their aversion to your Lord bringing you out of your house. So the disputing in this interpretation is equivalent to the aversion, and thus the comparison occurs in meaning. The one who says this claims that the disputers are the polytheists."

The sixth opinion: al-Farra' said: "The meaning is: Proceed according to your command regarding the spoils, and give the extra share (nafl) to whomever you wish, even if they dislike it, just as your Lord brought you out." End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The expression 'proceed according to your command and give the extra share to whomever you wish' is not well formulated. My own clarification of this meaning is that this kaf likens this story, which is his going out of his house, to the earlier story, which is their question about the spoils. It is as if they asked about the extra share and disputed, so Allah removed that from them, and this was the choice. Just as they disliked in this story the Prophet ﷺ setting out, when Allah brought him out of his house, and in that was the choice, so their disputing over the extra share is equivalent to their aversion here to going out. And Allah's judgment regarding the spoils, that they belong to Allah and the Messenger, is equivalent to His bringing out His Prophet from his house. Then the choice in both stories was from what Allah did. According to this interpretation, His words ﴿they dispute with you﴾ may be a new sentence, meaning the disbelievers: they dispute with you about the law of Islam after the truth has become clear in it, as if they were being driven to death while calling them to faith. What I have mentioned, that ﴿they dispute with you﴾ refers to the disbelievers, is explicitly stated." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "These are two consistent opinions, by which the meaning is completed and the wording is praised." By the two opinions we mean the opinion of al-Farra' and the opinion of al-Kisa'i. The discussion about these two statements has been extensive, but they are not evident, nor do they fit together from the standpoint of the function of the conjunction (al-'atif).

The seventh opinion: al-Akhfash said: the kaf is an adjective (na't) for ḥaqqan ("truly"), and the meaning is: "They are the believers in truth, just as He brought you out." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The meaning according to this interpretation, 'as He brought you out', does not harmonize."

The eighth opinion: the kaf is in the nominative position (raf') and the meaning is: "Just as your Lord brought you out, so fear Allah." It is as if it were a beginning and predicate. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This meaning was invented by this exegete, and it is not among the wordings of the verse, neither in its source nor in its outcome."

The ninth opinion: al-Zajjaj said: the kaf is in the accusative position (nasb), and the meaning is: "The spoils are established for Allah with a firm establishment, just as your Lord brought you out." This view was taken up and praised by al-Zamakhshari, who said: it is in the accusative as a qualifier (sifah) of a verbal noun (masdar) for the verb assumed in His words ﴿The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾ (8:1). That is: "The spoils have been settled for Allah and the Messenger and have been confirmed despite their aversion, with a confirmation like the confirmation of your Lord's bringing you out of your house while they were averse." End of quote. This has a distance (bu'd) in it because of the great separation between the likened and that to which it is likened, and no great meaning appears in comparing this with that. Rather, even if the two were close, no great benefit would appear in the comparison.

The tenth opinion: the kaf is in the nominative position, and the meaning is: "For them are degrees with their Lord, and forgiveness, and generous provision; this is a true promise, just as He brought you out." This involves the omission of a subject and predicate, and if it were stated explicitly the comparison would not fit and would not be good.

The eleventh opinion: the kaf is also in the nominative position, and the meaning is: "And set right the state of affairs among yourselves; that is better for you, just as He brought you out." So the kaf is an adjective of the predicate of an omitted subject. This too contains omission and length, as it separates His words "and set right" from "just as He brought you out."

The twelfth opinion: He likened the aversion of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to his going out from Madinah, when they became certain of the departure of Quraysh to defend Abu Sufyan and protect his caravan. Their aversion was to having the spoils taken from their hands and given to the Messenger, or to the extra share from them. This opinion was taken up and praised by al-Zamakhshari, who said: "The place of the kaf is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, its assumed meaning being: 'This situation is like the situation of your going out.' He means that their state in disliking what you saw of the distribution of the spoils is like their state in disliking going out to war." This is the view stated by this speaker, which al-Zamakhshari praised, and it is what Ibn 'Atiyyah explained of al-Farra's opinion with his words: "This kaf likened this story, which is his going out of his house, to the earlier story, which is their question about the spoils," and so on to the end of his statement.

The thirteenth opinion: the meaning is: "Your division of the spoils is true, just as your going out was true."

The fourteenth opinion: the comparison occurs between two goings out, namely: your Lord bringing you out of your house, which is Makkah, while you were averse to your going out; and the outcome of that was good, victory, and triumph, like the bringing out of your Lord from Madinah. And some of the believers being averse will be followed by victory and triumph.

The fifteenth opinion: the kaf is for comparison in the figurative sense (majaz), like the saying of a speaker to his slave: "Just as I directed you against my enemies and they overpowered you, and you asked for reinforcement and I reinforced you and strengthened you and removed your impediments, so now seize them and punish them with such and such; and just as I clothed you and provided you with sustenance, so act such and such; and just as I did good to you, do not thank me for it." Thus the meaning of the verse is: "Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth, and He covered you with drowsiness as a security from Him" (8:11), meaning by it Himself and those with Him; "and sent down water from the sky to purify you by it" (8:11); "and sent down upon you from the sky angels in succession" (8:9, 12), "so strike above the necks and strike from them every fingertip" (8:12). It is as if He says: "I have removed your impediments and reinforced you with the angels, so strike them in these places," and this is killing, so that you may reach Allah's purpose of establishing the truth and nullifying falsehood. The summary of this long statement is that ﴿just as He brought you out﴾ is connected to His words "so strike," and in this there is what is clearly distant and separated. These are the fifteen opinions that we have come across.

Whoever is inclined toward the weaving of speech, who turns in the composition of its varieties, and who practices eloquence and rhetoric, will not find any of these opinions good, even though some of their proponents had a standing (imamah) in the science of grammar and a firm foothold in it. But he did not attend closely to the wording of the speech, nor was it in his nature to shape it in the finest form, nor to exercise, in examining it, the eloquence through which inimitability (i'jaz) becomes apparent. Before writing down these opinions here, I came upon a number of them, and none of them settled in my mind. Then I saw in a dream that I was walking along a path with a man with whom I was discussing His words: ﴿Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾. I said to him: "No difficulty like this has passed before me, and perhaps there is an omitted element through which the meaning is made sound. I have not found in any exegete anything of substance on this." Then I said to him: "It has just become clear to me how to derive it, and that the omitted element is: 'He gave you victory' (nasaraka)." Both I and that man found this derivation good. Then I woke from sleep, still recalling it. The assumed meaning is: "So it is as if it were said: 'Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth,' that is, because of the manifestation of the religion of Allah and the exaltation of His law, and they were averse to your going out, out of dread of fighting and fear of death, since the command of the Prophet ﷺ for their going out was sudden, and they were not prepared for going out, and they disputed with you about the truth after its clarity. Allah gave you victory and reinforced you with His angels." The speech that follows indicates this omitted element, namely His words, exalted is He: ﴿when you sought help from your Lord, and He answered you﴾ (8:9), and so on in the verses. It appears that the kaf in this dream-based derivation is not merely for comparison, but contains the meaning of causation (ta'lil). The grammarians have explicitly stated that it may produce the meaning of causation, and they derived on this basis His words: ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾ (2:198). They also cited the verse:

"Do not revile people, just as you would not wish to be reviled."

i.e., because people insult you, do not insult them back. A common expression with this meaning is: "As you obey God, He will admit you to Paradise," meaning: because of your obedience to God, He will admit you to Paradise. The sense is therefore: if you go out to exalt the religion of God and kill its enemies, God will help you and reinforce you with angels. The waw in "wa-inna fariqan" is the waw of the circumstantial clause (waw al-hal). Apparently "min baytika" refers to the place of his residence; it is also said to be Medina, because it is his place of emigration (muhajar) and is specific to him; and it is also said to be Mecca, though this is remote, because the apparent meaning is that this is a report about his going out to Badr, so turning it to going out from Mecca is not apparent. The object of "la-karihun" is the going out, i.e., "they were truly averse to going out with you." Their aversion to that is either due to the natural revulsion of temperament, or because they had not been called to march (istanfaru), or the shift from the caravan (al-'ir) to the armed encounter (al-nafir), because of the strength of seizing wealth in that, and because of the killing and fighting in this; or because of leaving Mecca, their homes and their property. These are four opinions.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun of the subject in "yujadilunaka" refers to the group of believers who were averse, and their disputing is their saying: "Our going out was only for the caravan; had we known, we would have prepared ourselves for battle." The truth here is the support of the religion of Islam. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the polytheists, and their disputing about the truth is concerning the law of Islam.

Abd Allah recited "ba'da ma bayyana" with a dammah on the ba' and without a ta'. In His saying "ba'da ma tabayyana" there is a great rebuke against them, because whoever disputes about a matter that has not become clear is less deserving of blame, but whoever contends about a matter that is clear is deserving of blame and reproach.

Then He likened their state in their extreme terror, while they were being driven toward victory and booty, to the state of one who is being led onto the cliff toward death, while he is witnessing its causes, looking at them, and not doubting in them. It is also said that their fear was due to the small number and that they were infantry; it is narrated that there were only two horsemen among them, and they were three hundred and thirteen, while the polytheists were about a thousand men. The story of Badr is recounted in full in the books of the Sirah, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah have summarized from it what can be found in their two books.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verse 2–6 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Only those are the believers whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely.﴾ It is recited "wajilat" (وجلت) with a fatha on the jim, which is a dialect form. Ibn Mas'ud read "fariqat" (فرقت), and Ubayy read "faza'at" (فزعت). These two readings should be taken as explanations (tafsir). Since the meaning of "in kuntum mu'minin" (﴿if you are believers﴾) [al-A'raf: 85] was present, He said: "innama al-mu'minun" (﴿only the believers﴾), meaning those whose faith is complete. Then He described them with a relative clause joined to three great stations: the station of fear, the station of increase in faith, and the station of reliance (tawakkul). His saying "idha dhukira Allah" (﴿when Allah is mentioned﴾) may mean that when His name is mentioned and pronounced, their hearts are startled by its mention, out of magnification, reverence and awe. This remembrance differs from the remembrance in His saying: ﴿Then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Zumar: 23], because the remembrance of Allah there is His kindness, mercy and reward. It is also possible that "dhikr Allah" is by omission of a modifier, meaning: the greatness of Allah, His power, and what He threatened those who disobey Him with, are mentioned. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Al-Suddi said: it refers to a man who intends to commit a sin, then remembers Allah and is restrained from it. In the hadith about the seven whom Allah will shade under His shade on the day when there is no shade but His: "A man whom a woman of beauty and high station invites, and he says: 'Indeed I fear Allah.'" The meaning of "zadat-hum iman" (﴿they increase them in faith﴾) is certainty and steadfastness, because the convergence and reinforcement of proofs is stronger for the tranquility signified and firmer for its footing. It was also said: the meaning is that if he had not heard a ruling from the rulings of the Qur'an revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he believed in it, his faith increased with respect to all that he had already believed in, since for each ruling there is a specific affirmation. For this reason Mujahid said: "increase in faith" is an expression for increase in knowledge and its rulings. It was also said: the increase of faith is a metaphor for increase in action. It is reported from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that faith has a sunnah, obligations and laws, and whoever completes them completes the faith. It was also said: this refers to the wrongdoer who is admonished and told: "Fear Allah," and he desists, and that increases him in faith. The apparent view is that His saying "wa 'ala Rabbihim yatawakkalun" (﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾) is part of the relative clause of "alladhina," as we said earlier. It was also said that it is a new independent clause. The arrangement of these stations is the best arrangement: He began with the station of fear, whether the fear of reverence and awe or the fear of punishment; second, with faith in the obligations revealed; third, with entrusting the matter to Allah, devoting oneself to Him, and disregarding everything else.

﴿Those who establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them﴾. It is best that "alladhina" (الَّذِينَ) be an attribute of the preceding "alladhina," so that it falls within the scope of the same subject. Thus it is a report about the believers with three things: the inward attribute, the bodily attribute, and the financial attribute. He used the plural for the actions of the hearts because they are more noble, and in the actions of the limbs He combined prayer and charity, because they are the two pillars of actions. Al-Hawfi and al-Tabrizi permitted that "alladhina" be a substitute (badal) for "alladhina," or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are those who... The apparent meaning of "wa mimma razaqnahum yunfiqun" (﴿and spend from what We have provided them﴾) is general, covering zakat, voluntary charity, maintaining kinship ties and other financial good deeds. A group of commentators restricted it to zakat because it is joined with prayer.

﴿Those are the believers in truth﴾. Ibn Atiyya said: "haqqan" (حقًّا) is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar), as Sibawayh explicitly stated; it is the non-transferred verbal noun, and its governing verb is "ahaqqa dhalika haqqan," end of quote. The meaning is that it is an emphasis on what the nominal sentence contains of predication, and that there is no metaphor in that predication. Al-Zamakhshari said: "haqqan" is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: ﴿Those are the believers﴾ with true faith, and it is an emphatic verbal noun for the sentence ﴿Those are the believers﴾, like his saying: "He is the servant of Allah, truly," meaning: "that is truly established." It is reported from al-Hasan that a man asked him: "Are you a believer?" He said: "Faith is of two kinds. If you are asking me about faith in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, Paradise and Hell, resurrection and reckoning, then I am a believer. But if you are asking me about His saying: ﴿Only the believers﴾, then by Allah I do not know whether I am among them." He who claimed that the sentence is complete at His saying ﴿Those are the believers﴾, and that "haqqan" is connected to what follows, meaning "for them truly are degrees," is far off, because the accusative of "haqqan" in this case would precede the completion of the nominal sentence, since it is an emphatic verbal noun for the content of the sentence, and so it is not permissible to place it first. Some have permitted it, but it is weak.

﴿For them are degrees with their Lord, and forgiveness and a generous provision﴾. Since three attributes were mentioned earlier, the heart-related, the bodily and the financial, three things were arranged upon them. The actions of the heart are matched with degrees, the bodily with forgiveness, and it is reported in a hadith that a man had approached a non-related woman in a way that a man does with his wife short of intercourse, and when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was informed of that, he asked him: "Did you pray with us?" He said: "Yes." He said to him: "Allah has forgiven you." The financial attribute is matched with "generous provision" (rizq karim). This type of correspondence is among the fine points of rhetoric (badi' 'ilm al-bayan). Ibn Atiyya and the majority said that the intended meaning is the levels and stations of Paradise and its ranks, according to their deeds. Al-Tabari reported from Mujahid that they are the degrees of worldly deeds. His saying "rizq karim" intends the foods and drinks of Paradise, and "karim" is an attribute that implies elevation of rank, as in the saying: "a noble garment" and "a noble lineage." Al-Zamakhshari said: degrees of honour and dignity, elevation of station and forgiveness, overlooking their misdeeds, and generous provision, meaning the good and lasting benefits of Paradise in a manner of exaltation, and this is the meaning of reward, end of quote. Ata' said: the degrees of Paradise they ascend by their deeds. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: seventy degrees, between every two degrees is the distance a galloping horse covers in seventy years. It was also said: they are levels and stations in Paradise, some above others. In a hadith: "The people of Paradise will see the people of the chambers as one sees a bright star." These three opinions indicate that the degrees are meant literally. It is reported from Mujahid that they are degrees of lofty deeds.

The first: the kaf (the "just as") is in the sense of the oath particle waw, and ma is in the sense of "the one who" (alladhi), referring to one who has knowledge, namely Allah, as it occurs in His words: ﴿and by Him who created the male and the female﴾ (al-Layl 3). The answer to the oath is ﴿they dispute with you﴾, and the intended meaning is: "By Allah, who brought you out of your house, they dispute with you concerning the truth." This was said by Abu 'Ubayda, who was weak in the science of grammar. al-Kirmani said: "This is an error." Ibn al-Anbari said: "The kaf is not one of the particles of oath." End of quote. In this view there is also the problem that the answer to the oath is in the affirmative present tense without the lam or the emphatic nun, and both are necessary in such a construction according to the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun, the grammarians of Basra), or the alternation of one of them with the other according to the Kufan grammarians (al-Kufiyyun, the grammarians of Kufa). As for its being devoid of both or of one of them, this is an opinion that contradicts what the Kufans and Basrans agreed upon (ijma', scholarly consensus).

The second opinion: the kaf is in the sense of idh ("when") and ma is extra (za'idah), the meaning being: "Remember when He brought you out." This is weak, because it has not been established that kaf means idh in the language of the Arabs, nor has it been established that ma is added after this except in the conditional sense, and likewise it is not added in the sense that is claimed for it.

The third opinion: the kaf is in the sense of 'ala ("upon") and ma is in the sense of alladhi, the meaning being: "Proceed upon that which your Lord brought you out of your house." This is weak, because it has not been established that kaf means 'ala, and because the relative pronoun requires a returning pronoun (a 'a'id), and this cannot be omitted in such a construction.

The fourth opinion: 'Ikrimah said: the meaning is: "Obey Allah and His Messenger if you are believers, just as your going out in obedience is good for you, just as your going out was good for them."

The fifth opinion: al-Kisa'i and others said: "Just as your Lord brought you out of your house, despite the aversion of a party among them, so they dispute with you concerning fighting the disbelievers of Makkah, and they wish for the unarmed party (ghayr dhat al-shawkah) after it has become clear to them that you are only doing what you were commanded, not what they desire." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The meaning according to this interpretation is: they dispute with you concerning the truth with a dispute that resembles their aversion to your Lord bringing you out of your house. So the disputing in this interpretation is equivalent to the aversion, and thus the comparison occurs in meaning. The one who says this claims that the disputers are the polytheists."

The sixth opinion: al-Farra' said: "The meaning is: Proceed according to your command regarding the spoils, and give the extra share (nafl) to whomever you wish, even if they dislike it, just as your Lord brought you out." End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The expression 'proceed according to your command and give the extra share to whomever you wish' is not well formulated. My own clarification of this meaning is that this kaf likens this story, which is his going out of his house, to the earlier story, which is their question about the spoils. It is as if they asked about the extra share and disputed, so Allah removed that from them, and this was the choice. Just as they disliked in this story the Prophet ﷺ setting out, when Allah brought him out of his house, and in that was the choice, so their disputing over the extra share is equivalent to their aversion here to going out. And Allah's judgment regarding the spoils, that they belong to Allah and the Messenger, is equivalent to His bringing out His Prophet from his house. Then the choice in both stories was from what Allah did. According to this interpretation, His words ﴿they dispute with you﴾ may be a new sentence, meaning the disbelievers: they dispute with you about the law of Islam after the truth has become clear in it, as if they were being driven to death while calling them to faith. What I have mentioned, that ﴿they dispute with you﴾ refers to the disbelievers, is explicitly stated." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "These are two consistent opinions, by which the meaning is completed and the wording is praised." By the two opinions we mean the opinion of al-Farra' and the opinion of al-Kisa'i. The discussion about these two statements has been extensive, but they are not evident, nor do they fit together from the standpoint of the function of the conjunction (al-'atif).

The seventh opinion: al-Akhfash said: the kaf is an adjective (na't) for ḥaqqan ("truly"), and the meaning is: "They are the believers in truth, just as He brought you out." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The meaning according to this interpretation, 'as He brought you out', does not harmonize."

The eighth opinion: the kaf is in the nominative position (raf') and the meaning is: "Just as your Lord brought you out, so fear Allah." It is as if it were a beginning and predicate. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This meaning was invented by this exegete, and it is not among the wordings of the verse, neither in its source nor in its outcome."

The ninth opinion: al-Zajjaj said: the kaf is in the accusative position (nasb), and the meaning is: "The spoils are established for Allah with a firm establishment, just as your Lord brought you out." This view was taken up and praised by al-Zamakhshari, who said: it is in the accusative as a qualifier (sifah) of a verbal noun (masdar) for the verb assumed in His words ﴿The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾ (8:1). That is: "The spoils have been settled for Allah and the Messenger and have been confirmed despite their aversion, with a confirmation like the confirmation of your Lord's bringing you out of your house while they were averse." Rather, even if the two were close, no great benefit would appear in the comparison.

The tenth opinion: the kaf is in the nominative position, and the meaning is: "For them are degrees with their Lord, and forgiveness, and generous provision; this is a true promise, just as He brought you out." This involves the omission of a subject and predicate, and if it were stated explicitly the comparison would not fit and would not be good.

The eleventh opinion: the kaf is also in the nominative position, and the meaning is: "And set right the state of affairs among yourselves; that is better for you, just as He brought you out." So the kaf is an adjective of the predicate of an omitted subject. This too contains omission and length, as it separates His words "and set right" from "just as He brought you out."

The twelfth opinion: He likened the aversion of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to his going out from Madinah, when they became certain of the departure of Quraysh to defend Abu Sufyan and protect his caravan. Their aversion was to having the spoils taken from their hands and given to the Messenger, or to the extra share from them. His saying "idha dhukira Allah" (﴿when Allah is mentioned﴾) may mean that when His name is mentioned and pronounced, their hearts are startled by its mention, out of magnification, reverence and awe. This remembrance differs from the remembrance in His saying: ﴿Then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Zumar: 23], because the remembrance of Allah there is His kindness, mercy and reward. It is also possible that "dhikr Allah" is by omission of a modifier, meaning: the greatness of Allah, His power, and what He threatened those who disobey Him with, are mentioned. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Al-Suddi said: it refers to a man who intends to commit a sin, then remembers Allah and is restrained from it. In the hadith about the seven whom Allah will shade under His shade on the day when there is no shade but His: "A man whom a woman of beauty and high station invites, and he says: 'Indeed I fear Allah.'" The meaning of "zadat-hum iman" (﴿they increase them in faith﴾) is certainty and steadfastness, because the convergence and reinforcement of proofs is stronger for the tranquility signified and firmer for its footing. It was also said: the meaning is that if he had not heard a ruling from the rulings of the Qur'an revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he believed in it, his faith increased with respect to all that he had already believed in, since for each ruling there is a specific affirmation. For this reason Mujahid said: "increase in faith" is an expression for increase in knowledge and its rulings. It was also said: the increase of faith is a metaphor for increase in action. It is reported from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that faith has a sunnah, obligations and laws, and whoever completes them completes the faith. It was also said: this refers to the wrongdoer who is admonished and told: "Fear Allah," and he desists, and that increases him in faith. The apparent view is that His saying "wa 'ala Rabbihim yatawakkalun" (﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾) is part of the relative clause of "alladhina," as we said earlier. It was also said that it is a new independent clause. The arrangement of these stations is the best arrangement: He began with the station of fear, whether the fear of reverence and awe or the fear of punishment; second, with faith in the obligations revealed; third, with entrusting the matter to Allah, devoting oneself to Him, and disregarding everything else.

It is best that "alladhina" (الَّذِينَ) be an attribute of the preceding "alladhina," so that it falls within the scope of the same subject. Thus it is a report about the believers with three things: the inward attribute, the bodily attribute, and the financial attribute. He used the plural for the actions of the hearts because they are more noble, and in the actions of the limbs He combined prayer and charity, because they are the two pillars of actions. Al-Hawfi and al-Tabrizi permitted that "alladhina" be a substitute (badal) for "alladhina," or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are those who... The apparent meaning of "wa mimma razaqnahum yunfiqun" (﴿and spend from what We have provided them﴾) is general, covering zakat, voluntary charity, maintaining kinship ties and other financial good deeds. A group of commentators restricted it to zakat because it is joined with prayer.

Some have permitted it, but it is weak.

It was also said: they are levels and stations in Paradise, some above others. In a hadith: "The people of Paradise will see the people of the chambers as one sees a bright star." Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verses 2–6 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth, though a party of the believers were averse. They dispute with you concerning the truth after it had become clear, as if they were being driven to death while they looked on.﴾ The exegetes (mufassirun) differed greatly over His words: ﴿Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾, and they gave fifteen opinions on it. The first: the kaf (the "just as") is in the sense of the oath particle waw, and ma is in the sense of "the one who" (alladhi), referring to one who has knowledge, namely Allah, as it occurs in His words: ﴿and by Him who created the male and the female﴾ (al-Layl 3). The answer to the oath is ﴿they dispute with you﴾, and the intended meaning is: "By Allah, who brought you out of your house, they dispute with you concerning the truth." This was said by Abu 'Ubayda, who was weak in the science of grammar. al-Kirmani said: "This is an error." Ibn al-Anbari said: "The kaf is not one of the particles of oath." End of quote. In this view there is also the problem that the answer to the oath is in the affirmative present tense without the lam or the emphatic nun, and both are necessary in such a construction according to the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun, the grammarians of Basra), or the alternation of one of them with the other according to the Kufan grammarians (al-Kufiyyun, the grammarians of Kufa). As for its being devoid of both or of one of them, this is an opinion that contradicts what the Kufans and Basrans agreed upon (ijma', scholarly consensus).

The second opinion: the kaf is in the sense of idh ("when") and ma is extra (za'idah), the meaning being: "Remember when He brought you out." This is weak, because it has not been established that kaf means idh in the language of the Arabs, nor has it been established that ma is added after this except in the conditional sense, and likewise it is not added in the sense that is claimed for it.

The third opinion: the kaf is in the sense of 'ala ("upon") and ma is in the sense of alladhi, the meaning being: "Proceed upon that which your Lord brought you out of your house." This is weak, because it has not been established that kaf means 'ala, and because the relative pronoun requires a returning pronoun (a 'a'id), and this cannot be omitted in such a construction.

The fourth opinion: 'Ikrimah said: the meaning is: "Obey Allah and His Messenger if you are believers, just as your going out in obedience is good for you, just as your going out was good for them."

The fifth opinion: al-Kisa'i and others said: "Just as your Lord brought you out of your house, despite the aversion of a party among them, so they dispute with you concerning fighting the disbelievers of Makkah, and they wish for the unarmed party (ghayr dhat al-shawkah) after it has become clear to them that you are only doing what you were commanded, not what they desire." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The meaning according to this interpretation is: they dispute with you concerning the truth with a dispute that resembles their aversion to your Lord bringing you out of your house. So the disputing in this interpretation is equivalent to the aversion, and thus the comparison occurs in meaning. The one who says this claims that the disputers are the polytheists."

The sixth opinion: al-Farra' said: "The meaning is: Proceed according to your command regarding the spoils, and give the extra share (nafl) to whomever you wish, even if they dislike it, just as your Lord brought you out." End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The expression 'proceed according to your command and give the extra share to whomever you wish' is not well formulated. My own clarification of this meaning is that this kaf likens this story, which is his going out of his house, to the earlier story, which is their question about the spoils. It is as if they asked about the extra share and disputed, so Allah removed that from them, and this was the choice. Just as they disliked in this story the Prophet ﷺ setting out, when Allah brought him out of his house, and in that was the choice, so their disputing over the extra share is equivalent to their aversion here to going out. And Allah's judgment regarding the spoils, that they belong to Allah and the Messenger, is equivalent to His bringing out His Prophet from his house. Then the choice in both stories was from what Allah did. According to this interpretation, His words ﴿they dispute with you﴾ may be a new sentence, meaning the disbelievers: they dispute with you about the law of Islam after the truth has become clear in it, as if they were being driven to death while calling them to faith. What I have mentioned, that ﴿they dispute with you﴾ refers to the disbelievers, is explicitly stated." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "These are two consistent opinions, by which the meaning is completed and the wording is praised." By the two opinions we mean the opinion of al-Farra' and the opinion of al-Kisa'i. The discussion about these two statements has been extensive, but they are not evident, nor do they fit together from the standpoint of the function of the conjunction (al-'atif).

The seventh opinion: al-Akhfash said: the kaf is an adjective (na't) for ḥaqqan ("truly"), and the meaning is: "They are the believers in truth, just as He brought you out." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The meaning according to this interpretation, 'as He brought you out', does not harmonize."

The eighth opinion: the kaf is in the nominative position (raf') and the meaning is: "Just as your Lord brought you out, so fear Allah." It is as if it were a beginning and predicate. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This meaning was invented by this exegete, and it is not among the wordings of the verse, neither in its source nor in its outcome."

The ninth opinion: al-Zajjaj said: the kaf is in the accusative position (nasb), and the meaning is: "The spoils are established for Allah with a firm establishment, just as your Lord brought you out." This view was taken up and praised by al-Zamakhshari, who said: it is in the accusative as a qualifier (sifah) of a verbal noun (masdar) for the verb assumed in His words ﴿The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾ (8:1). That is: "The spoils have been settled for Allah and the Messenger and have been confirmed despite their aversion, with a confirmation like the confirmation of your Lord's bringing you out of your house while they were averse." End of quote. This has a distance (bu'd) in it because of the great separation between the likened and that to which it is likened, and no great meaning appears in comparing this with that. Rather, even if the two were close, no great benefit would appear in the comparison.

The tenth opinion: the kaf is in the nominative position, and the meaning is: "For them are degrees with their Lord, and forgiveness, and generous provision; this is a true promise, just as He brought you out." This involves the omission of a subject and predicate, and if it were stated explicitly the comparison would not fit and would not be good.

The eleventh opinion: the kaf is also in the nominative position, and the meaning is: "And set right the state of affairs among yourselves; that is better for you, just as He brought you out." So the kaf is an adjective of the predicate of an omitted subject. This too contains omission and length, as it separates His words "and set right" from "just as He brought you out."

The twelfth opinion: He likened the aversion of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to his going out from Madinah, when they became certain of the departure of Quraysh to defend Abu Sufyan and protect his caravan. Their aversion was to having the spoils taken from their hands and given to the Messenger, or to the extra share from them. This opinion was taken up and praised by al-Zamakhshari, who said: "The place of the kaf is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, its assumed meaning being: 'This situation is like the situation of your going out.' He means that their state in disliking what you saw of the distribution of the spoils is like their state in disliking going out to war." This is the view stated by this speaker, which al-Zamakhshari praised, and it is what Ibn 'Atiyyah explained of al-Farra's opinion with his words: "This kaf likened this story, which is his going out of his house, to the earlier story, which is their question about the spoils," and so on to the end of his statement.

The thirteenth opinion: the meaning is: "Your division of the spoils is true, just as your going out was true."

The fourteenth opinion: the comparison occurs between two goings out, namely: your Lord bringing you out of your house, which is Makkah, while you were averse to your going out; and the outcome of that was good, victory, and triumph, like the bringing out of your Lord from Madinah. And some of the believers being averse will be followed by victory and triumph.

The fifteenth opinion: the kaf is for comparison in the figurative sense (majaz), like the saying of a speaker to his slave: "Just as I directed you against my enemies and they overpowered you, and you asked for reinforcement and I reinforced you and strengthened you and removed your impediments, so now seize them and punish them with such and such; and just as I clothed you and provided you with sustenance, so act such and such; and just as I did good to you, do not thank me for it." Thus the meaning of the verse is: "Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth, and He covered you with drowsiness as a security from Him" (8:11), meaning by it Himself and those with Him; "and sent down water from the sky to purify you by it" (8:11); "and sent down upon you from the sky angels in succession" (8:9, 12), "so strike above the necks and strike from them every fingertip" (8:12). It is as if He says: "I have removed your impediments and reinforced you with the angels, so strike them in these places," and this is killing, so that you may reach Allah's purpose of establishing the truth and nullifying falsehood. The summary of this long statement is that ﴿just as He brought you out﴾ is connected to His words "so strike," and in this there is what is clearly distant and separated. These are the fifteen opinions that we have come across.

Whoever is inclined toward the weaving of speech, who turns in the composition of its varieties, and who practices eloquence and rhetoric, will not find any of these opinions good, even though some of their proponents had a standing (imamah) in the science of grammar and a firm foothold in it. But he did not attend closely to the wording of the speech, nor was it in his nature to shape it in the finest form, nor to exercise, in examining it, the eloquence through which inimitability (i'jaz) becomes apparent. Before writing down these opinions here, I came upon a number of them, and none of them settled in my mind. Then I saw in a dream that I was walking along a path with a man with whom I was discussing His words: ﴿Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾. I said to him: "No difficulty like this has passed before me, and perhaps there is an omitted element through which the meaning is made sound. I have not found in any exegete anything of substance on this." Then I said to him: "It has just become clear to me how to derive it, and that the omitted element is: 'He gave you victory' (nasaraka)." Both I and that man found this derivation good. Then I woke from sleep, still recalling it. The assumed meaning is: "So it is as if it were said: 'Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth,' that is, because of the manifestation of the religion of Allah and the exaltation of His law, and they were averse to your going out, out of dread of fighting and fear of death, since the command of the Prophet ﷺ for their going out was sudden, and they were not prepared for going out, and they disputed with you about the truth after its clarity. Allah gave you victory and reinforced you with His angels." The speech that follows indicates this omitted element, namely His words, exalted is He: ﴿when you sought help from your Lord, and He answered you﴾ (8:9), and so on in the verses. It appears that the kaf in this dream-based derivation is not merely for comparison, but contains the meaning of causation (ta'lil). The grammarians have explicitly stated that it may produce the meaning of causation, and they derived on this basis His words: ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾ (2:198). They also cited the verse:

"Do not revile people, just as you would not wish to be reviled."

i.e., because people insult you, do not insult them back. A common expression with this meaning is: "As you obey God, He will admit you to Paradise," meaning: because of your obedience to God, He will admit you to Paradise. The sense is therefore: if you go out to exalt the religion of God and kill its enemies, God will help you and reinforce you with angels. The waw in "wa-inna fariqan" is the waw of the circumstantial clause (waw al-hal). Apparently "min baytika" refers to the place of his residence; it is also said to be Medina, because it is his place of emigration (muhajar) and is specific to him; and it is also said to be Mecca, though this is remote, because the apparent meaning is that this is a report about his going out to Badr, so turning it to going out from Mecca is not apparent. The object of "la-karihun" is the going out, i.e., "they were truly averse to going out with you." Their aversion to that is either due to the natural revulsion of temperament, or because they had not been called to march (istanfaru), or the shift from the caravan (al-'ir) to the armed encounter (al-nafir), because of the strength of seizing wealth in that, and because of the killing and fighting in this; or because of leaving Mecca, their homes and their property. These are four opinions.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun of the subject in "yujadilunaka" refers to the group of believers who were averse, and their disputing is their saying: "Our going out was only for the caravan; had we known, we would have prepared ourselves for battle." The truth here is the support of the religion of Islam. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the polytheists, and their disputing about the truth is concerning the law of Islam.

Abd Allah recited "ba'da ma bayyana" with a dammah on the ba' and without a ta'. In His saying "ba'da ma tabayyana" there is a great rebuke against them, because whoever disputes about a matter that has not become clear is less deserving of blame, but whoever contends about a matter that is clear is deserving of blame and reproach.

Then He likened their state in their extreme terror, while they were being driven toward victory and booty, to the state of one who is being led onto the cliff toward death, while he is witnessing its causes, looking at them, and not doubting in them. It is also said that their fear was due to the small number and that they were infantry; it is narrated that there were only two horsemen among them, and they were three hundred and thirteen, while the polytheists were about a thousand men. The story of Badr is recounted in full in the books of the Sirah, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah have summarized from it what can be found in their two books.
