In this view there is also the problem that the answer to the oath is in the affirmative present tense without the lam or the emphatic nun, and both are necessary in such a construction according to the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun, the grammarians of Basra), or the alternation of one of them with the other according to the Kufan grammarians (al-Kufiyyun, the grammarians of Kufa). As for its being devoid of both or of one of them, this is an opinion that contradicts what the Kufans and Basrans agreed upon (ijma', scholarly consensus).

The second opinion: the kaf is in the sense of idh ("when") and ma is extra (za'idah), the meaning being: "Remember when He brought you out." This is weak, because it has not been established that kaf means idh in the language of the Arabs, nor has it been established that ma is added after this except in the conditional sense, and likewise it is not added in the sense that is claimed for it.

The third opinion: the kaf is in the sense of 'ala ("upon") and ma is in the sense of alladhi, the meaning being: "Proceed upon that which your Lord brought you out of your house." This is weak, because it has not been established that kaf means 'ala, and because the relative pronoun requires a returning pronoun (a 'a'id), and this cannot be omitted in such a construction.

The fourth opinion: 'Ikrimah said: the meaning is: "Obey Allah and His Messenger if you are believers, just as your going out in obedience is good for you, just as your going out was good for them."

The fifth opinion: al-Kisa'i and others said: "Just as your Lord brought you out of your house, despite the aversion of a party among them, so they dispute with you concerning fighting the disbelievers of Makkah, and they wish for the unarmed party (ghayr dhat al-shawkah) after it has become clear to them that you are only doing what you were commanded, not what they desire." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The meaning according to this interpretation is: they dispute with you concerning the truth with a dispute that resembles their aversion to your Lord bringing you out of your house. So the disputing in this interpretation is equivalent to the aversion, and thus the comparison occurs in meaning. The one who says this claims that the disputers are the polytheists."

The sixth opinion: al-Farra' said: "The meaning is: Proceed according to your command regarding the spoils, and give the extra share (nafl) to whomever you wish, even if they dislike it, just as your Lord brought you out." End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The expression 'proceed according to your command and give the extra share to whomever you wish' is not well formulated. My own clarification of this meaning is that this kaf likens this story, which is his going out of his house, to the earlier story, which is their question about the spoils. It is as if they asked about the extra share and disputed, so Allah removed that from them, and this was the choice. Just as they disliked in this story the Prophet ﷺ setting out, when Allah brought him out of his house, and in that was the choice, so their disputing over the extra share is equivalent to their aversion here to going out. And Allah's judgment regarding the spoils, that they belong to Allah and the Messenger, is equivalent to His bringing out His Prophet from his house. Then the choice in both stories was from what Allah did. According to this interpretation, His words ﴿they dispute with you﴾ may be a new sentence, meaning the disbelievers: they dispute with you about the law of Islam after the truth has become clear in it, as if they were being driven to death while calling them to faith. What I have mentioned, that ﴿they dispute with you﴾ refers to the disbelievers, is explicitly stated." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "These are two consistent opinions, by which the meaning is completed and the wording is praised." By the two opinions we mean the opinion of al-Farra' and the opinion of al-Kisa'i. The discussion about these two statements has been extensive, but they are not evident, nor do they fit together from the standpoint of the function of the conjunction (al-'atif).

The seventh opinion: al-Akhfash said: the kaf is an adjective (na't) for ḥaqqan ("truly"), and the meaning is: "They are the believers in truth, just as He brought you out." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The meaning according to this interpretation, 'as He brought you out', does not harmonize."

The eighth opinion: the kaf is in the nominative position (raf') and the meaning is: "Just as your Lord brought you out, so fear Allah." It is as if it were a beginning and predicate. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This meaning was invented by this exegete, and it is not among the wordings of the verse, neither in its source nor in its outcome."

The ninth opinion: al-Zajjaj said: the kaf is in the accusative position (nasb), and the meaning is: "The spoils are established for Allah with a firm establishment, just as your Lord brought you out." This view was taken up and praised by al-Zamakhshari, who said: it is in the accusative as a qualifier (sifah) of a verbal noun (masdar) for the verb assumed in His words ﴿The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾ (8:1). That is: "The spoils have been settled for Allah and the Messenger and have been confirmed despite their aversion, with a confirmation like the confirmation of your Lord's bringing you out of your house while they were averse." End of quote. This has a distance (bu'd) in it because of the great separation between the likened and that to which it is likened, and no great meaning appears in comparing this with that. Rather, even if the two were close, no great benefit would appear in the comparison.

The tenth opinion: the kaf is in the nominative position, and the meaning is: "For them are degrees with their Lord, and forgiveness, and generous provision; this is a true promise, just as He brought you out." This involves the omission of a subject and predicate, and if it were stated explicitly the comparison would not fit and would not be good.

The eleventh opinion: the kaf is also in the nominative position, and the meaning is: "And set right the state of affairs among yourselves; that is better for you, just as He brought you out." So the kaf is an adjective of the predicate of an omitted subject. This too contains omission and length, as it separates His words "and set right" from "just as He brought you out."

The twelfth opinion: He likened the aversion of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to his going out from Madinah, when they became certain of the departure of Quraysh to defend Abu Sufyan and protect his caravan. Their aversion was to having the spoils taken from their hands and given to the Messenger, or to the extra share from them. This opinion was taken up and praised by al-Zamakhshari, who said: "The place of the kaf is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, its assumed meaning being: 'This situation is like the situation of your going out.' He means that their state in disliking what you saw of the distribution of the spoils is like their state in disliking going out to war." This is the view stated by this speaker, which al-Zamakhshari praised, and it is what Ibn 'Atiyyah explained of al-Farra's opinion with his words: "This kaf likened this story, which is his going out of his house, to the earlier story, which is their question about the spoils," and so on to the end of his statement.

The thirteenth opinion: the meaning is: "Your division of the spoils is true, just as your going out was true."

The fourteenth opinion: the comparison occurs between two goings out, namely: your Lord bringing you out of your house, which is Makkah, while you were averse to your going out; and the outcome of that was good, victory, and triumph, like the bringing out of your Lord from Madinah. And some of the believers being averse will be followed by victory and triumph.

The fifteenth opinion: the kaf is for comparison in the figurative sense (majaz), like the saying of a speaker to his slave: "Just as I directed you against my enemies and they overpowered you, and you asked for reinforcement and I reinforced you and strengthened you and removed your impediments, so now seize them and punish them with such and such; and just as I clothed you and provided you with sustenance, so act such and such; and just as I did good to you, do not thank me for it." Thus the meaning of the verse is: "Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth, and He covered you with drowsiness as a security from Him" (8:11), meaning by it Himself and those with Him; "and sent down water from the sky to purify you by it" (8:11); "and sent down upon you from the sky angels in succession" (8:9, 12), "so strike above the necks and strike from them every fingertip" (8:12). It is as if He says: "I have removed your impediments and reinforced you with the angels, so strike them in these places," and this is killing, so that you may reach Allah's purpose of establishing the truth and nullifying falsehood. The summary of this long statement is that ﴿just as He brought you out﴾ is connected to His words "so strike," and in this there is what is clearly distant and separated. These are the fifteen opinions that we have come across.

Whoever is inclined toward the weaving of speech, who turns in the composition of its varieties, and who practices eloquence and rhetoric, will not find any of these opinions good, even though some of their proponents had a standing (imamah) in the science of grammar and a firm foothold in it. But he did not attend closely to the wording of the speech, nor was it in his nature to shape it in the finest form, nor to exercise, in examining it, the eloquence through which inimitability (i'jaz) becomes apparent. Before writing down these opinions here, I came upon a number of them, and none of them settled in my mind. Then I saw in a dream that I was walking along a path with a man with whom I was discussing His words: ﴿Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾. I said to him: "No difficulty like this has passed before me, and perhaps there is an omitted element through which the meaning is made sound. I have not found in any exegete anything of substance on this." Then I said to him: "It has just become clear to me how to derive it, and that the omitted element is: 'He gave you victory' (nasaraka)." Both I and that man found this derivation good. Then I woke from sleep, still recalling it. The assumed meaning is: "So it is as if it were said: 'Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth,' that is, because of the manifestation of the religion of Allah and the exaltation of His law, and they were averse to your going out, out of dread of fighting and fear of death, since the command of the Prophet ﷺ for their going out was sudden, and they were not prepared for going out, and they disputed with you about the truth after its clarity. Allah gave you victory and reinforced you with His angels." The speech that follows indicates this omitted element, namely His words, exalted is He: ﴿when you sought help from your Lord, and He answered you﴾ (8:9), and so on in the verses. It appears that the kaf in this dream-based derivation is not merely for comparison, but contains the meaning of causation (ta'lil). The grammarians have explicitly stated that it may produce the meaning of causation, and they derived on this basis His words: ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾ (2:198). They also cited the verse:

"Do not revile people, just as you would not wish to be reviled."

i.e., because people insult you, do not insult them back. A common expression with this meaning is: "As you obey God, He will admit you to Paradise," meaning: because of your obedience to God, He will admit you to Paradise. The sense is therefore: if you go out to exalt the religion of God and kill its enemies, God will help you and reinforce you with angels. The waw in "wa-inna fariqan" is the waw of the circumstantial clause (waw al-hal). Apparently "min baytika" refers to the place of his residence; it is also said to be Medina, because it is his place of emigration (muhajar) and is specific to him; and it is also said to be Mecca, though this is remote, because the apparent meaning is that this is a report about his going out to Badr, so turning it to going out from Mecca is not apparent. The object of "la-karihun" is the going out, i.e., "they were truly averse to going out with you." Their aversion to that is either due to the natural revulsion of temperament, or because they had not been called to march (istanfaru), or the shift from the caravan (al-'ir) to the armed encounter (al-nafir), because of the strength of seizing wealth in that, and because of the killing and fighting in this; or because of leaving Mecca, their homes and their property. These are four opinions.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun of the subject in "yujadilunaka" refers to the group of believers who were averse, and their disputing is their saying: "Our going out was only for the caravan; had we known, we would have prepared ourselves for battle." The truth here is the support of the religion of Islam. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the polytheists, and their disputing about the truth is concerning the law of Islam.

Abd Allah recited "ba'da ma bayyana" with a dammah on the ba' and without a ta'. In His saying "ba'da ma tabayyana" there is a great rebuke against them, because whoever disputes about a matter that has not become clear is less deserving of blame, but whoever contends about a matter that is clear is deserving of blame and reproach.

Then He likened their state in their extreme terror, while they were being driven toward victory and booty, to the state of one who is being led onto the cliff toward death, while he is witnessing its causes, looking at them, and not doubting in them. It is also said that their fear was due to the small number and that they were infantry; it is narrated that there were only two horsemen among them, and they were three hundred and thirteen, while the polytheists were about a thousand men. The story of Badr is recounted in full in the books of the Sirah, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah have summarized from it what can be found in their two books.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verse 2–6 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Only those are the believers whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely.﴾ It is recited "wajilat" (وجلت) with a fatha on the jim, which is a dialect form. Ibn Mas'ud read "fariqat" (فرقت), and Ubayy read "faza'at" (فزعت). These two readings should be taken as explanations (tafsir). Since the meaning of "in kuntum mu'minin" (﴿if you are believers﴾) [al-A'raf: 85] was present, He said: "innama al-mu'minun" (﴿only the believers﴾), meaning those whose faith is complete. Then He described them with a relative clause joined to three great stations: the station of fear, the station of increase in faith, and the station of reliance (tawakkul). His saying "idha dhukira Allah" (﴿when Allah is mentioned﴾) may mean that when His name is mentioned and pronounced, their hearts are startled by its mention, out of magnification, reverence and awe. This remembrance differs from the remembrance in His saying: ﴿Then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Zumar: 23], because the remembrance of Allah there is His kindness, mercy and reward. It is also possible that "dhikr Allah" is by omission of a modifier, meaning: the greatness of Allah, His power, and what He threatened those who disobey Him with, are mentioned. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Al-Suddi said: it refers to a man who intends to commit a sin, then remembers Allah and is restrained from it. In the hadith about the seven whom Allah will shade under His shade on the day when there is no shade but His: "A man whom a woman of beauty and high station invites, and he says: 'Indeed I fear Allah.'" The meaning of "zadat-hum iman" (﴿they increase them in faith﴾) is certainty and steadfastness, because the convergence and reinforcement of proofs is stronger for the tranquility signified and firmer for its footing. It was also said: the meaning is that if he had not heard a ruling from the rulings of the Qur'an revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he believed in it, his faith increased with respect to all that he had already believed in, since for each ruling there is a specific affirmation. For this reason Mujahid said: "increase in faith" is an expression for increase in knowledge and its rulings. It was also said: the increase of faith is a metaphor for increase in action. It is reported from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that faith has a sunnah, obligations and laws, and whoever completes them completes the faith. It was also said: this refers to the wrongdoer who is admonished and told: "Fear Allah," and he desists, and that increases him in faith. The apparent view is that His saying "wa 'ala Rabbihim yatawakkalun" (﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾) is part of the relative clause of "alladhina," as we said earlier. It was also said that it is a new independent clause. The arrangement of these stations is the best arrangement: He began with the station of fear, whether the fear of reverence and awe or the fear of punishment; second, with faith in the obligations revealed; third, with entrusting the matter to Allah, devoting oneself to Him, and disregarding everything else.

﴿Those who establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them﴾. It is best that "alladhina" (الَّذِينَ) be an attribute of the preceding "alladhina," so that it falls within the scope of the same subject. Thus it is a report about the believers with three things: the inward attribute, the bodily attribute, and the financial attribute. He used the plural for the actions of the hearts because they are more noble, and in the actions of the limbs He combined prayer and charity, because they are the two pillars of actions. Al-Hawfi and al-Tabrizi permitted that "alladhina" be a substitute (badal) for "alladhina," or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are those who... The apparent meaning of "wa mimma razaqnahum yunfiqun" (﴿and spend from what We have provided them﴾) is general, covering zakat, voluntary charity, maintaining kinship ties and other financial good deeds. A group of commentators restricted it to zakat because it is joined with prayer.

﴿Those are the believers in truth﴾. Ibn Atiyya said: "haqqan" (حقًّا) is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar), as Sibawayh explicitly stated; it is the non-transferred verbal noun, and its governing verb is "ahaqqa dhalika haqqan," end of quote. The meaning is that it is an emphasis on what the nominal sentence contains of predication, and that there is no metaphor in that predication. Al-Zamakhshari said: "haqqan" is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: ﴿Those are the believers﴾ with true faith, and it is an emphatic verbal noun for the sentence ﴿Those are the believers﴾, like his saying: "He is the servant of Allah, truly," meaning: "that is truly established." It is reported from al-Hasan that a man asked him: "Are you a believer?" He said: "Faith is of two kinds. If you are asking me about faith in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, Paradise and Hell, resurrection and reckoning, then I am a believer. But if you are asking me about His saying: ﴿Only the believers﴾, then by Allah I do not know whether I am among them." He who claimed that the sentence is complete at His saying ﴿Those are the believers﴾, and that "haqqan" is connected to what follows, meaning "for them truly are degrees," is far off, because the accusative of "haqqan" in this case would precede the completion of the nominal sentence, since it is an emphatic verbal noun for the content of the sentence, and so it is not permissible to place it first. Some have permitted it, but it is weak.

﴿For them are degrees with their Lord, and forgiveness and a generous provision﴾. Since three attributes were mentioned earlier, the heart-related, the bodily and the financial, three things were arranged upon them. The actions of the heart are matched with degrees, the bodily with forgiveness, and it is reported in a hadith that a man had approached a non-related woman in a way that a man does with his wife short of intercourse, and when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was informed of that, he asked him: "Did you pray with us?" He said: "Yes." He said to him: "Allah has forgiven you." The financial attribute is matched with "generous provision" (rizq karim). This type of correspondence is among the fine points of rhetoric (badi' 'ilm al-bayan). Ibn Atiyya and the majority said that the intended meaning is the levels and stations of Paradise and its ranks, according to their deeds. Al-Tabari reported from Mujahid that they are the degrees of worldly deeds. His saying "rizq karim" intends the foods and drinks of Paradise, and "karim" is an attribute that implies elevation of rank, as in the saying: "a noble garment" and "a noble lineage." Al-Zamakhshari said: degrees of honour and dignity, elevation of station and forgiveness, overlooking their misdeeds, and generous provision, meaning the good and lasting benefits of Paradise in a manner of exaltation, and this is the meaning of reward, end of quote. Ata' said: the degrees of Paradise they ascend by their deeds. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: seventy degrees, between every two degrees is the distance a galloping horse covers in seventy years. It was also said: they are levels and stations in Paradise, some above others. In a hadith: "The people of Paradise will see the people of the chambers as one sees a bright star." These three opinions indicate that the degrees are meant literally. It is reported from Mujahid that they are degrees of lofty deeds.

Thus the meaning of the verse is: "Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth, and He covered you with drowsiness as a security from Him" (8:11), meaning by it Himself and those with Him; "and sent down water from the sky to purify you by it" (8:11); "and sent down upon you from the sky angels in succession" (8:9, 12), "so strike above the necks and strike from them every fingertip" (8:12). It is as if He says: "I have removed your impediments and reinforced you with the angels, so strike them in these places," and this is killing, so that you may reach Allah's purpose of establishing the truth and nullifying falsehood. The summary of this long statement is that ﴿just as He brought you out﴾ is connected to His words "so strike," and in this there is what is clearly distant and separated. These are the fifteen opinions that we have come across.

Whoever is inclined toward the weaving of speech, who turns in the composition of its varieties, and who practices eloquence and rhetoric, will not find any of these opinions good, even though some of their proponents had a standing (imamah) in the science of grammar and a firm foothold in it. But he did not attend closely to the wording of the speech, nor was it in his nature to shape it in the finest form, nor to exercise, in examining it, the eloquence through which inimitability (i'jaz) becomes apparent. Before writing down these opinions here, I came upon a number of them, and none of them settled in my mind. Then I saw in a dream that I was walking along a path with a man with whom I was discussing His words: ﴿Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾. I said to him: "No difficulty like this has passed before me, and perhaps there is an omitted element through which the meaning is made sound. I have not found in any exegete anything of substance on this." Then I said to him: "It has just become clear to me how to derive it, and that the omitted element is: 'He gave you victory' (nasaraka)." Both I and that man found this derivation good. Then I woke from sleep, still recalling it. The assumed meaning is: "So it is as if it were said: 'Just as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth,' that is, because of the manifestation of the religion of Allah and the exaltation of His law, and they were averse to your going out, out of dread of fighting and fear of death, since the command of the Prophet ﷺ for their going out was sudden, and they were not prepared for going out, and they disputed with you about the truth after its clarity. Allah gave you victory and reinforced you with His angels." The speech that follows indicates this omitted element, namely His words, exalted is He: ﴿when you sought help from your Lord, and He answered you﴾ (8:9), and so on in the verses. It appears that the kaf in this dream-based derivation is not merely for comparison, but contains the meaning of causation (ta'lil). The grammarians have explicitly stated that it may produce the meaning of causation, and they derived on this basis His words: ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾ (2:198). They also cited the verse:

"Do not revile people, just as you would not wish to be reviled."

i.e., because people insult you, do not insult them back. A common expression with this meaning is: "As you obey God, He will admit you to Paradise," meaning: because of your obedience to God, He will admit you to Paradise. The sense is therefore: if you go out to exalt the religion of God and kill its enemies, God will help you and reinforce you with angels. The waw in "wa-inna fariqan" is the waw of the circumstantial clause (waw al-hal). Apparently "min baytika" refers to the place of his residence; it is also said to be Medina, because it is his place of emigration (muhajar) and is specific to him; and it is also said to be Mecca, though this is remote, because the apparent meaning is that this is a report about his going out to Badr, so turning it to going out from Mecca is not apparent. The object of "la-karihun" is the going out, i.e., "they were truly averse to going out with you." Their aversion to that is either due to the natural revulsion of temperament, or because they had not been called to march (istanfaru), or the shift from the caravan (al-'ir) to the armed encounter (al-nafir), because of the strength of seizing wealth in that, and because of the killing and fighting in this; or because of leaving Mecca, their homes and their property. These are four opinions.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun of the subject in "yujadilunaka" refers to the group of believers who were averse, and their disputing is their saying: "Our going out was only for the caravan; had we known, we would have prepared ourselves for battle." The truth here is the support of the religion of Islam. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the polytheists, and their disputing about the truth is concerning the law of Islam.

Abd Allah recited "ba'da ma bayyana" with a dammah on the ba' and without a ta'. In His saying "ba'da ma tabayyana" there is a great rebuke against them, because whoever disputes about a matter that has not become clear is less deserving of blame, but whoever contends about a matter that is clear is deserving of blame and reproach.

Then He likened their state in their extreme terror, while they were being driven toward victory and booty, to the state of one who is being led onto the cliff toward death, while he is witnessing its causes, looking at them, and not doubting in them. It is also said that their fear was due to the small number and that they were infantry; it is narrated that there were only two horsemen among them, and they were three hundred and thirteen, while the polytheists were about a thousand men. The story of Badr is recounted in full in the books of the Sirah, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah have summarized from it what can be found in their two books.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 8, verses 7–9:**

﴿And when Allah promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours, and you wished that the unarmed one would be yours, while Allah intended to establish the truth by His words and to cut off the roots of the disbelievers, so that He might establish the truth and nullify falsehood, even though the criminals disliked it.﴾

﴿One of the two groups﴾ is unspecified. The two groups were the caravan of Quraysh, which carried great merchandise for them and was accompanied by forty riders, among them Abu Sufyan, Amr ibn al-As, and Amr ibn Hisham, and the group whom Abu Jahl had called out, who were in the number we have mentioned. ﴿The unarmed one﴾ is the caravan, because it was not armed for fighting; it was only an easy booty. The meaning of establishing the truth is making it firm and exalting it. ﴿By His words﴾ means by His revealed verses concerning the fight against the armed group, and by what He commanded the angels of descent for support, and by what He decreed of their capture, their killing, and their being thrown into the well of Badr, and by what the Prophet (ﷺ) had informed of and which then became manifest. Cutting off the roots is an expression for total destruction. The meaning is: you desired the preservation of the immediate gain, the safety of your situations, and trivial matters, whereas He desired the exaltation of the truth and success in both abodes, and how far apart the two aims are. For this reason He chose for you the armed group and showed them to you plainly; He humiliated them and gave you victory, and He abased them and exalted you, and He obtained for you what was greater than the outcome of the caravan and what was nearer than it, and better than both.

Maslamah ibn Muharib recited ﴿يَعِدْكم﴾ with a sukun on the dal to avoid successive vowels (tawali al-harakat). Ibn Muhaysin recited ﴿اللَّهُ احْدى﴾ by dropping the hamza of ﴿إحْدى﴾ contrary to analogy. Also from him: ﴿أحَدَ﴾ in the masculine, since the feminine of ﴿الطّائِفَةِ﴾ is metaphorical. Abu Amr assimilated ﴿الشَّوْكَة تَّكُونُ﴾. Muslim ibn Muharib recited ﴿بِكَلِمَتِهِ﴾ in the singular; Ibn Atiyyah reported it from Shayba, Abu Ja'far, and Nafi', with differing reports from them. The singular was used with the meaning of the plural, since its meaning is known, or it may refer to the word of creation of things, which is "Be" (kun). It was said: His words are what He promised His Prophet in Surah al-Dukhan, when He said: ﴿On the day We shall strike with the greatest blow, indeed We will take retribution﴾ (44:16), meaning upon Abu Jahl and his companions. It was said: they are His commands and prohibitions. It was said: they are His promises of victory, triumph, and conquest over one of the two groups. It was said: they are His words that preceded in eternity. The meaning of ﴿لِيُحِقَّ الحَقَّ﴾ is that He may make manifest what must be made manifest, which is Islam. ﴿And nullify falsehood﴾: He did that. It was said: the truth is the Qur'an and the falsehood is Iblis. This lam is connected to an omitted element whose estimated form is: "so that He might establish the truth and nullify falsehood, He did that," that is, He did not do it except for these two, which is the establishment of Islam and its manifestation, and the nullification of disbelief and its erasure. This is not a repetition, because the two meanings differ: the first is a clarification of the two wills; the second is an explanation of what was done in choosing the armed group over others for them and in giving them victory over it, and that He did not give them victory, nor abase those [who were] so numerous, except for this purpose, which is the most sublime of purposes. Estimating the governed element as coming later is better. Al-Zamakhshari said: The omitted element must be estimated as coming later so that it conveys the meaning of exclusivity and fits the meaning. End of his words. That is according to his doctrine that the fronting of the object and the prepositional phrase indicates exclusivity and restriction. According to us, that does not indicate this; it only indicates attention to and concern for what has been fronted, not specification or restriction. The discussion with him on this has preceded. It was said: ﴿لِيُحِقَّ﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿ويَقْطَعَ﴾. Ibn Atiyyah said: ﴿وَلَوْ كَرِهَ﴾, meaning: and your aversion is occurring, so it is a circumstantial clause (jumlah fi mawdi' al-hal). End of his words. The discussion with him on this has already preceded, and the verification of it is that the waw is for coordination with an omitted element, which in the position of a circumstantial clause, and what is coordinated with a circumstantial clause is also circumstantial. We illustrated that with the saying: "Give to the beggar even if he comes on a horse," meaning: in every state, even in this state which contradicts giving charity to the beggar. Here ﴿أنْ﴾ and ﴿وَلَوْ﴾ come to exhaust what is hidden, because it is not included in the generality of what precedes it, owing to the contrast between this state and the predicate that precedes both of them. Al-Hasan said: these two verses precede in revelation the saying ﴿as your Lord brought you forth﴾ (8:5), and the recitation after them, for the truth is contrasted with the truth and aversion with aversion. End of his words. This is a claim without evidence, and there is no need to compel us to affirm it.

﴿When you sought help from your Lord, and He answered you: I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another.﴾

Istaghatha means he sought relief. When they knew that fighting was inevitable, they began to seek relief from Allah and to supplicate for help. The apparent meaning is that it is an address to those who were addressed in His saying ﴿And when He promised you﴾ and ﴿you wished﴾, and that the address in His saying ﴿as He brought you forth﴾ and ﴿they dispute with you﴾ is an address to the Messenger, which is why it is singular; so the two addresses differ. It was said: the one seeking relief was the Prophet (ﷺ). It was narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated to me: "When the day of Badr came, [the Prophet] looked at his companions, who were three hundred and some, and at the polytheists, who were a thousand, so he faced the qibla, stretched out his hands, and said: 'O Allah, fulfil for me what You have promised me. O Allah, if You destroy this band, You will not be worshipped on earth.' He remained thus until his cloak fell off, and Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) returned it to him, saying: 'Enough, O Messenger of Allah, your entreating Allah; He will surely fulfil for you what He has promised you.'" They said: thus it is an address of the single exalted one being an address of all. It is also narrated that when the people lined up, Abu Jahl said: "O Allah, whichever of us is more honored by the truth, help him." ﴿Idh﴾ is a substitute for ﴿idh yaʿiduкum﴾; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyyah said so, though he had earlier stated that the governing element in ﴿idh yaʿiduкum﴾ is "remember." Al-Tabari said: it is connected to ﴿yuhiqqa wa-yubtila﴾. Al-Hawfi permitted it to be in the accusative governed by ﴿yaʿiduкum﴾, and al-Hawfi also permitted it to be a new independent sentence with the implied "and remember." Abu al-Baqa' permitted it to be an adverbial of time governed by ﴿tawaddūna﴾.

The verb ﴿استغاث﴾ transitively takes its object directly, as it does here, and it takes it with a preposition, as appears in Sibawayh's wording in the chapter on istighathah, and in Ibn Malik's grammar the object is ﴿المُسْتَغاثُ﴾, and he does not say ﴿المُسْتَغاثُ بِهِ﴾. Perhaps when he saw that it takes its object directly in the Qur'an, he said ﴿المُسْتَغاثُ﴾ without governing it with the bāʾ as Sibawayh and the grammarians did. He claimed that the speech of the Arabs is otherwise, and his speech is heard from the speech of the Arabs. What came governed with the bāʾ is the saying of the poet:

*Until he sought relief with water that has no rope, among the valleys, in its need, the (camel-)herds.*

*Enclosed by the roots of plants, the wind weaving it, a burning wind, for the morning sun of its water, a ripple.*

*As the grave of ʿAnṭalah sought relief with something, fearing the eyes, and the dry bones were not looked at by it.*

The majority recited ﴿أنِّي﴾ with a fatḥah, meaning ﴿بِأنِّي﴾. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar narrated it from Abu ʿAmr: ﴿وإنِّي﴾ with a kasrah, by the implied verb of saying according to the Basran school, or by quotation after ﴿استجاب﴾, treating it as a verb since it is equal to it in meaning. The discussion of the explanation of ﴿استجاب﴾ has preceded.

The majority recited ﴿بِألْفٍ﴾ in the singular; al-Jahdari recited ﴿بِآلُفٍ﴾ on the pattern of ﴿أفْلُسٍ﴾; and from him and from al-Suddi ﴿بِآلافٍ﴾. The combination of the singular and the plural may be understood by taking the singular to refer to those among them who fought, or to the leaders whom the others follow.

Nafi' and a group from the people of Madinah and others recited ﴿مُرْدَفِينَ﴾ with a fatḥah on the dāl; the rest of the seven and al-Hasan and Mujahid recited it with a kasrah, meaning: following one another. It was narrated from Ibn Abbas: behind each angel is an angel following him. Some of the Makkans, as reported by al-Khalil ibn Ahmad from him and cited by Ibn Atiyyah, recited ﴿مُرَدِّفِينَ﴾ with a fatḥah on the rāʾ and a shadda on the dāl with a kasrah; its origin is ﴿مُرْتَدِفِينَ﴾, which was assimilated. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: it is also possible to have a fatḥah on the rāʾ, fleeing to the lightest vowel, or because of the heaviness of the vowel of the tāʾ moving to the rāʾ upon assimilation, though no trace of this is known. It was narrated from al-Khalil that the rāʾ is pronounced with a ḍammah, following the vowel of the mīm, as in their saying ﴿مُخَضَّمٌ﴾; and it was recited likewise, except with a kasrah on the rāʾ, following the vowel of the dāl, or it is vocalized with a kasrah according to the original rule for meeting two sukuns. Ibn Atiyyah said: with this recitation, a kasrah on the mīm would also be fitting, but I do not know it as a recitation, like their saying ﴿مُخَضَّمٌ﴾.

The discussion of the number of the angels and whether they fought or did not fight has preceded in Surah Al ʿImran. The verse did not address their fighting. The apparent meaning is that the reading of whoever recited ﴿مُرْدِفِينَ﴾ with a sukun on the rāʾ and a fatḥah on the dāl is that it is an adjective of ﴿بِألْفٍ﴾, meaning: some of them followed others. Ibn Atiyyah said: it is also possible that by ﴿المُرْدَفِينَ﴾ is meant the believers, that is, they were reinforced with the angels, so ﴿مُرْدَفِينَ﴾ in this case is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ardaftuhu iyyāhu" means when you followed him, and it is said "ardaftuhu," as you say "atbaʿtuhu" when you come after him. So the one with a kasrah on the dāl cannot be free of meaning "following" or "being followed." If it means "following," then it is either following one another, or following one another in the sense of some following others, or meaning the believers following them, that is, they precede them and the believers follow them, or following them to escort and send them forward before them while they are at their rear, so that they are under their eyes and protection; or meaning they follow themselves as other angels, or following other angels. This view is supported by His saying in Surah Al ʿImran: ﴿with three thousand angels sent down﴾ (3:124), ﴿with five thousand angels marked﴾ (3:125). End of his words. This is excessive elaboration in speech. Its summary is that ﴿اتَّبَعَ﴾ with doubled ʿayn is transitive to one object; ﴿أتْبَعَ﴾ without doubling is transitive to two objects; and ﴿أرْدَفَ﴾ conveys the meaning of both. The object of ﴿تَبِعَ﴾ is omitted, and the two objects of ﴿تَبِعَ﴾ are omitted, so what makes the meaning sound is to be estimated. His saying "or following them, the believers" is not one of the places where a separate pronoun is used; rather it is one that is attached and the nūn is dropped for it. One does not say "these are clothing you (singular) with a garment," but "they clothe you." The correct form would be: "or meaning following them, the believers," or he should say: "or meaning following themselves, the believers."

The majority recited ﴿بِألْفٍ﴾ in the singular; al-Jahdari recited ﴿بِآلُفٍ﴾ on the pattern of ﴿أفْلُسٍ﴾; and from him and from al-Suddi ﴿بِآلافٍ﴾. The combination of the singular and the plural may be understood by taking the singular to refer to those among them who fought, or to the leaders whom the others follow.

Nafi' and a group from the people of Madinah and others recited ﴿مُرْدَفِينَ﴾ with a fatḥah on the dāl; the rest of the seven and al-Hasan and Mujahid recited it with a kasrah, meaning: following one another. It was narrated from Ibn Abbas: behind each angel is an angel following him. Some of the Makkans, as reported by al-Khalil ibn Ahmad from him and cited by Ibn Atiyyah, recited ﴿مُرَدِّفِينَ﴾ with a fatḥah on the rāʾ and a shadda on the dāl with a kasrah; its origin is ﴿مُرْتَدِفِينَ﴾, which was assimilated. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: it is also possible to have a fatḥah on the rāʾ, fleeing to the lightest vowel, or because of the heaviness of the vowel of the tāʾ moving to the rāʾ upon assimilation, though no trace of this is known. It was narrated from al-Khalil that the rāʾ is pronounced with a ḍammah, following the vowel of the mīm, as in their saying ﴿مُخَضَّمٌ﴾; and it was recited likewise, except with a kasrah on the rāʾ, following the vowel of the dāl, or it is vocalized with a kasrah according to the original rule for meeting two sukuns. Ibn Atiyyah said: with this recitation, a kasrah on the mīm would also be fitting, but I do not know it as a recitation, like their saying ﴿مُخَضَّمٌ﴾.

The discussion of the number of the angels and whether they fought or did not fight has preceded in Surah Al ʿImran. The verse did not address their fighting. The apparent meaning is that the reading of whoever recited ﴿مُرْدِفِينَ﴾ with a sukun on the rāʾ and a fatḥah on the dāl is that it is an adjective of ﴿بِألْفٍ﴾, meaning: some of them followed others. Ibn Atiyyah said: it is also possible that by ﴿المُرْدَفِينَ﴾ is meant the believers, that is, they were reinforced with the angels, so ﴿مُرْدَفِينَ﴾ in this case is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ardaftuhu iyyāhu" means when you followed him, and it is said "ardaftuhu," as you say "atbaʿtuhu" when you come after him. So the one with a kasrah on the dāl cannot be free of meaning "following" or "being followed." If it means "following," then it is either following one another, or following one another in the sense of some following others, or meaning the believers following them, that is, they precede them and the believers follow them, or following them to escort and send them forward before them while they are at their rear, so that they are under their eyes and protection; or meaning they follow themselves as other angels, or following other angels. This view is supported by His saying in Surah Al ʿImran: ﴿with three thousand angels sent down﴾ (3:124), ﴿with five thousand angels marked﴾ (3:125). End of his words. This is excessive elaboration in speech. Its summary is that ﴿اتَّبَعَ﴾ with doubled ʿayn is transitive to one object; ﴿أتْبَعَ﴾ without doubling is transitive to two objects; and ﴿أرْدَفَ﴾ conveys the meaning of both. The object of ﴿تَبِعَ﴾ is omitted, and the two objects of ﴿تَبِعَ﴾ are omitted, so what makes the meaning sound is to be estimated. His saying "or following them, the believers" is not one of the places where a separate pronoun is used; rather it is one that is attached and the nūn is dropped for it. One does not say "these are clothing you (singular) with a garment," but "they clothe you." The correct form would be: "or meaning following them, the believers," or he should say: "or meaning following themselves, the believers."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 8, verses 7–9:**

﴿And when Allah promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours, and you wished that the unarmed one would be yours, while Allah intended to establish the truth by His words and to cut off the roots of the disbelievers, so that He might establish the truth and nullify falsehood, even though the criminals disliked it.﴾

﴿One of the two groups﴾ is unspecified. The two groups were the caravan of Quraysh, which carried great merchandise for them and was accompanied by forty riders, among them Abu Sufyan, Amr ibn al-As, and Amr ibn Hisham, and the group whom Abu Jahl had called out, who were in the number we have mentioned. ﴿The unarmed one﴾ is the caravan, because it was not armed for fighting; it was only an easy booty. The meaning of establishing the truth is making it firm and exalting it. ﴿By His words﴾ means by His revealed verses concerning the fight against the armed group, and by what He commanded the angels of descent for support, and by what He decreed of their capture, their killing, and their being thrown into the well of Badr, and by what the Prophet (ﷺ) had informed of and which then became manifest. Cutting off the roots is an expression for total destruction. The meaning is: you desired the preservation of the immediate gain, the safety of your situations, and trivial matters, whereas He desired the exaltation of the truth and success in both abodes, and how far apart the two aims are. For this reason He chose for you the armed group and showed them to you plainly; He humiliated them and gave you victory, and He abased them and exalted you, and He obtained for you what was greater than the outcome of the caravan and what was nearer than it, and better than both.

Maslamah ibn Muharib recited ﴿يَعِدْكم﴾ with a sukun on the dal to avoid successive vowels (tawali al-harakat). Ibn Muhaysin recited ﴿اللَّهُ احْدى﴾ by dropping the hamza of ﴿إحْدى﴾ contrary to analogy. Also from him: ﴿أحَدَ﴾ in the masculine, since the feminine of ﴿الطّائِفَةِ﴾ is metaphorical. Abu Amr assimilated ﴿الشَّوْكَة تَّكُونُ﴾. Muslim ibn Muharib recited ﴿بِكَلِمَتِهِ﴾ in the singular; Ibn Atiyyah reported it from Shayba, Abu Ja'far, and Nafi', with differing reports from them. The singular was used with the meaning of the plural, since its meaning is known, or it may refer to the word of creation of things, which is "Be" (kun). It was said: His words are what He promised His Prophet in Surah al-Dukhan, when He said: ﴿On the day We shall strike with the greatest blow, indeed We will take retribution﴾ (44:16), meaning upon Abu Jahl and his companions. It was said: they are His commands and prohibitions. It was said: they are His promises of victory, triumph, and conquest over one of the two groups. It was said: they are His words that preceded in eternity. The meaning of ﴿لِيُحِقَّ الحَقَّ﴾ is that He may make manifest what must be made manifest, which is Islam. ﴿And nullify falsehood﴾: He did that. It was said: the truth is the Qur'an and the falsehood is Iblis. This lam is connected to an omitted element whose estimated form is: "so that He might establish the truth and nullify falsehood, He did that," that is, He did not do it except for these two, which is the establishment of Islam and its manifestation, and the nullification of disbelief and its erasure. This is not a repetition, because the two meanings differ: the first is a clarification of the two wills; the second is an explanation of what was done in choosing the armed group over others for them and in giving them victory over it, and that He did not give them victory, nor abase those [who were] so numerous, except for this purpose, which is the most sublime of purposes. Estimating the governed element as coming later is better. Al-Zamakhshari said: The omitted element must be estimated as coming later so that it conveys the meaning of exclusivity and fits the meaning. End of his words. That is according to his doctrine that the fronting of the object and the prepositional phrase indicates exclusivity and restriction. According to us, that does not indicate this; it only indicates attention to and concern for what has been fronted, not specification or restriction. The discussion with him on this has preceded. It was said: ﴿لِيُحِقَّ﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿ويَقْطَعَ﴾. Ibn Atiyyah said: ﴿وَلَوْ كَرِهَ﴾, meaning: and your aversion is occurring, so it is a circumstantial clause (jumlah fi mawdi' al-hal). End of his words. The discussion with him on this has already preceded, and the verification of it is that the waw is for coordination with an omitted element, which in the position of a circumstantial clause, and what is coordinated with a circumstantial clause is also circumstantial. We illustrated that with the saying: "Give to the beggar even if he comes on a horse," meaning: in every state, even in this state which contradicts giving charity to the beggar. Here ﴿أنْ﴾ and ﴿وَلَوْ﴾ come to exhaust what is hidden, because it is not included in the generality of what precedes it, owing to the contrast between this state and the predicate that precedes both of them. Al-Hasan said: these two verses precede in revelation the saying ﴿as your Lord brought you forth﴾ (8:5), and the recitation after them, for the truth is contrasted with the truth and aversion with aversion. End of his words. This is a claim without evidence, and there is no need to compel us to affirm it.

﴿When you sought help from your Lord, and He answered you: I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another.﴾

Istaghatha means he sought relief. When they knew that fighting was inevitable, they began to seek relief from Allah and to supplicate for help. The apparent meaning is that it is an address to those who were addressed in His saying ﴿And when He promised you﴾ and ﴿you wished﴾, and that the address in His saying ﴿as He brought you forth﴾ and ﴿they dispute with you﴾ is an address to the Messenger, which is why it is singular; so the two addresses differ. It was said: the one seeking relief was the Prophet (ﷺ). It was narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated to me: "When the day of Badr came, [the Prophet] looked at his companions, who were three hundred and some, and at the polytheists, who were a thousand, so he faced the qibla, stretched out his hands, and said: 'O Allah, fulfil for me what You have promised me. O Allah, if You destroy this band, You will not be worshipped on earth.' He remained thus until his cloak fell off, and Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) returned it to him, saying: 'Enough, O Messenger of Allah, your entreating Allah; He will surely fulfil for you what He has promised you.'" They said: thus it is an address of the single exalted one being an address of all. It is also narrated that when the people lined up, Abu Jahl said: "O Allah, whichever of us is more honored by the truth, help him." ﴿Idh﴾ is a substitute for ﴿idh yaʿiduкum﴾; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyyah said so, though he had earlier stated that the governing element in ﴿idh yaʿiduкum﴾ is "remember." Al-Tabari said: it is connected to ﴿yuhiqqa wa-yubtila﴾. Al-Hawfi permitted it to be in the accusative governed by ﴿yaʿiduкum﴾, and al-Hawfi also permitted it to be a new independent sentence with the implied "and remember." Abu al-Baqa' permitted it to be an adverbial of time governed by ﴿tawaddūna﴾.

The verb ﴿استغاث﴾ transitively takes its object directly, as it does here, and it takes it with a preposition, as appears in Sibawayh's wording in the chapter on istighathah, and in Ibn Malik's grammar the object is ﴿المُسْتَغاثُ﴾, and he does not say ﴿المُسْتَغاثُ بِهِ﴾. Perhaps when he saw that it takes its object directly in the Qur'an, he said ﴿المُسْتَغاثُ﴾ without governing it with the bāʾ as Sibawayh and the grammarians did. He claimed that the speech of the Arabs is otherwise, and his speech is heard from the speech of the Arabs. What came governed with the bāʾ is the saying of the poet:

*Until he sought relief with water that has no rope, among the valleys, in its need, the (camel-)herds.*

*Enclosed by the roots of plants, the wind weaving it, a burning wind, for the morning sun of its water, a ripple.*

*As the grave of ʿAnṭalah sought relief with something, fearing the eyes, and the dry bones were not looked at by it.*
