**Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 8, verses 10–11 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Allah did not make it except as good news, and so that your hearts might be reassured thereby. Victory is not except from Allah. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.﴾ The tafsir (exegesis) of a parallel of this verse has already been given. The meaning is: "except as good news for you," and it was stated in full in Al 'Imran because the story there is elaborate, whereas here it is concise, so omission (al-hadhf) suits this place. Here the word order is "Allah did not make it," while there it is "and victory is not except from Allah," for the sake of variety (al-tafannun) and breadth in speech. Here ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise﴾ comes to observe the rhyme of the verse-endings (ma"ra'at al-awakhir al-ayy). There, it is not the last verse, because "yaqta'a" (so that He might cut off) is connected to what precedes it, so it suits that "al-'Aziz al-Hakim" (the Almighty, the All-Wise) comes as a descriptive attribute (sifah). Both forms indicate causation ('ulliyyah), as you say: "Honour Zayd, the scholarly one," and "Honour Zayd, for he is scholarly."

The pronoun in ﴿ما جَعَلَهُ﴾ refers to the reinforcement (al-imdad) implied by ﴿أنِّي مُمِدُّكُمْ﴾ [al-Anfal: 9], or to the aid (al-madad), or to the promise implied by "Allah promises you one of the two groups" (yaʿidukum ihda al-ta'ifatayn), or to the thousand (al-alf), or to the response (al-istijabah), or to the reinforcement by riding (al-irdaf), or to the report of the reinforcement (al-khabar bi-l-imdad), or to Jibril. These are possible opinions that have been stated, the most apparent of which is the first. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention any other.

﴿When He covers you with drowsiness as a security from Him, and sends down upon you water from the sky to purify you thereby, and to remove from you the defilement of Satan, and to strengthen your hearts and make your feet firm thereby.﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a second apposition (badal) to "idh yaʿiduкum" (when He promised you), or it is in the accusative governed by "al-nasr" (victory), or by what is in "ʿinda Allah" (from Allah) of the meaning of a verb, or by "ma ja'alahu Allah" (what Allah made), or by implying "udhkur" (remember). End of quote.

As for it being a second apposition to "idh yaʿiduкum," Ibn 'Atiyyah agreed with him, since the governing element of "idh" is the same as the governing element of "wa-idh yaʿiduкum," with the repetition of that element being understood. The sharing of the first governing element itself can only occur with a conjunction particle (harf 'atf), and the intention is only to enumerate His favours upon the believers on the day of Badr. So He says: "Remember when We did such-and-such to you; remember when We did such-and-such."

As for it being in the accusative governed by "al-nasr" (victory), it is weak in several respects. First: it is a verbal noun (masdar) with "al" (the definite article), and regarding its governing function there is disagreement; the Kufans held that it is not permissible for it to govern. Second: it is a noun with a following complement (mawsul), and it has been separated from its object (ma'mul) by the predicate, which is "except from Allah," and that is a form of governing that is not permissible. One does not say "daraba Zayd shadid 'Amran" (Zayd's striking is severe, Amr). Third: it would entail the governing of what precedes "illa" (except) over what follows it, without that object being either an exception (mustathna), an element from which something is excepted (mustathna minhu), or a qualifier of it; and "idh" is none of these three. Therefore it is not permissible to say: "ma qama illa Zayd yawm al-Jum'ah" (none stood up except Zayd on Friday). Al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash permitted this.

As for it being in the accusative governed by what is in "ʿinda Allah" of the meaning of a verb, the meaning weakens it, because the stability of victory would become restricted by the time adverb, whereas victory from Allah is absolute, at the time of the covering by drowsiness and at other times.

As for it being in the accusative governed by "ma ja'alahu Allah," al-Hawfi preceded others in this, and it is also weak, because of the long separation and because it is an object of what precedes "illa," and it is not one of those three.

Al-Tabari said: The governing element of "idh" is His saying "wa-li-tatma'inna" (and that your hearts might be reassured). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This, despite its possibility, is weak.

Abu al-Baqa' said: It is permissible for it to be an adverb of time (zarf) for what "ʿAzizun Hakim" (Almighty, All-Wise) indicates. Ibn 'Atiyyah had preceded him to something close to this, saying: If the governing element of "idh" is made to be something that connects it to what precedes it, then the better option is for "Hakim" to govern "idh," because the casting of drowsiness upon them and making it a security is a wisdom from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. End of quote.

The best of these opinions is that it is an apposition (badal).

Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read: ﴿yaghshakumu al-nu'as﴾, as the present tense of "ghashiya" (to cover), with "al-nu'as" (drowsiness) in the nominative case as its subject.

Al-A'raj, Ibn Nisah, Abu Hafs and Nafi' read: ﴿yughashshikum﴾, as the present tense of "aghsha" (to cover).

ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Abu Raja', Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans read: ﴿yughashshikum﴾, as the present tense of "ghashshā" (to cover intensively). In these two readings, "al-nu'as" is in the accusative case, and the subject is the pronoun referring to Allah.

The reading of Nafi' harmonizes with His saying "yaghsha ta'ifatan minkum" (covers a group among you), and the reading of the rest with ﴿wa-yunazzilu﴾ (and sends down), since the subject does not differ.

The meaning of "yughashshikum" is "gives you by it," and this is a metaphor (isti'arah): what overcame them of drowsiness was made to be a covering for them. The explanation of "al-nu'as" and "amanah" has already been given in Al 'Imran.

The pronoun in ﴿minhu﴾ refers to Allah. The word ﴿amanah﴾ is in the accusative case; it has been said that it is a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "so you became secure in security." The more apparent view is that it is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu, object of purpose) in the reading ﴿yughashshikum﴾, because the agent who covers and the agent who grants security is Allah, Exalted. As for the reading "yaghshakum," the subject differs, since the subject of "yaghshakum" is drowsiness and the one who grants security is Allah. The permissibility of the object of purpose when the subject differs is a matter of disagreement.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Was it not obligatory that the agent of the verb being explained and the reason be one? I say: Yes, but since the meaning of "yaghshakumu al-nu'as" is "you are covered over" (tataghashsha'un), "amanah" is put in the accusative on the basis that the drowsiness and the security are for you. The meaning is: "when you are covered over with security," meaning "safety" (amnan), that is, for your safety. And "minhu" is a qualifier of it, meaning: a security obtained for you from Allah, Exalted. (If you ask): Is it permissible for it to be in the accusative on the basis that the security is for the drowsiness which is "yaghshakum," meaning: "drowsiness covers you for its security," with the attribution of security to drowsiness being a metaphorical attribution, while it actually belongs to those who are drowsy? Or on the basis that it is your security at that time, for it was the right of the drowsiness at that fearful time not to come upon you, and it only covered you as a security obtained from Allah, Exalted, which, had it not been for that, it would not have covered you, in the manner of representation (tamthil) and imagination (takhyil)? (I say): The eloquence of the Qur'an does not go beyond admitting this, and it has parallels in it. Indeed, one who touched on this said:

*"Sleep is awed to cover eyes that are awed by you; it is a fleeing, scattering wanderer."*

It was also read as ﴿أَمْنَةً﴾ (*amnatan*) with a sukūn on the mīm. Its parallel is *amina amanatan* (أَمِنَ أَمَنَةً), like *ḥiyiya ḥayāatan* (حَيِيَ حَيَاةً), and like *amina amnatan* (أَمِنَ أَمْنَةً) and *raḥima raḥmatan* (رَحِمَ رَحْمَةً). The meaning is that the fear they had been feeling was preventing them from sleeping. When God, exalted is He, calmed their hearts, He gave them security and they settled down. From Ibn ʿAbbās: "Drowsiness during fighting is a security from God, exalted is He, while drowsiness during prayer is a whisper from Satan." End of quote. A similar statement is reported from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: "Drowsiness when battle is imminent is a sign of security from the enemy, and it is from God, exalted is He. Drowsiness during prayer is from Satan." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This is only the way of revelation, so he must ascribe it [to the Prophet]." End of quote. The one who read ﴿أَمْنَةً﴾ with the sukūn on the mīm was Ibn Muḥayṣin, and it is also transmitted from al-Nakhaʿī and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmur.

As for the drowsiness overtaking them, it is said that it happened at the moment the two lines met, and a similar event is mentioned at the Battle of Uhud in Āl ʿImrān. It is also said that it was the night before the battle, when God bestowed upon them sleep along with the serious matter they would face the next day, so that they could rest that night, be energetic the following day for the fighting, and have their terror dispelled. It is said: "Security causes sleep, and fear causes wakefulness." The most fitting view is that the sequence of these clauses in time matches their sequence in recitation, so the sending down of rain came after the onset of drowsiness. From Ibn Najīḥ, however, it is reported that the rain came before the drowsiness, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya preferred this, saying: "The descent of water was before the covering of drowsiness, and the verse is not arranged in that order, since its purpose is only to enumerate the blessings."

Ṭalḥa read ﴿وَيُنَزِّلُ﴾ with the shadda (intensive form, *wa-yunazzilu*). The majority read ﴿مَاءً﴾ with the long vowel (*mā'an*). Al-Shaʿbī read *mā* without a hamza, a reading related by Ibn Jinnī, the author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* on the irregular recitations (*shawādhdh al-qirāʾāt*, readings that are not transmitted with the standard chain of the seven or ten canonical recitations). Both of them explained this reading as *mā* being a relative pronoun meaning "that which." Its relative clause, according to the author of *al-Lawāmiḥ*, is the prepositional phrase *li-yuṭahhirakum* (لِيُطَهِّرَكُم), and the returning pronoun is *hu* (هُوَ). Its meaning is: "that which is for purifying you with it." The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* said this. The apparent sense of this explanation is faulty, because the *lām* of purpose (*lām kay*, the "lam" meaning "in order that") cannot function as a relative clause, and because he made the pronoun *hu* while saying the meaning is "that which is for purifying you," and the *lām kay* cannot be the relative clause; rather the relative clause is *hu* together with the *lām* of the genitive and what it governs. Ibn Jinnī said: *mā* is a relative pronoun, and its relative clause is the preposition with what it governs, so it is as if he said "that which is for purification." This involves what we have said about *lām kay* coming as a relative clause.

It is possible to explain this reading in another way: *mā* is not a relative pronoun but means *māʾan*, "water," in its indefinite form. This is because they relate that the Arabs dropped this hamza, saying *mā yā hādhā* (مًا يَا هَذَا), dropping the hamza and pronouncing the *mīm* with tanwīn. This can be explained on this basis, except that they treated the connected form as the pause form, so they dropped the tanwīn. For when you pause on *sharibtu mā* (شَرِبْتُ مًا), you say *sharibtu mā*, dropping the tanwīn and keeping the alif, whether it is the alif of the connection, which replaces the wāw and is the root of the word, or the alif which replaces the tanwīn in the accusative case.

Ibn al-Musayyab read ﴿لِيُطَهِّرَكُمْ﴾ with the sukūn on the ṭāʾ, meaning *li-yuṭhirakum* (لِيُطْهِرَكُم), "to purify you" from the states of major ritual impurity (*janābāt*). The believers had been afflicted, most of them, with major impurity during their journey, and they lacked water. Between them and the water of Badr lay a long distance of soft, yielding sand in which feet sank. The polytheists had reached the water of Badr before them. It is also said that rather the believers had reached the water at Badr first, and the rain had come before that. What is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and others is that on the day of Badr the unbelievers got to the water of Badr before the believers, camped by it, and the believers were left without water. Their souls were troubled, they became thirsty and in a state of major impurity, and they prayed in that condition. Some of them said to themselves, through Satan's insinuation: "We claim to be the friends of God, and the Messenger of God is among us, and our state is this, while the polytheists are at the water?" So God sent down rain on the night of Badr, the seventeenth of Ramadan, until the valleys flowed. The people drank, purified themselves, and watered their mounts. The salt flat that lay between them and the polytheists became firm, so that the feet of the Muslims stood firm in it at the time of fighting. Before the rain, feet had sunk in it, but when the rain fell it became packed. They said: "This is the meaning of His saying, ﴿to purify you thereby﴾," that is, from major impurity, ﴿and remove from you the defilement of Satan﴾, that is, his punishment upon you through his whispering. *Rijz* means punishment. It is also said that his *rijz* is his plotting and his whispering. It is also said that major impurity from wet dreams is from Satan, and it is reported: "No prophet has ever had a wet dream; wet dreams are only from Satan."

ʿĪsā ibn ʿAmr read ﴿يُذْهِبْ﴾ with the jazm on the bāʾ (*yudhhib*). Ibn Muḥayṣin read *rujza* (رُجْزَ) with a ḍamma on the rāʾ, and Abū al-ʿĀliya read *rijsa* (رِجْسَ) with a sīn.

The meaning of "binding upon the hearts" (*al-rabṭ ʿalā al-qalb*) is the gathering of resolve, encouragement to meet the enemy, and patience in confronting the enemy. *Al-rabṭ* means tying or binding. It is literal in the case of physical bodies, and it is borrowed from that for what occurs in the heart of firmness and tranquility after agitation. Its requirement is that binding. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is patience. Muqātil said: it is faith. It is also said: it is the sending down of rain, and this is the apparent view, because His saying ﴿so that He may purify you﴾ and what follows it is the reason for the sending down of rain. The apparent meaning of "making the feet firm" is literal: the place where the encounter happened was sand in which feet sank, and the rain packed it down until feet could stand upon it. The pronoun in *bihi* (بِهِ) refers to the rain. It is also said that making the feet firm is figurative, and what is meant is that a person does not flee at the time of fighting; the pronoun in *bihi* then refers to the verbal noun implied by ﴿wa-liyarbiṭa﴾.

Consider the eloquence of the arrangement of these causes. He began first with the manifest cause, which is purifying them from major impurity, a physical act, namely their washing from major impurity. He then joined to it, without the particle of causation, what necessarily follows from purification, which is the removal of Satan's defilement, since he whispered to them that they were praying without having washed from major impurity. Then He joined, with the particle of causation, what is not a physical act but an act whose locus is the heart: encouragement, tranquility, and patience in facing the encounter. He joined to it, without the particle of causation, what necessarily follows from it, namely that they do not flee at the time of war. So when He mentioned the outward physical cause and the inward cause of the heart, the particle of causation appeared, and when He mentioned what follows from them, He did not emphasize it with the particle of causation. He began with purification first, because it is the most emphatic and the earliest in action, and because it is the act by which the best acts of worship are performed and by which hearts come to life.

**Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 8, verses 10–11 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Allah did not make it except as good news, and so that your hearts might be reassured thereby. Victory is not except from Allah. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.﴾ The tafsir (exegesis) of a parallel of this verse has already been given. The meaning is: "except as good news for you," and it was stated in full in Al 'Imran because the story there is elaborate, whereas here it is concise, so omission (al-hadhf) suits this place. Here the word order is "Allah did not make it," while there it is "and victory is not except from Allah," for the sake of variety (al-tafannun) and breadth in speech. Here ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise﴾ comes to observe the rhyme of the verse-endings (ma"ra'at al-awakhir al-ayy). There, it is not the last verse, because "yaqta'a" (so that He might cut off) is connected to what precedes it, so it suits that "al-'Aziz al-Hakim" (the Almighty, the All-Wise) comes as a descriptive attribute (sifah). Both forms indicate causation ('ulliyyah), as you say: "Honour Zayd, the scholarly one," and "Honour Zayd, for he is scholarly."

The pronoun in ﴿ما جَعَلَهُ﴾ refers to the reinforcement (al-imdad) implied by ﴿أنِّي مُمِدُّكُمْ﴾ [al-Anfal: 9], or to the aid (al-madad), or to the promise implied by "Allah promises you one of the two groups" (yaʿidukum ihda al-ta'ifatayn), or to the thousand (al-alf), or to the response (al-istijabah), or to the reinforcement by riding (al-irdaf), or to the report of the reinforcement (al-khabar bi-l-imdad), or to Jibril. These are possible opinions that have been stated, the most apparent of which is the first. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention any other.

﴿When He covers you with drowsiness as a security from Him, and sends down upon you water from the sky to purify you thereby, and to remove from you the defilement of Satan, and to strengthen your hearts and make your feet firm thereby.﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a second apposition (badal) to "idh yaʿiduкum" (when He promised you), or it is in the accusative governed by "al-nasr" (victory), or by what is in "ʿinda Allah" (from Allah) of the meaning of a verb, or by "ma ja'alahu Allah" (what Allah made), or by implying "udhkur" (remember). End of quote.

As for it being a second apposition to "idh yaʿiduкum," Ibn 'Atiyyah agreed with him, since the governing element of "idh" is the same as the governing element of "wa-idh yaʿiduкum," with the repetition of that element being understood. The sharing of the first governing element itself can only occur with a conjunction particle (harf 'atf), and the intention is only to enumerate His favours upon the believers on the day of Badr. So He says: "Remember when We did such-and-such to you; remember when We did such-and-such."

As for it being in the accusative governed by "al-nasr" (victory), it is weak in several respects. First: it is a verbal noun (masdar) with "al" (the definite article), and regarding its governing function there is disagreement; the Kufans held that it is not permissible for it to govern. Second: it is a noun with a following complement (mawsul), and it has been separated from its object (ma'mul) by the predicate, which is "except from Allah," and that is a form of governing that is not permissible. One does not say "daraba Zayd shadid 'Amran" (Zayd's striking is severe, Amr). Third: it would entail the governing of what precedes "illa" (except) over what follows it, without that object being either an exception (mustathna), an element from which something is excepted (mustathna minhu), or a qualifier of it; and "idh" is none of these three. Therefore it is not permissible to say: "ma qama illa Zayd yawm al-Jum'ah" (none stood up except Zayd on Friday). Al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash permitted this.

As for it being in the accusative governed by what is in "ʿinda Allah" of the meaning of a verb, the meaning weakens it, because the stability of victory would become restricted by the time adverb, whereas victory from Allah is absolute, at the time of the covering by drowsiness and at other times.

As for it being in the accusative governed by "ma ja'alahu Allah," al-Hawfi preceded others in this, and it is also weak, because of the long separation and because it is an object of what precedes "illa," and it is not one of those three.

Al-Tabari said: The governing element of "idh" is His saying "wa-li-tatma'inna" (and that your hearts might be reassured). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This, despite its possibility, is weak.

Abu al-Baqa' said: It is permissible for it to be an adverb of time (zarf) for what "ʿAzizun Hakim" (Almighty, All-Wise) indicates. Ibn 'Atiyyah had preceded him to something close to this, saying: If the governing element of "idh" is made to be something that connects it to what precedes it, then the better option is for "Hakim" to govern "idh," because the casting of drowsiness upon them and making it a security is a wisdom from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. End of quote.

The best of these opinions is that it is an apposition (badal).

Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read: ﴿yaghshakumu al-nu'as﴾, as the present tense of "ghashiya" (to cover), with "al-nu'as" (drowsiness) in the nominative case as its subject.

Al-A'raj, Ibn Nisah, Abu Hafs and Nafi' read: ﴿yughashshikum﴾, as the present tense of "aghsha" (to cover).

ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Abu Raja', Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans read: ﴿yughashshikum﴾, as the present tense of "ghashshā" (to cover intensively). In these two readings, "al-nu'as" is in the accusative case, and the subject is the pronoun referring to Allah.

The reading of Nafi' harmonizes with His saying "yaghsha ta'ifatan minkum" (covers a group among you), and the reading of the rest with ﴿wa-yunazzilu﴾ (and sends down), since the subject does not differ.

The meaning of "yughashshikum" is "gives you by it," and this is a metaphor (isti'arah): what overcame them of drowsiness was made to be a covering for them. The explanation of "al-nu'as" and "amanah" has already been given in Al 'Imran.

The pronoun in ﴿minhu﴾ refers to Allah. The word ﴿amanah﴾ is in the accusative case; it has been said that it is a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "so you became secure in security." The more apparent view is that it is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu, object of purpose) in the reading ﴿yughashshikum﴾, because the agent who covers and the agent who grants security is Allah, Exalted. As for the reading "yaghshakum," the subject differs, since the subject of "yaghshakum" is drowsiness and the one who grants security is Allah. The permissibility of the object of purpose when the subject differs is a matter of disagreement.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Was it not obligatory that the agent of the verb being explained and the reason be one? I say: Yes, but since the meaning of "yaghshakumu al-nu'as" is "you are covered over" (tataghashsha'un), "amanah" is put in the accusative on the basis that the drowsiness and the security are for you. The meaning is: "when you are covered over with security," meaning "safety" (amnan), that is, for your safety. And "minhu" is a qualifier of it, meaning: a security obtained for you from Allah, Exalted. (If you ask): Is it permissible for it to be in the accusative on the basis that the security is for the drowsiness which is "yaghshakum," meaning: "drowsiness covers you for its security," with the attribution of security to drowsiness being a metaphorical attribution, while it actually belongs to those who are drowsy? Or on the basis that it is your security at that time, for it was the right of the drowsiness at that fearful time not to come upon you, and it only covered you as a security obtained from Allah, Exalted, which, had it not been for that, it would not have covered you, in the manner of representation (tamthil) and imagination (takhyil)? (I say): The eloquence of the Qur'an does not go beyond admitting this, and it has parallels in it. Indeed, one who touched on this said:

*"Sleep is awed to cover eyes that are awed by you; it is a fleeing, scattering wanderer."*

It was also read as ﴿أَمْنَةً﴾ (*amnatan*) with a sukūn on the mīm. Its parallel is *amina amanatan* (أَمِنَ أَمَنَةً), like *ḥiyiya ḥayāatan* (حَيِيَ حَيَاةً), and like *amina amnatan* (أَمِنَ أَمْنَةً) and *raḥima raḥmatan* (رَحِمَ رَحْمَةً). The meaning is that the fear they had been feeling was preventing them from sleeping. When God, exalted is He, calmed their hearts, He gave them security and they settled down. From Ibn ʿAbbās: "Drowsiness during fighting is a security from God, exalted is He, while drowsiness during prayer is a whisper from Satan." End of quote. A similar statement is reported from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: "Drowsiness when battle is imminent is a sign of security from the enemy, and it is from God, exalted is He. Drowsiness during prayer is from Satan." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This is only the way of revelation, so he must ascribe it [to the Prophet]." End of quote. The one who read ﴿أَمْنَةً﴾ with the sukūn on the mīm was Ibn Muḥayṣin, and it is also transmitted from al-Nakhaʿī and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmur.

As for the drowsiness overtaking them, it is said that it happened at the moment the two lines met, and a similar event is mentioned at the Battle of Uhud in Āl ʿImrān. It is also said that it was the night before the battle, when God bestowed upon them sleep along with the serious matter they would face the next day, so that they could rest that night, be energetic the following day for the fighting, and have their terror dispelled. It is said: "Security causes sleep, and fear causes wakefulness." The most fitting view is that the sequence of these clauses in time matches their sequence in recitation, so the sending down of rain came after the onset of drowsiness. From Ibn Najīḥ, however, it is reported that the rain came before the drowsiness, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya preferred this, saying: "The descent of water was before the covering of drowsiness, and the verse is not arranged in that order, since its purpose is only to enumerate the blessings."

Ṭalḥa read ﴿وَيُنَزِّلُ﴾ with the shadda (intensive form, *wa-yunazzilu*). The majority read ﴿مَاءً﴾ with the long vowel (*mā'an*). Al-Shaʿbī read *mā* without a hamza, a reading related by Ibn Jinnī, the author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* on the irregular recitations (*shawādhdh al-qirāʾāt*, readings that are not transmitted with the standard chain of the seven or ten canonical recitations). Both of them explained this reading as *mā* being a relative pronoun meaning "that which." Its relative clause, according to the author of *al-Lawāmiḥ*, is the prepositional phrase *li-yuṭahhirakum* (لِيُطَهِّرَكُم), and the returning pronoun is *hu* (هُوَ). Its meaning is: "that which is for purifying you with it." The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* said this. The apparent sense of this explanation is faulty, because the *lām* of purpose (*lām kay*, the "lam" meaning "in order that") cannot function as a relative clause, and because he made the pronoun *hu* while saying the meaning is "that which is for purifying you," and the *lām kay* cannot be the relative clause; rather the relative clause is *hu* together with the *lām* of the genitive and what it governs. Ibn Jinnī said: *mā* is a relative pronoun, and its relative clause is the preposition with what it governs, so it is as if he said "that which is for purification." This involves what we have said about *lām kay* coming as a relative clause.

It is possible to explain this reading in another way: *mā* is not a relative pronoun but means *māʾan*, "water," in its indefinite form. This is because they relate that the Arabs dropped this hamza, saying *mā yā hādhā* (مًا يَا هَذَا), dropping the hamza and pronouncing the *mīm* with tanwīn. This can be explained on this basis, except that they treated the connected form as the pause form, so they dropped the tanwīn. For when you pause on *sharibtu mā* (شَرِبْتُ مًا), you say *sharibtu mā*, dropping the tanwīn and keeping the alif, whether it is the alif of the connection, which replaces the wāw and is the root of the word, or the alif which replaces the tanwīn in the accusative case.

Ibn al-Musayyab read ﴿لِيُطَهِّرَكُمْ﴾ with the sukūn on the ṭāʾ, meaning *li-yuṭhirakum* (لِيُطْهِرَكُم), "to purify you" from the states of major ritual impurity (*janābāt*). The believers had been afflicted, most of them, with major impurity during their journey, and they lacked water. Between them and the water of Badr lay a long distance of soft, yielding sand in which feet sank. The polytheists had reached the water of Badr before them. It is also said that rather the believers had reached the water at Badr first, and the rain had come before that. What is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and others is that on the day of Badr the unbelievers got to the water of Badr before the believers, camped by it, and the believers were left without water. Their souls were troubled, they became thirsty and in a state of major impurity, and they prayed in that condition. Some of them said to themselves, through Satan's insinuation: "We claim to be the friends of God, and the Messenger of God is among us, and our state is this, while the polytheists are at the water?" So God sent down rain on the night of Badr, the seventeenth of Ramadan, until the valleys flowed. The people drank, purified themselves, and watered their mounts. The salt flat that lay between them and the polytheists became firm, so that the feet of the Muslims stood firm in it at the time of fighting. Before the rain, feet had sunk in it, but when the rain fell it became packed. They said: "This is the meaning of His saying, ﴿to purify you thereby﴾," that is, from major impurity, ﴿and remove from you the defilement of Satan﴾, that is, his punishment upon you through his whispering. *Rijz* means punishment. It is also said that his *rijz* is his plotting and his whispering. It is also said that major impurity from wet dreams is from Satan, and it is reported: "No prophet has ever had a wet dream; wet dreams are only from Satan."

ʿĪsā ibn ʿAmr read ﴿يُذْهِبْ﴾ with the jazm on the bāʾ (*yudhhib*). Ibn Muḥayṣin read *rujza* (رُجْزَ) with a ḍamma on the rāʾ, and Abū al-ʿĀliya read *rijsa* (رِجْسَ) with a sīn.

The meaning of "binding upon the hearts" (*al-rabṭ ʿalā al-qalb*) is the gathering of resolve, encouragement to meet the enemy, and patience in confronting the enemy. *Al-rabṭ* means tying or binding. It is literal in the case of physical bodies, and it is borrowed from that for what occurs in the heart of firmness and tranquility after agitation. Its requirement is that binding. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is patience. Muqātil said: it is faith. It is also said: it is the sending down of rain, and this is the apparent view, because His saying ﴿so that He may purify you﴾ and what follows it is the reason for the sending down of rain. The apparent meaning of "making the feet firm" is literal: the place where the encounter happened was sand in which feet sank, and the rain packed it down until feet could stand upon it. The pronoun in *bihi* (بِهِ) refers to the rain. It is also said that making the feet firm is figurative, and what is meant is that a person does not flee at the time of fighting; the pronoun in *bihi* then refers to the verbal noun implied by ﴿wa-liyarbiṭa﴾.

Consider the eloquence of the arrangement of these causes. He began first with the manifest cause, which is purifying them from major impurity, a physical act, namely their washing from major impurity. He then joined to it, without the particle of causation, what necessarily follows from purification, which is the removal of Satan's defilement, since he whispered to them that they were praying without having washed from major impurity. Then He joined, with the particle of causation, what is not a physical act but an act whose locus is the heart: encouragement, tranquility, and patience in facing the encounter. He joined to it, without the particle of causation, what necessarily follows from it, namely that they do not flee at the time of war. So when He mentioned the outward physical cause and the inward cause of the heart, the particle of causation appeared, and when He mentioned what follows from them, He did not emphasize it with the particle of causation. He began with purification first, because it is the most emphatic and the earliest in action, and because it is the act by which the best acts of worship are performed and by which hearts come to life.

**[p-470]** This is also one of the enumerations of blessings. The revelation to the angels, that He is with them, meaning that He will support and aid them, and His command to them to make the believers steadfast, together with the report of what would follow, namely the casting of terror into the hearts of their enemies, and the command to strike above the necks and strike every finger of them, is among the greatest of blessings. It also indicates that victory, triumph and the final outcome belong to the believers.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Idh yuhi﴾ (when your Lord revealed to the angels) may be a third substitute (badal) for ﴿idh yaʿiduкum﴾ (when He promised you), and it may be in the accusative governed by ﴿thabbitu﴾ (make steadfast).

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: The governing element of ﴿idh﴾ is the first governing element, as mentioned previously. If we took it as close, then His saying ﴿wa-yuthabbita﴾ (and to make firm) [al-Anfal: 11] would be on the interpretation that the pronoun refers to the binding. As for its referring to the water, it is possible that ﴿wa-yuthabbita﴾ [al-Anfal: 11] governs ﴿idh﴾. End of quote. For him, this is possible because the time of the making firm differs from the time of this revelation, since the time of the sending down of the rain and what is connected to it of its causes preceded the covering with drowsiness, and the revelation occurred at the time of fighting.

This revelation is either by inspiration (ilham) or by notification (iʿlam). ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, with a variant reading from him, recited ﴿innī maʿakum﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, on the basis of an implied verb of saying according to the school of the Basrans (al-Basriyyun), or on the basis of treating ﴿yuhi﴾ as if it were ﴿taqul﴾ (you say) according to the school of the Kufans (al-Kufiyyun). The angels are those by whom the believers were reinforced. Since what preceded was an enumeration of blessings upon the believers, the address to them came with ﴿yaghshākum﴾ (He covers you), ﴿yunazzilu ʿalaykum﴾ (He sends down upon you), ﴿yuṭahhirakum﴾ (He purifies you), ﴿yudhhiba rijza﴾ (and removes the filth), and ﴿liyarbiṭa ʿalā qulūbikum﴾ (and that He may bind your hearts), since these are matters that do not befit the station of the Messenger. When He mentioned the revelation to the angels, He addressed the Messenger alone, saying ﴿idh yuhi rabbuka﴾ (when your Lord revealed), and in that there is an honour (tashrif) by addressing him alone with the speech: that is, your Lord, the one who nurtures you and watches over your welfare, and ﴿yuthabbitu alladhina amanu﴾ (makes firm those who believed).

Al-Hasan said: by fighting, that is, fight. Muqatil said: give them the good news of victory. So the angel would walk in front of the row in the form of a man saying, "Rejoice, for Allah is your helper." Al-Zajjaj mentioned that they make them firm with things they cast into their hearts by which they are strengthened. Al-Tha'labi and others said: they set right their resolve and intentions toward jihad. Ibn ʿAtiyya said something similar, saying: It is also possible that the making firm commanded is what the angel casts into the heart of a person of the thought of victory and of belittling the unbelievers, and the promptings of encouragement that run through him. This interpretation is strengthened by the correspondence of His saying ﴿sa-ulqī fī qulūb alladhīna kafarū al-rūʿb﴾ (I shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved), although the casting of terror corresponds to making firm in whatever form the making firm takes; but it is more akin to this, since they are of one kind. On this interpretation, His saying ﴿sa-ulqī fī qulūb alladhīna kafarū al-rūʿb﴾ comes as an address to the angels. Then His saying ﴿fa-ḍribū fawqa al-aʿnāq﴾ (so strike above the necks) has the form of a command but the meaning of a report about the state of affairs, just as you say when describing to one you are addressing: "We met the people and defeated them, so strike with your sword wherever you wish, and kill and take your captive," meaning: this was the description of the situation. It is also possible that ﴿sa-ulqī﴾ up to the end of the verse is a report addressed to the believers about what He will do to the unbelievers in the future, as He did in the past, and then He commanded them to strike the necks and the fingers, encouraging them and urging them to support the religion.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: I am helping you to make them firm, so make them firm. Thus His saying "I shall cast" and "so strike" may be an explanation of His saying "that I am with you, so make firm." There is no help greater than casting terror into the hearts of the disbelievers, and no making firm more effective than striking their necks; the combination of the two is the utmost of support. It may also be not an explanation, and what is meant by making firm is that they bring to their minds what will strengthen their hearts, and make their resolves and intentions sound, and that they show what they are certain of, namely that they are being reinforced by the angels. It was also said: the angel would take the form of a man whom they knew by face, and come and say: "I heard the polytheists saying, 'By Allah, if they attack us, we will surely break,'" and he would walk between the two rows saying, "Rejoice, for Allah is your helper, because you worship Him and these do not worship Him." End of quote. Then he said: It may also be that His saying "I shall cast" up to His saying "every finger" follows His saying ﴿fa-thabbitū alladhīna āmanū﴾ (so make firm those who believed), as an instruction to the angels and to what they should make the believers firm with, as if He had said: "Tell them: I shall cast," and those who strike on this view are the believers. End of quote.

What appears is that what comes after ﴿idh yuhi rabbuka ilā al-malāʾika﴾ (when your Lord revealed to the angels) is part of what was revealed, and that the angels are the ones addressed with making the believers firm and with striking above the necks and every finger.

Al-Sa'ib ibn Yasar said: Whenever we asked Yazid ibn ʿAmir al-Sawwari about the terror which Allah cast into the hearts of the polytheists, how it was, he would take pebbles and throw them at the basin, and it would ring out, and he would say: "We used to find in our bellies something like this."

Ibn ʿAmir, al-Kisa'i and al-Aʿraj recited ﴿al-rūʿb﴾ with a damma on the ʿayn. Regarding ﴿fawqa﴾, al-Akhfash said it is superfluous (zāʾida), meaning: "strike the necks," and this is the view of ʿAtiyya and al-Dahhak, so the necks would be the object of ﴿ḍribū﴾. This is not good, because ﴿fawq﴾ is a noun of place (ism ẓarf), and nouns are not made superfluous.

Abu ʿUbayda said: ﴿fawq﴾ means ʿalā (on), as you say: "I struck him above the head" and "on the head," and the object of ﴿fa-ḍribū﴾ on this view is omitted, meaning: "strike them above the necks." This is a good view, as it keeps ﴿fawq﴾ in its meaning of location.

Ibn Qutayba said: ﴿fawq﴾ means dūn (below). Ibn ʿAtiyya said: This is a clear error; the confusion arose only from His saying ﴿baʿūḍatan fa-mā fawqahā﴾ (a gnat or what is above it) [al-Baqara: 26], in smallness and littleness, so it resembled the meaning of dūn. End of quote. On Ibn Qutayba's view the object is omitted, meaning: "strike them."

ʿIkrima said: ﴿fawq﴾ is on its original sense, and he meant the heads, since they are above the necks. Al-Zamakhshari said: He means striking the skulls. The poet said:

*"And I strike the skull of the brave man who charges."*

Another said:

*"I came upon him while he was in a dense, brave host, with a keen sword that struck the middle of the head so it split."*

End of quote. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: This interpretation is the noblest of them. In my opinion it may be intended by His saying "above the necks" a description of the most forceful and most precise blows to the neck, namely the blow that falls above the bone of the neck and below the bone of the head at the joint. This meaning is reflected in the saying of Duraid ibn al-Simma al-Jushami to Ibn al-Daghina al-Sulami when he said to him: "Take my sword, raise it above the bone and lower it away from the brain, for thus I used to strike the necks of the brave," and in the saying of the poet:

*"I placed the sword between his neck and between the fine cheek and its sideburn."*

On this view ﴿fawqa al-aʿnāq﴾ comes firmly in place. End of quote.

If ʿIkrima's saying is an explanation of meaning, it is good, and the object of ﴿fa-ḍribū﴾ is omitted. If he meant that ﴿fawq﴾ is the thing struck, then it is not good, because ﴿fawq﴾ is among the adverbs that are not inflected: it cannot be a subject, an object, or a noun governed by a preposition in the way of an inflected noun; it is only used with a preposition of jarr, as in His saying ﴿min fawqihim ẓulalun﴾ (above them are layers) [al-Zumar: 16]. This is the correct view regarding ﴿fawq﴾. Some have permitted ﴿fawq﴾ in the verse to be a direct object and permitted its inflection, saying: one says ﴿fawquka raʾsuka﴾ with nominative, and ﴿fawqaka qalansuwatuka﴾ with accusative. This view appears from al-Zamakhshari, who said: "Above the necks" means the upper parts of the necks, which are the places of slaughter, since they are joints; so striking them is cutting and sending the head flying. End of quote.

As for ﴿al-banān﴾ (the fingers), its discussion has been treated in the lexical section (al-mufradat). A group, including al-Dahhak, said: ﴿al-banān﴾ are the joints wherever they are among the limbs. Another group said: ﴿al-banān﴾ are the fingers of the two hands and the two feet. It was also said: the fingers and other limbs. The preferred view is that they are the fingers.

ʿAntara al-ʿAbsi said:

*"The young man of battle who defends its protection, and strikes at the moment of distress every finger."*

He also said:

*"And death is the throwing down of my hand when I join its fingers with the Indian sword."*

Striking the unbelievers is prescribed at every place on them, but it aimed at the most effective places and those where the vital points lie. For when one aims at the head or the extremities, one remains steady of heart and careful about what one places one's weapon of war in, whether a sword, a spear or others, by which the encounter takes place. Striking the head is the most distracting of all distractions from fighting and frequently leads to death, while striking the fingers disables the one struck from fighting, unlike other limbs.

Al-Farra' said: He taught them the places for striking, saying: strike the heads, the hands and the feet. It is as if He said: strike the upper parts if you are able to strike them; if you cannot, strike them in the middle; if you cannot, strike them in the lower parts. For striking the upper parts quickly brings them to death, striking the middle quickly leads to their no longer resisting, and striking the lower parts prevents them from advancing and retreating, so that the result is either their complete destruction or your gaining control over them. End of quote. In al-Farra's statement there is a loading of the words of the Qur'an with what they cannot bear.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: strike the vital points and the extremities, since a blow either lands on a vital point or on a non-vital one, so He commanded them to combine both types together. End of quote.

﴿That is because they opposed God and His Messenger.﴾ The demonstrative (al-ishara) refers to what befell them of having terror cast into their hearts and what they suffered of striking and killing. The kaf (the "-ka" in "dhalika") is addressed either to the Messenger, or to every listener, or to the disbelievers by way of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person). "Dhalika" is the subject (mubtada'), "bi-annahum" is the predicate (khabar), and the pronoun refers to the disbelievers. The discussion of opposition (mushaqqa) has already occurred in His words: ﴿so they are only in opposition﴾ [al-Baqarah: 137]. Here "mushaqqa" takes the form of mufa'ala, so it is as if, when God legislated laws and commanded commands and they denied them and turned away, what lay between them grew distant, separated and split. The exegetes, in His words "opposed God," expressed it as: they came to be in a split other than His split.

﴿And whoever opposes God and His Messenger, indeed God is severe in punishment.﴾ The scholars agreed on the fakk (separate writing, i.e., the two identical letters not being merged) in "yushaqiq," following the script of the Mushaf. This is the dialect of the Hijaz, while idgham (assimilation of the two identical letters into one) is the dialect of Tamim, as came in the other verse: ﴿And whoever opposes God [yushaqqi Allaha]﴾ [al-Hashr: 4]. It was also said that there is an omitted modifier in it, its estimate being: they opposed (p-472) the friends of God. "Man" is a conditional (shartiyya), the response (jawab) is "fa-inna" and what follows it, and the returning pronoun to "man" is omitted, i.e., "severe in punishment for him." It contains a warning and a threat, and He began with the worldly punishment, namely killing, capture and subjugation of them.

﴿That, so taste it, and that for the disbelievers is the punishment of the Fire.﴾ He combined the two punishments: the worldly punishment, which is hastened, and the punishment of the Hereafter, which is deferred. The demonstrative "dhalikum" refers to the worldly punishment that befell them, and the address is to the opponents. Since the worldly punishment is slight in comparison with the punishment of the Hereafter, He called what befell them of it a "taste" (dhawq), because taste is what one recognises flavour by, and it is small so that by it the state of a great quantity of food may be known, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Then indeed you, O astray deniers,﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 51] ﴿will surely eat from a tree of zaqqum﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 52] ﴿and fill your bellies with it﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 53]. So what came to them of punishment in this world is like a small taste compared with what has been prepared for them in the Hereafter of great punishment.

"Dhalikum" is in the nominative case, either as a beginning (mubtada') with an omitted predicate, i.e., "that is the punishment," or as a predicate (khabar) with an omitted subject, i.e., "the punishment is that." These are two estimates given by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: that is, "that is the striking and killing and what God inflicted upon them on the day of Badr," as if he said: "the matter is that, so taste it," end of quote. This is the estimate of al-Zajjaj. Al-Zamakhshari said: it may be in the accusative case by an implied "'alaykum" (upon you): "that, so taste it," like your saying "Zayd, so strike him." End of quote. This estimate is not permissible, because "'alaykum" is among the ism al-fi'l (verb-like nouns), and ism al-fi'l are not made implicit. His comparing it to your saying "Zayd, so strike him" is not sound, because they did not estimate it as "'alayka Zayd, so strike him"; rather this is in the accusative by ishtighal (the verb being occupied with the pronoun). Some have permitted that it be in the accusative by ishtighal. Some others said: it is not permissible for "dhalikum" to be a mubtada' with "fa-dhuqu hu" as its khabar, because what follows the fa' cannot be a khabar for a mubtada' unless the mubtada' is an ism mawsul (relative pronoun) or an indefinite modified noun, such as: "Whoever comes to me, then for him is a dirham," and "Every man in the house, then he is honoured," end of quote. What he said is correct. The matter of ishtighal rests on the soundness of permitting that "dhalikum" be a mubtada', which is possible. However, their saying "Zayd, fa-idribhu" and "Zayd fa-idribhu" — the fa' here is not like the fa' in "the one who comes to me, then for him is a dirham," because this fa' entered to include in the mubtada' the meaning of the conditional noun, and for that there are conditions mentioned in grammar. The fa' in "Zayd fa-idribhu" is the response to an omitted command, and it is postponed from an earlier position. The estimate is: "Attend! Then Zayd, strike him." The Arabs said "Zaydan fa-idribhu," and the grammarians estimated: "Attend, then strike Zayd." The ishtighal in "Zaydan fa-idribhu" is built on this estimate, so the difference between the two fa's is clear. Without this estimate it would not be permissible to say "Zaydan fa-idrib," but rather the construction would be "Zaydan idrib," as is the case when there is no omitted command of attention estimated there.

Ibn 'Amir and the majority read "wa-anna" with a fatha on the hamza. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is conjoined to "dhalikum" in its two aspects, or it is in the accusative with the waw meaning "together with": "Taste this punishment, the hastened together with the deferred that is yours in the Hereafter," so the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun, i.e., in place of "wa-inna lakum" and "wa-inna lil-kafirin." Ibn 'Atiyya said: either by estimating "wa-hatmun anna" (and it is a certainty that), so the estimate of an omitted mubtada' whose khabar is it; or by estimating "wa-i'lamu anna" (and know that), in which case it is in the accusative position. End of quote. Sibawayh said: the estimate is "the matter is that, so taste it." Al-Hasan, Zayd ibn 'Ali and Sulayman al-Taymi read "wa-inna" with a kasra on the hamza, as a resumption of the statement (isti'naf al-akhbar).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verses 15–16 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who believe, when you meet those who disbelieve advancing in ranks, do not turn your backs to them.﴾ ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day, unless he is swerving for battle or joining a company, has indeed incurred anger from Allah, and his refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾ ﴿So you did not kill them, but Allah killed them. And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw, so that He might test the believers with a fine trial from Him. Indeed, Allah is Hearing, Knowing.﴾ [al-Anfal: 17] ﴿That is so, and that Allah weakens the plot of the disbelievers.﴾ [al-Anfal: 18] ﴿If you seek a decision, the decision has already come to you. And if you desist, it is better for you. And if you return, We will return. And your company will not avail you anything, even if it is numerous. And indeed, Allah is with the believers.﴾ [al-Anfal: 19] ﴿O you who believe, obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you hear.﴾ [al-Anfal: 20] ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear.﴾ [al-Anfal: 21] ﴿Indeed, the worst of creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and the dumb who do not reason.﴾ [al-Anfal: 22] ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while they were averse.﴾ [al-Anfal: 23] ﴿O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life. And know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart, and that to Him you will be gathered.﴾ [al-Anfal: 24] ﴿And beware of a trial that will not strike only those among you who have done wrong. And know that Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ [al-Anfal: 25] ﴿And remember when you were few and oppressed in the land, fearing that people would snatch you away. So He sheltered you, strengthened you with His help, and provided you with good things, that perhaps you would be grateful.﴾ [al-Anfal: 26] ﴿O you who believe, do not betray Allah and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts while you know.﴾ [al-Anfal: 27] ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial, and that with Allah is a great reward.﴾ [al-Anfal: 28] ﴿O you who believe, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion, and will expiate your misdeeds from you, and will forgive you. And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾ [al-Anfal: 29] ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to confine you, or kill you, or expel you, they plotted, and Allah plotted. And Allah is the best of plotters.﴾ [al-Anfal: 30] ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, they say, "We have heard. If we wished, we could say the like of this. This is nothing but the tales of the ancients."﴾ [al-Anfal: 31] ﴿And when they said, "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."﴾ [al-Anfal: 32] ﴿But Allah would not punish them while you were among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness.﴾ [al-Anfal: 33] ﴿And why would Allah not punish them, when they bar access to the Sacred Mosque, and they are not its guardians? Its guardians are only the righteous, but most of them do not know.﴾ [al-Anfal: 34] ﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping. So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve.﴾ [al-Anfal: 35] ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert [people] from the way of Allah. They will spend it, then it will become a regret for them, then they will be overcome. And those who disbelieve will be gathered to Hell.﴾ [al-Anfal: 36] ﴿That Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good, and place the wicked on top of one another, pile them all up together, and cast them into Hell. Those are the losers.﴾ [al-Anfal: 37] ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them; but if they return, the precedent of the former peoples has already passed.﴾ [al-Anfal: 38]

Al-Layth said: "The company of people walking toward their enemy is the zahf (advance in ranks)." Al-A'sha said:

*Whose are these howdahs? Their going is a slow advance; the ship of the desert drags, when it lags and holds back, it plows the ground.*

Al-Farra' said: "Al-zahf is drawing near little by little. It is said: zahafa ilayhi yazhafu zahfan, when he walked toward him. And azhaftu al-qawm means I drew near to fight them. Likewise tazahhafa and tazahafa. Azhif lana 'aduwwana izhafan means: they began advancing to fight us. Fa-izdahafa al-qawm izdihafan means: some of them walked toward others."

Tha'lab said: "From this comes al-zihaf in poetry, which is when one of the two letters drops out and one of them creeps toward the other." The large army was called al-zahf (the advance) because of its multitude, as if it creeps toward me, crawling slowly, from zahafa al-sabiyyu, when the child crawls on his buttocks little by little. Its original sense is the verbal noun of zahafa. Azhaf has the plural zuhuf. Al-Hudhali, describing a watering place, said:

*As if the tracks of the serpents in it, before the dawn, were the marks of whips.*

Al-mutahayyiz is the one who joins himself to a side. Abu 'Ubayda said: "Al-tahayyuz and al-tahawwuz mean withdrawing aside." Al-Layth said: "Ma laka mutahawwizan" means when you do not settle on the ground. Its root is from al-hawz, which is gathering. It is said: huztuhu fi al-tarsi fa-nhaza, meaning I gathered it in the writing and it was gathered. Tahayyaza means it gathered and came together. Tahawwazat al-hayya means the snake coiled up and gathered. Withdrawing aside was called tahayyuz, because the one who withdraws from a side gathers himself away from it and joins others. The form tahayyaza is of the pattern tafay'ala, its original form being tahayway, a yā' and a wāw came together, one of them was preceded by a sukūn, so the wāw was changed into a yā' and the yā' was assimilated into it. Tahawwaza is of the pattern tafa''ala, its middle radical being doubled.

Al-ramy (throwing) is well known, and it may be with an arrow, a stone, or dust. Al-muka' is whistling. 'Antara said:

*And a friend of a flirtatious woman, I left him a corpse, his chest pulsing like the cheek of a one-eyed man.*

That is, it makes a sound. From this comes makat-i al-dabbah, when the animal's rear released wind. Al-Suddi said: "Al-muka' is whistling in the tune of a white bird in the Hijaz, called al-makka'. A poet said:

*When the makka' warbles in a place other than a garden, woe to the people of the water-skins and the red camels.*

Zahfan is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). It is said that it comes from the object (the maf'ūl), meaning: when you meet them while they are a large host and you are few, do not flee, let alone that you should approach them in number or equal them. It is also said that it comes from the subject (the fā'il), meaning: while you are a body of advancing troops. This was an indication of what would later happen from them on the day of Hunayn, when they fled, although they were twelve thousand, after He had forbidden them from fleeing that day. It is also said: this was at the beginning of Islam, when the command was to endure, that one Muslim should stand against ten disbelievers. Then it was lightened, so that one was set against two. The ruling concerning the believing woman who flees from her weakness will come in the verse of lightening. How well al-Harith ibn Hisham made an excuse when he fled, and it was said about him:
"He left his beloved ones, not fighting in front of them, and escaped with the head of a swift horse and its bridle."

al-Harith also said, from a set of verses:
"And I know that if I fight a single man, I will be killed, and my presence will not harm my enemy."

The judge (al-Qadi) used this conditional sentence as evidence for the threat against wrongdoers among the people of prayer, because it shows that whoever flees, except in these two states, deserves Allah's wrath, and his refuge is Hell. He said: The Murji'a cannot apply this to the disbelievers, as they did with the verses of threat, because this begins with the people of prayer, which is His saying: ﴿O you who have believed﴾. End of quote.

There is no proof in this, because it is a general statement that is specified (*'amm makhsus*). It is apparent that *tahayyuz* (retreating to a group) is permitted whether the army is large or not. It was also said: It is not permitted if the army is large. It is apparent that fleeing from the battlefield without its conditions is a major sin, because of the threat. And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw, so that He might test the believers with a fine trial from Him. Indeed, Allah is Hearing, Knowing.﴾ [al-Anfal: 17] ﴿That is so, and that Allah weakens the plot of the disbelievers.﴾ [al-Anfal: 18] ﴿If you seek a decision, the decision has already come to you. And if you desist, it is better for you. And if you return, We will return. And your company will not avail you anything, even if it is numerous. And indeed, Allah is with the believers.﴾ [al-Anfal: 19] ﴿O you who believe, obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you hear.﴾ [al-Anfal: 20] ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear.﴾ [al-Anfal: 21] ﴿Indeed, the worst of creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and the dumb who do not reason.﴾ [al-Anfal: 22] ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while they were averse.﴾ [al-Anfal: 23] ﴿O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life. And know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart, and that to Him you will be gathered.﴾ [al-Anfal: 24] ﴿And beware of a trial that will not strike only those among you who have done wrong. And know that Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ [al-Anfal: 25] ﴿And remember when you were few and oppressed in the land, fearing that people would snatch you away. So He sheltered you, strengthened you with His help, and provided you with good things, that perhaps you would be grateful.﴾ [al-Anfal: 26] ﴿O you who believe, do not betray Allah and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts while you know.﴾ [al-Anfal: 27] ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial, and that with Allah is a great reward.﴾ [al-Anfal: 28] ﴿O you who believe, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion, and will expiate your misdeeds from you, and will forgive you. And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾ [al-Anfal: 29] ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to confine you, or kill you, or expel you, they plotted, and Allah plotted. And Allah is the best of plotters.﴾ [al-Anfal: 30] ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, they say, "We have heard. If we wished, we could say the like of this. This is nothing but the tales of the ancients."﴾ [al-Anfal: 31] ﴿And when they said, "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."﴾ [al-Anfal: 32] ﴿But Allah would not punish them while you were among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness.﴾ [al-Anfal: 33] ﴿And why would Allah not punish them, when they bar access to the Sacred Mosque, and they are not its guardians? Its guardians are only the righteous, but most of them do not know.﴾ [al-Anfal: 34] ﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping. So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve.﴾ [al-Anfal: 35] ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert [people] from the way of Allah. They will spend it, then it will become a regret for them, then they will be overcome. And those who disbelieve will be gathered to Hell.﴾ [al-Anfal: 36] ﴿That Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good, and place the wicked on top of one another, pile them all up together, and cast them into Hell. Those are the losers.﴾ [al-Anfal: 37] ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them; but if they return, the precedent of the former peoples has already passed.﴾ [al-Anfal: 38]

"And I know that if I fight a single man, I will be killed, and my presence will not harm my enemy."

The judge (al-Qadi) used this conditional sentence as evidence for the threat against wrongdoers among the people of prayer, because it shows that whoever flees, except in these two states, deserves Allah's wrath, and his refuge is Hell. He said: The Murji'a cannot apply this to the disbelievers, as they did with the verses of threat, because this begins with the people of prayer, which is His saying: ﴿O you who have believed﴾. End of quote.

There is no proof in this, because it is a general statement that is specified (*'amm makhsus*). It is apparent that *tahayyuz* (retreating to a group) is permitted whether the army is large or not. It was also said: It is not permitted if the army is large. It is apparent that fleeing from the battlefield without its conditions is a major sin, because of the threat. For this reason, Ibn al-Qasim said: Do not accept the testimony of one who fled from the battlefield, even if he fled in front of them. Whoever flees should seek Allah's forgiveness. In al-Tirmidhi: "Whoever says, 'I seek forgiveness from Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting,' will be forgiven, even if he fled from the battlefield."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verses 17–18:

﴿So you did not kill them, but it was Allah who killed them. And you did not throw when you threw, but it was Allah who threw, so that He might bestow upon the believers from Him a fine favour. Indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ When the Companions returned from Badr, they began to boast of their exploits, so one of them would say: "I killed and I took captives." Then this was revealed. Al-Zamakhshari said: The fa' (فاء) is the answer to an elided conditional clause, its implied sense being: "If you boast of killing them, then you did not kill them, but Allah killed them, because it is He who sent down the angels, cast terror into their hearts, willed victory and triumph, strengthened your hearts, and removed from them fear and dismay." End of quotation. But the fa' is not the answer to an elided conditional clause as he claimed. Rather, it serves to link the sentences, because when He said: ﴿So strike above the necks and strike from them every fingertip﴾ [al-Anfal: 12], carrying out what they were commanded became a cause of killing. So it was said: "So you did not kill them," meaning: you did not act independently in killing, because the decrees concerning it and its Creator is only Allah; the slayer has no share in it. Rather, He caused it to occur through his hand (p-477). Thus the creation of the killing is denied of them and affirmed for Allah. This is a refutation of those who claim that the actions of servants are created by them. The coming of lakinna (لكنّ, "but") here is most fitting, since it stands between a negation and an affirmation: what is affirmed for Allah is what is negated of them, namely the reality of the killing. As for one who claims that the actions of servants are created by them, he must interpret the statement as meaning: "They did not cause your killing of them, but Allah killed them, because it is He who sent down the angels," and so on to the end of his statement. He conjoined the negated clause introduced by mā with the negated clause introduced by lam, because lam negates the past even though it takes the form of the present. For negating the past there are two methods: one is to place mā before the verb's form, and the other is to negate it with lam, bringing the present form. The original is the first, since negation should correspond to affirmation. There is emphasis in the sentence in two respects. The first: the negation came in a form corresponding to the affirmation in wording. The second: He negated what He had explicitly affirmed, namely His words: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾. In His words ﴿So you did not kill them﴾ He did not explicitly say: "when you killed them." This emphasis was made because throwing was a matter beyond the normal course of things, a miraculous sign (mu'jiza) from the signs of Allah, in whatever manner throwing is interpreted. They differed concerning it. Ibn 'Abbas said: "On the day of Badr the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took a handful of dust and said: 'May the faces be disfigured,' meaning: may they be made ugly. So no polytheist remained except that some of it entered his eyes, his mouth and his nostrils." Hakim ibn Hizam said: "We heard a sound from the sky, as if it were the sound of a pebble falling into a basin, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) threw that throw, and they fled." Anas said: "He threw three pebbles on the day of Badr: one at the right wing of the people, one at their left wing, and a third among them. And he said: 'May the faces be disfigured,' and they fled." It was also said: the throwing here refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) throwing a spear at Ubayy ibn Khalaf on the day of Uhud. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is weak, because the verse was revealed right after Badr, and on this view it would be unconnected to what precedes and follows it, which is far-fetched. It was also said: the intended meaning is the arrow that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) shot at the fortress of Khaybar, which travelled through the air until it struck Ibn Abi al-Huqayq. This is corrupt, and the sound account of the slaying of Ibn Abi al-Huqayq is other than this. His words ﴿And you did not throw﴾ are a negation, and ﴿when you threw﴾ is an affirmation, so an interpretation is needed, namely that one distinguishes between the two throws: what is negated is the hitting and the victory, while what is affirmed is the sending forth. It was also said: what is negated is the taking of life, and what is affirmed is the effect of the throw, which is the wounding. These two views are close to each other. It was also said: "You did not seize the throwing by yourself when you sent the dust, because seizing it in this way is the act of Allah in reality, while the sending of the dust is attributed to him as an acquisition (kasb, كسب)." The meaning would then be: "You did not throw the sufficient throw when you threw." A similar expression is the verse of al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas:

*"I was in war one who was hard-pressed, yet I was given nothing and I withheld nothing."*

That is, I was not given anything worthy of praise. It was also said: the object of the negation is the terror, and the object of the affirmation is the pebbles; that is, "You did not cast terror into their hearts when you threw the pebbles." Al-Zamakhshari said: He means that the throw you threw was not truly thrown by you, for if you had thrown it, its effect would not have reached beyond what a human throw reaches. Rather it was the throw of Allah, since it produced that great effect. Thus He affirmed the throwing for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) because the outward form of throwing was found in him, and He negated it of him because its effect, which no human can bear, is the act of Allah. So Allah the Exalted was the true doer of the throwing, as if it had never existed from the Messenger at all. End of quotation. This returns to the meaning of the two views mentioned earlier. The disagreement of al-Farra' concerning lakinna and what follows it was mentioned under His words: ﴿But the devils disbelieved﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102].

﴿That He might bestow upon the believers from Him a fine favour﴾. Al-Suddi said: He gives them victory and bestows blessings upon them. It is said: abla-hu (أبلاه) when he bestowed a favour upon him, and balla-hu (بلاه) when he tested him. The word balā' (بلاء) is used for both good and evil. Describing it as ḥasan (حسن, fine) indicates victory and honour. Al-Zamakhshari said: "And that He might give them a beautiful gift, as the poet said:

*'So he gave them both the best of trials, the trial that tries.'*"

End of quotation. The fine balā' has been said to mean victory and spoils. It has also been said to mean martyrdom for those who were martyred on the day of Badr, who were fourteen men, among them 'Ubayda ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, Mihja' the freedman of 'Umar, and Mu'adh and 'Amr, the two sons of 'Afra' — that (p-478) he said: "Were it not that the commentators agreed on taking balā' here to mean blessing, it could bear the meaning of trial, for the obligation of what follows it, namely the jihad, so that it might be said that what He did on the day of Badr was the cause of a hard obligation upon them in the expeditions that came after it." End of quotation. But the context rules out that balā' means trial, because He said: ﴿That He might bestow upon the believers from Him a fine favour﴾, meaning He did that, namely the killing and throwing of the disbelievers, and attributed it to Allah. This was the cause of their defeat, of victory over them, and of making them spoil for the believers. This is not a trial but a gift. ﴿Indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ Since they had been occupied with boasting of killing those they killed and capturing those they captured, or since perhaps the deed was not free of some fighters, either out of zealous fervour or for defence of self, or since the verse was concluded with these two attributes, it was said: "Indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing": He hears your words and what you boast of, and He knows what the hearts conceal. And [He knows] who fights so that the word of Allah may be the highest.

﴿That, and that Allah weakens the plot of the disbelievers﴾. He said: ﴿That﴾ is a reference to the fine favour, and its place in the grammar is nominative (raf'). ﴿And that Allah weakens﴾ is conjoined to ﴿That He might bestow﴾, meaning that the purpose is the bestowing of favour upon the believers and the weakening of the plot of the disbelievers. End of quotation. Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿That﴾ refers to what was mentioned earlier of Allah's killing and His throwing of them. Its position in grammar is nominative. Sibawayh said: the estimated sense is: "The matter is that." Some grammarians said: it may be in the accusative position, with the estimate: "We did that," and (wa-anna, وأنّ) is conjoined to ﴿that﴾. It may also be the predicate of an elided subject, its estimate being: "And it is decreed, established and fixed," or something similar. End of quotation. Al-Hawfi said: ﴿That﴾ is nominative as the subject, with an elided predicate, the estimate being: "That is the matter." It may also be that ﴿That﴾ is the predicate and ﴿the matter﴾ is the subject. It may also be in the accusative position, the estimate being: "We did that." The reference is to the killing and to the bestowing of the fine favour upon the believers. Regarding the opening of anna (أنّ) there are two possibilities, accusative and nominative, conjoined to ﴿that﴾ according to the two estimates, or by supposing a verb, the estimate being: "And know that Allah weakens." End of quotation. The two Harams (Makkah and Madinah) and Abu 'Amr read muwahhinu (مُوَهِّنُ), from wahhana (وهّن), and transitivity by doubling in a verb whose middle radical is a guttural letter other than the hamza is rare, as in ḍa'‌‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‌‌‍ّfta (ضعّفت, I weakened) and wahhantu (وهّنت, I weakened). Its usual method is transitivity by hamza, as in adhhaltu-hu (أذهلته, I bewildered him), awhantu-hu (أوهنته, I weakened him), and alhamtu-hu (ألحمته, I fed him flesh). The remaining seven readers, al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and al-A'mash, and Ibn Muhaysin read mūhinu (مُوهِنُ), from awhana (أوهن), and Hafs transmitted it with the idafa (إضافة, annexation) construction.
