Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verse 19:

﴿If you seek victory, then victory has indeed come to you. And if you desist, it is better for you. And if you return, We will return. And your company will not avail you anything, however numerous it is. And indeed Allah is with the believers.﴾ The mention of the believers and the disbelievers has preceded, and the address to the believers had come earlier with His words: ﴿So you did not kill them﴾ [al-Anfal: 17] and with His words: ﴿That is [your due]﴾ [al-Anfal: 18]. So a group took it to be an address to the believers, and His words ﴿then victory has indeed come to you﴾ support this, since this address befits only the believers, on the meaning of seeking victory through the opening (istiftah, i.e., seeking a decision or victory). As for taking it to mean clarification and judgment, it fits as an address to both the disbelievers and the believers. If it is an address to the believers, then the meaning is: if you seek help, then help has indeed come to you; and if you desist from the like of what you did regarding the spoils and the captives before the permission, it is better for you; and if you return to the like of that, We will return to rebuke you, as He said: ﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had already preceded﴾ [al-Anfal: 68], and so on. Then He informed them that the company (fi'ah), which is the group, does not avail, however numerous it is, except by the help and support of Allah. Then He comforted them by informing them that He, the Exalted, is with the believers.

Most of the scholars said: it is an address to the people of Mecca in the manner of mockery. That is because when they wanted to set out, they clung to the curtains of the Ka'bah and said: "O Allah, grant victory to the one who is most generous to the guest, who is most joined to the kin, and who most frees the captive. If Muhammad is upon the truth, then give him victory; and if we are upon the truth, then give us victory." It is also narrated that they said: "O Allah, grant victory to the higher of the two armies, the more guided of the two groups, and the more honorable of the two parties." It is also narrated that Abu Jahl said on the morning of the Battle of Badr: "O Allah, whichever of us was more severing of kinship and more wrongful, then destroy him today" (fahnih al-yawm), meaning: destroy him. It is narrated from him that he supplicated something similar to this. Al-Hasan, Mujahid and others said: this statement was from the Quraysh at the time of their departure to defend the caravan. Al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], and the verse, and he was among those killed on the Day of Badr. According to this view, the meaning of His words (p-479) ﴿then victory has indeed come to you﴾ is that it was for the Muslims against you. It was also said: its meaning is: then there has come to you that by which the matter became clear for you, the judgment was settled by it, and the truth was revealed to you through it; and the seeking of opening (istiftah) on this view means judgment and decision. "And if they desist from disbelief" and "if you return to this statement and fighting Muhammad thereafter, We will return to the support of the believers and your forsaking."

A group said: ﴿If you seek victory﴾ is an address to the believers, and ﴿if you desist﴾ is an address to the disbelievers, meaning: if you desist from enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it is better for you; and if you return to fighting him, We will return to his support against you. Al-Kirmani said: "And if you desist from the matter of the spoils and the ransoming of the captives at Badr, and if you return to disobedience to Allah, We will return to the rejection (of your deeds)."

It was recited: ﴿وَلَنْ يُغْنِيَ﴾ with the yā' (yughnī), because the feminine marking is metaphorical; al-Fadl considered it good. Al-Sahibani (Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr) and Hafs read ﴿وأنَّ اللَّهَ﴾ with the hamza opened (fatha), while the rest of the seven read it with the hamza kasra. Ibn Mas'ud read: "and Allah is with the believers."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on Surah 8, verse 20:

﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you hear.﴾ When His saying "And if you cease" had preceded, and the pronoun's apparent reference was to the believers, He addressed them and urged them to obey Allah and His Messenger. The apparent meaning is that this is an address and a direct speech to the sincere believers, urging them by command to obey Allah and His Messenger. Since the verse before it was directed toward the matter of *jihad* (struggle in the way of Allah), it was said that the meaning of "obey him" is: in what he calls you to of *jihad*. It was also said: in complying with commands and prohibitions. He singled them out with the command to elevate their status, although others are also commanded to obey Allah and His Messenger. This is the view of the majority. As for one who said that His saying "And if you cease" is an address to the disbelievers, he holds that this verse was revealed because of their dispute over the spoils (*nafl*), their argument over the truth, and their boasting about killing the disbelievers and inflicting harm upon them. As for one who went to the view that it is an address to the hypocrites, meaning "O you who have believed with their tongues," he was far from the correct view, because describing them with faith, which is affirmation (*tasdiq*), does not suit them, since the hypocrites have no share of affirmation. And one who went to the view that it is an address to the Children of Israel was also far off, because that would be extraneous to the verses.

The original form of "wa-la tawallaw" is "wa-la tatawallaw." The disagreement concerning the letter *ta'* in such forms has been mentioned earlier: is it the prefixed letter of the imperfect (*harf al-mudara'a*), or is it the *ta'* of the form *tafa'\'ala*?

As for the pronoun in "'anhu" (from him), al-Zamakhshari said: it refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because the meaning is "obey the Messenger of Allah," like His saying: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62]; and because obedience to the Messenger and obedience to Allah are one thing: "Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah" [al-Nisa': 80]. So the pronoun's returning to one of the two is like its returning to both, as when you say: "Kindness and generosity do not benefit so-and-so." It is also permissible for it to refer to the command to obey: "and do not turn away from this command and its compliance while you hear it," or: "and do not turn away from the Messenger of Allah, and do not oppose him, while you hear," meaning: you affirm, because you are believers; you are not like the deaf, the deniers among the disbelievers. End of quotation.

It returned to the Messenger because turning away is only properly applied to the Messenger when they turn away from him; this holds if "tawalli" is taken literally (*haqiqa*). If it returns to the command, the usage is figurative (*majaz*). It was also said that it refers to obedience, and it was said that it refers to Allah. Al-Kirmani said, in substance: since the dual form is not used for Allah alone, He (Exalted) is not joined with another in a single pronoun referring to them, unlike the plural, which is used for His own person as an expression of magnification; so He joined Himself with another in the pronoun. There are parallels to this in the Qur'an, among them: ﴿When He calls you﴾ [al-Anfal: 24], and among them ﴿that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62]. In the hadith there is a condemnation of one who joins the two in a dual pronoun, and instruction that he should say: "Whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger."

"While you hear" is a circumstantial clause (*jumla haliyya*), meaning: your hearing does not suit turning away, nor does it coexist with it. Concerning its object there are several views: first, Allah's admonition to you; second, the command and prohibition; third, the expression of hearing as referring to intellect and understanding; fourth, the expression of affirmation, which is faith.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verse 21–22:

﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear.﴾ He forbade them from being like those who claimed to hear. The ones likened to them are the Jews, or the hypocrites, or the polytheists, or those who said, "We have indeed heard; had we wished, we would have said the like of this," or the Banu Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy, of whom only two men embraced Islam, Mus'ab ibn Umayr and Suwayd ibn Harmala, or al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and those who followed him: six opinions. Since their hearing was of no benefit and had no effect on them, (p-480) He negated hearing from them because its fruit was absent. The fruit of hearing revelation is affirming it and believing in it. The meaning is: you profess belief in the Qur'an and the prophethood, but when there comes from you a turning away from obedience, your professed belief becomes like non-belief, so your hearing resembles the hearing of one who does not believe. The negating sentence came in a form other than the affirmative: it did not come as "and they did not hear," because the past tense (al-madi) does not indicate the continuation or permanence of a state, unlike the negation of the present tense (al-mudari'). Just as its affirmation indicates permanence in the saying "he gives and withholds," so too its negation is expressed in this way. The particle of negation "la" (لا) was used because it is broader in the scope of the present tense than "ma" (ما), and more indicative of the absence of hearing in the future, i.e., they are among those who do not accept hearing.

﴿Indeed, the most evil of creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and the dumb who do not reason.﴾ When God the Exalted informed that those likened to them do not hear, He informed that the most evil of living creatures that crawl are the deaf, or that the most evil of beasts are the deaf. He combined these people with the category of "creatures" (dawabb) and informed that they are the most evil of living beings absolutely. The meaning of "deaf" is deafness to what is recited to them of the Qur'an, and "dumb" is muteness regarding the affirmation of faith and what in it is their salvation. Then He mentioned the negation of the attribute that produces for them the deafness and dumbness arising from it, which is reason ('aql). The beginning was with deafness because dumbness arises from it, for it necessarily follows that every deaf person would be created mute, since speech is only acquired and learned by one whose sense of hearing is intact. This corresponds to the saying of God the Exalted, ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not reason﴾ [al-Baqarah: 171], except that in this verse He added the attribute of blindness. All these attributes are metaphors for the absence of their acceptance of faith and their turning away from what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought. The apparent sense of these statements is general. It is said that it was revealed concerning a group of the Banu Abd al-Dar who used to say, "We are deaf, dumb, and blind to what Muhammad brings; we neither hear it nor respond to it." They were all killed at Badr, and they were the standard-bearers. Ibn Jurayj said they are the hypocrites, and al-Hasan said they are the People of the Book.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verse 21–22:

﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear.﴾ He forbade them from being like those who claimed to hear. The ones likened to them are the Jews, or the hypocrites, or the polytheists, or those who said, "We have indeed heard; had we wished, we would have said the like of this," or the Banu Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy, of whom only two men embraced Islam, Mus'ab ibn Umayr and Suwayd ibn Harmala, or al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and those who followed him: six opinions. They were all killed at Badr, and they were the standard-bearers. Ibn Jurayj said they are the hypocrites, and al-Hasan said they are the People of the Book.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verse 23:

﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while being averse.﴾ Ibn 'Atiyya said: Allah the Exalted informed that their not hearing and their lack of guidance is only because of what Allah knew of them and what preceded from His decree concerning them. Thus this came in an eloquent expression of censure against them. "And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear": the intended meaning is that He would have made them hear with understanding and guidance. Then, Mighty and Majestic is He, He began the report about them with what they are upon of being sealed with disbelief, saying: "And if He had made them hear," meaning: if He had made them understand, "they would have turned away while being averse," due to the preceding decree concerning them, and they would have turned away from the guidance that had become clear to them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "And if Allah had known any good in these deaf and dumb ones," meaning: benefit from divine grace (al-luṭf), "He would have made them hear the grace toward them, until they heard as those who believe." Then he said: "And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away," meaning: if He had shown grace toward them, it would not have benefited them. Therefore He withheld His graces from them. That is, if He had shown grace toward them and they had believed, they would have apostatized after that, denied, and not remained upright.

Al-Zajjaj said: "He would have made them hear" is the answer to everything they asked for.

Ibn al-Jawzi related: "He would have made them hear" the speech of the dead whom they asked to be revived, because they asked for the revival of Qusayy ibn Kilab and others so that they would bear witness to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: The expression of its non-existence in itself is by the non-knowledge of Allah of its existence. The sense of the statement is: if good had occurred in them, Allah would have made them hear the proofs and admonitions with a hearing of instruction that conveys understanding. "And if He had made them hear," since He knew that there was no good in them, they would not have benefited from them, and they would have turned away while being averse. He also said: Allah's knowledge (ma'lumat) is of four kinds. First: the totality of existing things. Second: the totality of non-existent things. Third: for each of the existing things, if it were non-existent, what would its state be. Fourth: for each of the non-existent things, if it were existent, what would its state be. The first two kinds are knowledge of what actually is, and the last two kinds are knowledge of what is possible but not actual. So His saying: "And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear" belongs to the second kind, which is knowledge of the possibles, and is not among the kinds of knowledge of actualities. Its parallel is the saying of the Exalted, reporting about the hypocrites: ﴿If you are expelled, we will surely go out with you﴾ [al-Hashr: 11] and ﴿if you are fought, we will surely support you﴾ [al-Hashr: 11]. Then He said: ﴿If they are expelled, they will not go out with them, and if they are fought, they will not support them, and if they support them, they will surely turn their backs; then they will not be helped﴾ [al-Hashr: 12]. So Allah's knowledge of the non-existent is that if it were existent, what would its state be. Also His saying: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28] reports about the non-existent that if it were existent, what would its state be (p. 481). End of quotation.

I say: the apparent sense of these two implications (mulazamatan) needs interpretation, because He reported that a making-to-hear would occur from Him for them on the supposition of His knowing good in them, then He reported that their turning away would occur on the supposition of His making them hear. So it follows that their turning away would occur on the supposition of His knowing good in them. This is through the intermediary particle, because what is ordered upon something is ordered upon what that thing is ordered upon. But this does not hold, because turning away does not occur on the supposition of His knowing good in them. The statement in the two clauses becomes as if it were a single statement, so the sense would be: "And if Allah had known good in them and made them hear, they would have turned away." It is known that if He had known good in them, they would not have turned away.

﴿O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾. The discussion of *istajaba* (to respond) has already been covered under ﴿so let them respond to Me﴾. The pronoun in *da'akum* (he calls you) is singular, as it is in ﴿and do not turn away from Him﴾, because mentioning one of them together with the other is only for emphasis. *Al-istijaba* here means *al-imtithal* (compliance, carrying out the command), and *al-du'a'* (calling) means urging and rousing toward that which gives them life. The apparent meaning of *istajibu* (respond) is obligation, and for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ubayy, when he called him while he was lingering in prayer: "What prevented you from responding? Were you not told in what was revealed to me: *respond to Allah and to the Messenger*?"

The apparent connection of *lima* (for what) is with *da'akum* (he calls you), since *da'a* is transitive with the preposition *lam*. A poet said:

*I called out for what befell me, Miswar*

Another said:

*And if I am called to the great calamity, I will be among its defenders.*

It has also been said that the *lam* means *ila* (to) and is connected to *istajibu*. Thus it is interpreted as *ila*, so that the two prepositions differ in meaning while both attach to one verb. Mujahid and the majority of scholars said: the meaning is respond to obedience and to what the Qur'an contains of commands and prohibitions, for in that is eternal life and everlasting blessing. It was also said that *ma yuhyikum* (that which gives you life) is fighting the disbelievers, for if they abandoned it, the disbelievers would overcome and kill them, and in retaliation (*qisas*) there is life for you. It was said that it is martyrdom, based on the verse ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord, provided for﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:169), as Ibn Ishaq said. It was also said that it is the knowledge of religions and laws, since knowledge is life just as ignorance is death. A poet said:

*Do not be impressed by the ignorant man's finery; he is dead, and his garment is a shroud.*

This is close to the saying of the majority and of Mujahid. Mujahid also said that *ma yuhyikum* is the truth. It was said that it is the restoration of their affairs, the goodness of their conditions in this world, and their elevation; one says *hayiyat halahu* when his state has risen. It was said that it is what they gain of spoils in jihad and live on. It was said that it is the body. What appears correct is the first opinion, because it is in the context of the statement ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:23). What gives life from ignorance is hearing what benefits from what He commanded and forbade, so that one carries out what is commanded and avoids what is forbidden, and thus he attains the two good lives, the worldly and the otherworldly.

﴿And know that Allah intervenes between a person and his heart, and that to Him you will be gathered﴾. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, controls all things and is able to prevent a person from what his heart desires. Therefore He is the One to whom one should respond when He calls, since the dominion (*malakut*) of everything and its reins are in His hand. This contains an urging toward vigilance, fear of Allah, and hastening to respond to Him. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: He intervenes between the believer and disbelief, and between the disbeliever and faith. Mujahid said: He intervenes between a person and his intellect, so he does not know what he is doing, as punishment for his obstinacy. In the revelation: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart﴾ (Qaf 50:37), meaning, has intellect. al-Suddi said: He intervenes between each person and his heart, so that he cannot have faith or disbelief except by His permission. Ibn al-Anbari said: between him and what he wishes. Ibn Qutayba said: between him and his desire. These two return to the first opinion. 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: it is that He takes him (causes him to die), and because the term (*ajal*) intervenes between him and the hope of his heart. This is an urging to seize the opportunity before death, which is the time one will find, namely the ability to sincerely purify the heart, to treat its diseases and afflictions, and to return it sound as Allah wishes. So seize this opportunity and make your hearts sincere in obedience to Allah [p. 482] and His Messenger. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), and 'Ali ibn 'Isa is al-Rummani, who was a Mu'tazili. al-Zamakhshari also said this.

It was also said: the meaning is that Allah may take hold of the servant's heart, so He reverses his resolutions, changes his intentions and aims, and replaces fear with security, security with fear, remembrance with forgetfulness, and forgetfulness with remembrance, and what is similar to that which is permissible for Allah, exalted is He. As for acts of the heart for which the servant is rewarded or punished, that is not so. The Jabriyyah (determinists) hold that He intervenes between a person and faith when he disbelieves, and between him and disbelief when he believes. Exalted is Allah above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation. This wretched man made the early leaders of this community wrongdoers, since the one who said this is Ibn 'Abbas, the interpreter of the Qur'an, and those mentioned with him from the masters of the Successors. It was also said: He changes cowardice into boldness. This is an encouragement to fight after the command to it in His words "respond." Its reality is revealed by his saying (ﷺ): "The heart of the son of Adam is between two of the fingers of the Most Merciful; He turns it however He wills." Its interpretation is: between two effects of His lordship. It was also said: He intervenes between the believer and the sins that his heart intends, by preserving him from them. It was also said: the meaning is that He is aware of everything that comes to a person's mind, nothing of his inner thoughts is hidden from Him, so it is as if He is between him and his heart. al-Tabari chose that the meaning is that Allah informed that He is more in control of the hearts of the servants than they are themselves, and that He intervenes between them and their hearts whenever He wills, so that a person perceives nothing except by His will, exalted is He.

Ibn Abi Ishaq read *bayna al-mir'i* with a kasra on the *mim*, following the vowel of the grammatical inflection (*i'rab*, the case endings of Arabic), since *al-mar'* has two dialects: a fatha on the *mim* in all cases, and following the case vowel. al-Hasan and al-Zuhri read *bayna al-marri* with a shadda on the *ra'* without a hamza. Its explanation is that he transferred the vowel of the hamza to the *ra'*, deleted the hamza, then doubled the *ra'* as is done in pausal (*waqf*) pronunciation, treating the connected speech as if it were pause. The Arabs often do this, treating connected speech as pause. This is an explanation of an anomalous reading.

﴿and that to Him you will be gathered﴾. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in *annahu* refers to Allah, though it may be the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*). When He commanded them to know His power and His intervening between a person and the intentions of his heart, He informed them that to Him He will gather them and reward them for their deeds. In this there is a reminder of what their affairs will lead to, namely resurrection and recompense with reward and punishment.

This address, on its apparent meaning, is general: guard against a trial that does not befall only the wrongdoer but affects both the righteous and the wicked. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "He commanded the believers not to tolerate wrongdoing among them, lest God afflict them all with punishment." In al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi [it is related] that "when people see the wrongdoer and do not take him by the hands, God is about to encompass them all with a punishment from Him." In Muslim, from the hadith of Zaynab bint Jahsh: she asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ), "Will we be destroyed while the righteous are among us?" He said: (p. 483) "Yes, when wickedness becomes widespread."

It is also said that the address is to the Companions; it is said to the people of Badr; it is said to 'Ali, 'Ammar, Talha and al-Zubayr; and it is said to two men of Quraysh, as reported by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, who did not name them. The trial here is fighting in the battle of the Camel, or misguidance, or failing to forbid evil, or [afflicting them] with wealth and children, or the spread of innovations, or punishment; these are the opinions. Al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam said on the day of the Camel: "I did not know that this verse was meant for us until today, and I used to think it applied only to those who were addressed by it at that time."

The clause "lā tuṣībanna" (lā tuṣībanna, "it will certainly not afflict") is declarative and is a qualifier of "fitnah" (a trial), meaning: a trial that does not afflict the wrongdoers alone. However, the attachment of the emphatic nun (nūn al-tawkīd, the energetic nun) to a negated verb with "lā" is disputed. The majority do not permit it and treat what has come of it as either a poetic necessity or a rarity. What we choose is that it is permissible, and this is the view of some grammarians. Since its attachment to a verb after "lā" without an intervening separator has been attested, as in the verse:

"Neither the one who enjoys bliss is left to his bliss,
nor does he refuse, if he is told 'praise me' and offered a bribe."

And:

"Nor is the one in misery left to his misery,
such that his complaint to Him benefits him if he complains."

Then its attachment with a separator is more likely, as in "lā tuṣībanna."

Al-Zamakhshari claimed that the clause is a qualifier and that it is a prohibition. He said: "Likewise, if you make it a qualifier with the sense of saying, it is as if it were said: 'Guard against a trial about which it is said: lā tuṣībanna.' A parallel to this is the verse:

'Until, when the darkness gathered and was mixed, they came with a mixture [of milk and water]: "Have you ever seen a wolf?"'

That is: with a mixture about which this statement is made, because in it there is the bluish color that is the meaning of 'wolf.'" End of quotation. The explanation is that the clause governs a deleted qualifier.

Al-Farra' claimed that the clause is an answer to the imperative, like your saying: "Get down from the animal, lest it throw you off" (lā taṭrahannaka), meaning: if you get down from it, it will not throw you off. He said: "From this is [the verse] 'Enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his soldiers crush you' [An-Naml: 18], meaning: if you enter, he will not crush you; and the nun entered because of the sense of conditionality in it." End of quotation. This example, with the verse "Enter your dwellings, lest they crush you" [An-Naml: 18], is not a parallel to "wa-ittaqū fitnatan," because the example fits the conditional form, while the verse is a condition and a consequence as he estimated; and this does not fit there. Do you not see that it is not valid to estimate: "If you guard against a trial, it will not afflict those among you who did wrong specifically"? Because in that case what follows the condition would be a consequence of the condition, whose intended meaning in terms of sense would be [different]. Al-Zamakhshari took al-Farra's opinion, added to its corruption, and became confused in it. He said: "His saying 'lā tuṣībanna' cannot be other than an answer to the imperative, or a prohibition after an imperative, or a qualifier of 'fitnah.' If it is an answer, the meaning is: if it befalls you, it will not befall the wrongdoers among you specifically, but it will encompass you all." End of quotation of this opinion. Observe how he estimated it to be an answer to the imperative "ittaqū," and then estimated the conditional particle attached to a non-imperfect form other than the imperfect of "ittaqū," saying: "The meaning is: if it befalls you, that is, the trial." Observe how al-Farra' estimated [the case of] "descend from the animal, lest it throw you off" and [the verse] "Enter your dwellings, lest they crush you," placing the conditional particle on the imperfect of an imperative verb. So too is estimated whatever is an answer to an imperative.

Some claimed that "lā tuṣībanna" is the answer to an implied oath. Others said that "lā" is a negation, and the negation was treated as affirmative, so the nun entered, as it entered in "latadribanna" (you will certainly strike). The estimate: "By God, it will certainly not afflict." According to the first opinion, that it is a qualifier, or an answer to an imperative, or an answer to an oath, the nun has entered a verb negated with "lā." Some grammarians held that it is the answer to an implied oath and that the clause is affirmative; the nun entered its place, the lām was lengthened and became "lā," and the meaning is "latuṣībanna" (it will surely afflict). This is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ali, Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Baqir, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Abu al-'Aliya: "latuṣībanna." In this there is a threat only to the wrongdoers. On this interpretation Ibn Jinni also explained the reading of the majority, "lā tuṣībanna," and that the lām was lengthened, so an alif came from it as a vowel-lengthening; for vowel-lengthening is characteristic of poetry. Ibn Jinni said regarding the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and those with him: it may be that this reading intends "lā tuṣībanna," with the alif deleted for lightness and by relying on the vowel, as they say: "am wallāhi" (by God). Al-Mahdawi said: "As the alif was deleted from 'mā,' which is a sister of 'lā,' in the phrase 'am wallāhi la-af'alanna' and the like." End of quotation. It is not a negation. Al-Naqqash related from Ibn Mas'ud that he read "fitnatan an tuṣība" (a trial that it befall), and from al-Zubayr: "latuṣībanna."

Al-Mubarrad, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj explained the reading "lā tuṣībanna" as a prohibition, and the speech is complete at "wa-ittaqū fitnatan," which is a general address to the believers, and the speech ends there. Then the prohibition of the wrongdoers in particular is begun, against exposing themselves to wrongdoing, so that the trial afflicts them specifically. The prohibition is expressed by attributing it to the trial. It is a transferred prohibition, as they say: "lā arayannaka hāhunā" (let me not see you here), meaning: do not be here, so that my seeing you occurs. The intended meaning here is: the wrongdoer should not expose himself to the trial, so that its affliction befalls him specifically. Al-Zamakhshari said, in estimating this aspect: "If it is a prohibition after an imperative, it is as if it were said: 'Beware of a sin or a punishment.' Then it was said: 'Do not expose yourselves to wrongdoing, lest punishment or the effect of sin befall those among you who did wrong specifically.'"

Al-Akhfash said: "lā tuṣībanna" is in the sense of supplication. End of quotation. What seems to have led him to this, God knows best, is the improbability of the energetic nun entering a negation with "lā," and the desire to replace its estimate with a prohibition; so he turned to making it a supplication, and the meaning becomes: "May the trial not afflict the wrongdoers specifically." This requires a supplication against those who are not wrongdoers, so the estimate becomes: "May it not afflict a wrongdoer or a non-wrongdoer." It is as if it were said: "Guard against a trial that God has not brought upon anyone."

Thus the opinions on the derivation of "lā tuṣībanna" are summarized as: supplication and prohibition on two estimates, an answer to an imperative on two estimates, and a qualifier.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how is it permissible for the energetic nun to enter the answer to an imperative?" I say: because it has the sense of wishing. When you say: "Get down from the animal, lest it throw you off," the form "lā tuṭrahannaka" is permissible for that reason, and so are "lā tuṣībanna" and "lā yaḥṭimannakum." End of quotation. If you say "lā taṭrahka" and make it an answer to your saying "inzil" (get down), with no prohibition in it but pure negation, then the answer to the imperative is negated with "lā" and apocopated as an answer, according to the disagreement over the answer to the imperative. As for the six verbs, the condition is an implied condition indicated by the imperative, and what is mentioned with it has the sense of a condition. When we follow the position of the majority, that the verb negated with "lā" does not take the emphatic nun, it is not permissible to say: "Get down from the animal, lest it throw you off [with the nun]."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of 'min' in His saying 'alladhīna ẓalamū minkum khāṣṣatan' (those among you who did wrong specifically)?" I say: it is partitive on the first aspect, and explanatory on the second, because the meaning is: "it will not afflict you specifically for your wrongdoing, because wrongdoing from you is more reprehensible than from the rest of people." End of quotation. By "the first" he means that it is an answer after an imperative, and by "the second" that it is a prohibition after an imperative.

"Khāṣṣatan" (specifically) originally is a qualifier of a deleted verbal noun, meaning: a specific affliction. It is a circumstantial state of the implied subject in "lā tuṣībanna." It is also possible that it is a circumstantial state of "alladhīna ẓalamū," meaning: singled out by it, but it afflicts them and others. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that 'khāṣṣatan' is a circumstantial state of the pronoun in 'ẓalamū.' I do not understand this aspect."

[The verse continues:] "And know that God is severe in punishment" [Al-Baqara]. This is a severe threat appropriate to His saying "lā tuṣībanna alladhīna ẓalamū minkum khāṣṣatan," since it encourages steadfastness out of fear of God's punishment. It may be asked: how does the Merciful, the Generous, bring trial and punishment upon one who has not sinned? I answer: because it is a disposition by the decree of the King, as He may bring poverty and sickness upon His servant at the outset, and it is good of Him to do so. Or because He knew that this contains an increase of reward for the one upon whom it falls.

This address, on its apparent meaning, is general: guard against a trial that does not befall only the wrongdoer but affects both the righteous and the wicked. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "He commanded the believers not to tolerate wrongdoing among them, lest God afflict them all with punishment." In al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi [it is related] that "when people see the wrongdoer and do not take him by the hands, God is about to encompass them all with a punishment from Him." In Muslim, from the hadith of Zaynab bint Jahsh: she asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ), "Will we be destroyed while the righteous are among us?" He said: (p. 483) "Yes, when wickedness becomes widespread."

It is also said that the address is to the Companions; it is said to the people of Badr; it is said to 'Ali, 'Ammar, Talha and al-Zubayr; and it is said to two men of Quraysh, as reported by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, who did not name them. The trial here is fighting in the battle of the Camel, or misguidance, or failing to forbid evil, or [afflicting them] with wealth and children, or the spread of innovations, or punishment; these are the opinions. Al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam said on the day of the Camel: "I did not know that this verse was meant for us until today, and I used to think it applied only to those who were addressed by it at that time."

The clause "lā tuṣībanna" (lā tuṣībanna, "it will certainly not afflict") is declarative and is a qualifier of "fitnah" (a trial), meaning: a trial that does not afflict the wrongdoers alone. However, the attachment of the emphatic nun (nūn al-tawkīd, the energetic nun) to a negated verb with "lā" is disputed. The majority do not permit it and treat what has come of it as either a poetic necessity or a rarity. What we choose is that it is permissible, and this is the view of some grammarians. Since its attachment to a verb after "lā" without an intervening separator has been attested, as in the verse:

"Neither the one who enjoys bliss is left to his bliss,
nor does he refuse, if he is told 'praise me' and offered a bribe."

And:

"Nor is the one in misery left to his misery,
such that his complaint to Him benefits him if he complains."

Then its attachment with a separator is more likely, as in "lā tuṣībanna."

Al-Zamakhshari claimed that the clause is a qualifier and that it is a prohibition. He said: "Likewise, if you make it a qualifier with the sense of saying, it is as if it were said: 'Guard against a trial about which it is said: lā tuṣībanna.' A parallel to this is the verse:

'Until, when the darkness gathered and was mixed, they came with a mixture [of milk and water]: "Have you ever seen a wolf?"'

That is: with a mixture about which this statement is made, because in it there is the bluish color that is the meaning of 'wolf.'" End of quotation. The explanation is that the clause governs a deleted qualifier.

Al-Farra' claimed that the clause is an answer to the imperative, like your saying: "Get down from the animal, lest it throw you off" (lā taṭrahannaka), meaning: if you get down from it, it will not throw you off. He said: "From this is [the verse] 'Enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his soldiers crush you' [An-Naml: 18], meaning: if you enter, he will not crush you; and the nun entered because of the sense of conditionality in it." End of quotation. This example, with the verse "Enter your dwellings, lest they crush you" [An-Naml: 18], is not a parallel to "wa-ittaqū fitnatan," because the example fits the conditional form, while the verse is a condition and a consequence as he estimated; and this does not fit there. Do you not see that it is not valid to estimate: "If you guard against a trial, it will not afflict those among you who did wrong specifically"? Because in that case what follows the condition would be a consequence of the condition, whose intended meaning in terms of sense would be [different]. Al-Zamakhshari took al-Farra's opinion, added to its corruption, and became confused in it. He said: "His saying 'lā tuṣībanna' cannot be other than an answer to the imperative, or a prohibition after an imperative, or a qualifier of 'fitnah.' If it is an answer, the meaning is: if it befalls you, it will not befall the wrongdoers among you specifically, but it will encompass you all." End of quotation of this opinion. Observe how he estimated it to be an answer to the imperative "ittaqū," and then estimated the conditional particle attached to a non-imperfect form other than the imperfect of "ittaqū," saying: "The meaning is: if it befalls you, that is, the trial." Observe how al-Farra' estimated [the case of] "descend from the animal, lest it throw you off" and [the verse] "Enter your dwellings, lest they crush you," placing the conditional particle on the imperfect of an imperative verb. So too is estimated whatever is an answer to an imperative.

Some claimed that "lā tuṣībanna" is the answer to an implied oath. Others said that "lā" is a negation, and the negation was treated as affirmative, so the nun entered, as it entered in "latadribanna" (you will certainly strike). The estimate: "By God, it will certainly not afflict." According to the first opinion, that it is a qualifier, or an answer to an imperative, or an answer to an oath, the nun has entered a verb negated with "lā." Some grammarians held that it is the answer to an implied oath and that the clause is affirmative; the nun entered its place, the lām was lengthened and became "lā," and the meaning is "latuṣībanna" (it will surely afflict). This is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ali, Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Baqir, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Abu al-'Aliya: "latuṣībanna." In this there is a threat only to the wrongdoers. On this interpretation Ibn Jinni also explained the reading of the majority, "lā tuṣībanna," and that the lām was lengthened, so an alif came from it as a vowel-lengthening; for vowel-lengthening is characteristic of poetry. Ibn Jinni said regarding the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and those with him: it may be that this reading intends "lā tuṣībanna," with the alif deleted for lightness and by relying on the vowel, as they say: "am wallāhi" (by God). Al-Mahdawi said: "As the alif was deleted from 'mā,' which is a sister of 'lā,' in the phrase 'am wallāhi la-af'alanna' and the like." End of quotation. It is not a negation. Al-Naqqash related from Ibn Mas'ud that he read "fitnatan an tuṣība" (a trial that it befall), and from al-Zubayr: "latuṣībanna."

Al-Mubarrad, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj explained the reading "lā tuṣībanna" as a prohibition, and the speech is complete at "wa-ittaqū fitnatan," which is a general address to the believers, and the speech ends there. Then the prohibition of the wrongdoers in particular is begun, against exposing themselves to wrongdoing, so that the trial afflicts them specifically. The prohibition is expressed by attributing it to the trial. It is a transferred prohibition, as they say: "lā arayannaka hāhunā" (let me not see you here), meaning: do not be here, so that my seeing you occurs. The intended meaning here is: the wrongdoer should not expose himself to the trial, so that its affliction befalls him specifically. Al-Zamakhshari said, in estimating this aspect: "If it is a prohibition after an imperative, it is as if it were said: 'Beware of a sin or a punishment.' Then it was said: 'Do not expose yourselves to wrongdoing, lest punishment or the effect of sin befall those among you who did wrong specifically.'"

Al-Akhfash said: "lā tuṣībanna" is in the sense of supplication. End of quotation. What seems to have led him to this, God knows best, is the improbability of the energetic nun entering a negation with "lā," and the desire to replace its estimate with a prohibition; so he turned to making it a supplication, and the meaning becomes: "May the trial not afflict the wrongdoers specifically." This requires a supplication against those who are not wrongdoers, so the estimate becomes: "May it not afflict a wrongdoer or a non-wrongdoer." It is as if it were said: "Guard against a trial that God has not brought upon anyone."

Thus the opinions on the derivation of "lā tuṣībanna" are summarized as: supplication and prohibition on two estimates, an answer to an imperative on two estimates, and a qualifier.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how is it permissible for the energetic nun to enter the answer to an imperative?" I say: because it has the sense of wishing. When you say: "Get down from the animal, lest it throw you off," the form "lā tuṭrahannaka" is permissible for that reason, and so are "lā tuṣībanna" and "lā yaḥṭimannakum." End of quotation. If you say "lā taṭrahka" and make it an answer to your saying "inzil" (get down), with no prohibition in it but pure negation, then the answer to the imperative is negated with "lā" and apocopated as an answer, according to the disagreement over the answer to the imperative. As for the six verbs, the condition is an implied condition indicated by the imperative, and what is mentioned with it has the sense of a condition. When we follow the position of the majority, that the verb negated with "lā" does not take the emphatic nun, it is not permissible to say: "Get down from the animal, lest it throw you off [with the nun]."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of 'min' in His saying 'alladhīna ẓalamū minkum khāṣṣatan' (those among you who did wrong specifically)?" I say: it is partitive on the first aspect, and explanatory on the second, because the meaning is: "it will not afflict you specifically for your wrongdoing, because wrongdoing from you is more reprehensible than from the rest of people." End of quotation. By "the first" he means that it is an answer after an imperative, and by "the second" that it is a prohibition after an imperative.

"Khāṣṣatan" (specifically) originally is a qualifier of a deleted verbal noun, meaning: a specific affliction. It is a circumstantial state of the implied subject in "lā tuṣībanna." It is also possible that it is a circumstantial state of "alladhīna ẓalamū," meaning: singled out by it, but it afflicts them and others. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that 'khāṣṣatan' is a circumstantial state of the pronoun in 'ẓalamū.' I do not understand this aspect."

[The verse continues:] "And know that God is severe in punishment" [Al-Baqara]. This is a severe threat appropriate to His saying "lā tuṣībanna alladhīna ẓalamū minkum khāṣṣatan," since it encourages steadfastness out of fear of God's punishment. It may be asked: how does the Merciful, the Generous, bring trial and punishment upon one who has not sinned? I answer: because it is a disposition by the decree of the King, as He may bring poverty and sickness upon His servant at the outset, and it is good of Him to do so. Or because He knew that this contains an increase of reward for the one upon whom it falls.

﴿Remember when you were few and oppressed in the land, fearing that people would snatch you away, but He sheltered you, strengthened you with His help, and provided you with good things, so that you might give thanks﴾ [al-Anfal: 26]. It was revealed right after Badr. It was said: this address is specifically to the Muhajirun (Emigrants) who were in Makkah, few in number and subdued there, fearing that the polytheists would seize them. Ibn 'Abbas said: "He sheltered them in Madinah, and strengthened them with victory on the day of Badr." The good things (al-tayyibat) are the spoils of war and what was opened for them through it. It was also said: the address is to the Messenger and the Companions, and this describes their condition on the day of Badr. The good things are the spoils of war. The people (al-nas) are the army of Makkah and the rest of the neighboring tribes. Strengthening (al-ta'yid) is reinforcement with angels and overcoming the numerical advantage. Wahb and Qatadah said: the address is to all the Arabs, for they were the most naked of people in body, the most hungry in stomach, and the least well off in condition. "The people" are Persia and Rome. The shelter is prophethood and the Law (al-shari'ah), strengthening with victory is the conquest of lands and the defeat of kings, and the good things encompass food, drink, and clothing.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this interpretation is refuted by the fact that the Arabs, at the time this verse was revealed, were disbelievers except for a few, and the circumstances that this interpreter mentions had not yet arisen. It would only have been possible to address the Arabs with this verse at the end of the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. If someone applies this verse to the condition of the Arabs, then his application is correct. But that the condition of the Arabs was the cause of the revelation of the verse is far-fetched, for the reason we have mentioned. End of quote. This verse is a reminder of Allah's blessings upon them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "idh antum" is in the accusative as an object of "udhkuru" (remember), being an adverbial of time (zarf). Meaning: remember the time when you were few and humble. End of quote. In this there is a treatment of "idh" by making it an object, whereas it is one of the adverbs that cannot be used in this way except when times are attached to it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "idh" is an adverb of time for the governed element of "udhkuru", its implied meaning being: remember your state which was, or which is established, when you were few. It is not permissible for "idh" to be an adverb of time for "udhkuru", for "udhkuru" is only used in the sense of "idh" if we consider it an object. End of quote. This is a good explanation. Al-Hufi said: "idh antum" is an adverb of time whose governing element is "udhkuru". This cannot be correct at all, because "udhkur" refers to the future, so its adverb of time can only be future, while "idh" is a past adverb of time, and it is impossible for the future to occur within it. The clause "la'allakum tashkurun" (so that you may give thanks) is connected to His saying "fa-awakum" (He sheltered you) and what follows, meaning: He did this kindness in order to desire your gratitude.

﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts while you know﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and most of the scholars said: it was revealed concerning Abu Lubabah, when the Quraydhah asked his counsel when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wanted to expel them to Adhri'at and Arihā, as he had done with the Banu al-Nadir. Abu Lubabah pointed to his throat, meaning: the Messenger has nothing but slaughter. This was his betrayal, in a long story. Jabir said: it was about a man among the hypocrites who wrote to Abu Sufyan with some news of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah said: it was about the killing of 'Uthman. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is likely that the verse applies to his killing, for his killing was a betrayal of Allah, His Messenger, and the trusts. End of quote. It was also said: it was about Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah when he wrote to the people of Makkah informing them of the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ departure toward them. It was also said: it was about people who used to hear the speech of the Messenger and spread it until it reached the polytheists. Their betrayal of Allah is in not carrying out His commands and doing what He forbade in secret. The betrayal of the Messenger is in what was entrusted to them. The betrayal of trusts is neglecting them and not regarding them. It was also said: "and betray those in charge of your trusts" (wa-takhunu dhawi amanatikum). "While you know" (wa-antum ta'lamun) is a circumstantial clause (jumlah hāliyyah), meaning: while you know the consequence and the harm of that. So that would be further from you falling into betrayal, because one who knows what follows from sin is the farthest of people from it. It was also said: "while you know" means you know that betrayal is committed by you deliberately, not by mistake. It was also said: "while you are knowing" means you know the ugliness of the ugly and the goodness of the good.

They permitted "wa-takhunu" to be jussive (majzūm, in the jussive mood), as a conjunction to "la takhunu" (do not betray), and to be accusative (mansūb, in the subjunctive mood) as an answer to the prohibition. Its being jussive is the more preferred, because the accusative implies prohibiting the combination, while the jussive implies prohibiting each one individually. Mujahid read "amanatakum" in the singular, and this is narrated from Abu 'Amr.

﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial, and that with Allah is a great reward﴾. That is: the cause of falling into trial, which is sin, or punishment, or a test, and an examination for you, and how you guard His limits regarding them. Therefore, in the fact that the great reward is with Him, there is an indication that a person should not be tempted by his wealth and children, so that he prefers his love for them over what is with Allah, and so he gathers wealth and loves children until he prefers that. This is just as Abu Lubabah did, because his wealth and children were with the Banu Quraydhah.

﴿O you who have believed, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion (furqan) and will remove from you your misdeeds and forgive you. And Allah is the possessor of great bounty﴾. Furqan: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Qutaybah, and Malik as narrated from Ibn Wahb, Ibn al-Qasim, and Ashhab said: it means a way out (makhraj). Malik recited: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Talaq: 2]. The meaning is a way out in religion from misguidance. Mizrad ibn Dirar said:

"He hastened to the horizon before it would set, but when the night grew dark, he did not find a furqan."

Another said:

"What is for you, from the length of grief, a furqan, after dwellers who departed and separated?"

Another said:

"How can I hope for eternity while death is seeking me, and for me from the cup of death there is no furqan?"

Ibn Zayd and Ibn Ishaq said: a separation between truth and falsehood. Qatadah and others said: deliverance. Al-Farra' said: victory and triumph. In the Hereafter it means He will admit you into Paradise and the disbelievers into the Fire. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: a distinction between your truth and the falsehood of those who dispute with you, meaning through victory and support over them. Furqan is a verbal noun from "faraqa bayna al-shay'ayn" (he separated between two things), meaning he came between them. Al-Zamakhshari said: victory, because truth is distinguished from falsehood, and disbelief is distinguished by humiliating its party and Islam by honoring its people, and from this is His saying: ﴿the Day of the Criterion (yawm al-furqan)﴾. Or it means clarity and manifestation, showing your matter and making your fame and traces known in all parts of the earth. You say: "I kept doing such-and-such until the furqan shone," meaning until dawn broke. Or it means a way out from doubts, success, and expansion of hearts. Or a differentiation between you and others among the adherents of religions, and superiority and excellence in this world and the Hereafter. End of quote. The word "furqanan" is unrestricted, so it is suitable for whatever creates a distinction between believers and disbelievers in the matters of this world and the Hereafter. If the piety here is from avoiding the major sins, then the misdeeds are the minor sins, so that the condition and the reward differ. Its expiation is in this world, and its forgiveness, meaning its removal, is on the Day of Resurrection. The two circumstances differ so that there is no repetition. The explanation of ﴿And Allah is the possessor of great bounty﴾ was given earlier, in al-Baqarah.
