It was said: this address is specifically to the Muhajirun (Emigrants) who were in Makkah, few in number and subdued there, fearing that the polytheists would seize them. Ibn 'Abbas said: "He sheltered them in Madinah, and strengthened them with victory on the day of Badr." The good things (al-tayyibat) are the spoils of war and what was opened for them through it. It was also said: the address is to the Messenger and the Companions, and this describes their condition on the day of Badr. The good things are the spoils of war. The people (al-nas) are the army of Makkah and the rest of the neighboring tribes. Strengthening (al-ta'yid) is reinforcement with angels and overcoming the numerical advantage. Wahb and Qatadah said: the address is to all the Arabs, for they were the most naked of people in body, the most hungry in stomach, and the least well off in condition. "The people" are Persia and Rome. The shelter is prophethood and the Law (al-shari'ah), strengthening with victory is the conquest of lands and the defeat of kings, and the good things encompass food, drink, and clothing.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this interpretation is refuted by the fact that the Arabs, at the time this verse was revealed, were disbelievers except for a few, and the circumstances that this interpreter mentions had not yet arisen. It would only have been possible to address the Arabs with this verse at the end of the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. If someone applies this verse to the condition of the Arabs, then his application is correct. But that the condition of the Arabs was the cause of the revelation of the verse is far-fetched, for the reason we have mentioned. End of quote. This verse is a reminder of Allah's blessings upon them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "idh antum" is in the accusative as an object of "udhkuru" (remember), being an adverbial of time (zarf). Meaning: remember the time when you were few and humble. End of quote. In this there is a treatment of "idh" by making it an object, whereas it is one of the adverbs that cannot be used in this way except when times are attached to it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "idh" is an adverb of time for the governed element of "udhkuru", its implied meaning being: remember your state which was, or which is established, when you were few. It is not permissible for "idh" to be an adverb of time for "udhkuru", for "udhkuru" is only used in the sense of "idh" if we consider it an object. End of quote. This is a good explanation. Al-Hufi said: "idh antum" is an adverb of time whose governing element is "udhkuru". This cannot be correct at all, because "udhkur" refers to the future, so its adverb of time can only be future, while "idh" is a past adverb of time, and it is impossible for the future to occur within it. The clause "la'allakum tashkurun" (so that you may give thanks) is connected to His saying "fa-awakum" (He sheltered you) and what follows, meaning: He did this kindness in order to desire your gratitude.

﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts while you know﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and most of the scholars said: it was revealed concerning Abu Lubabah, when the Quraydhah asked his counsel when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wanted to expel them to Adhri'at and Arihā, as he had done with the Banu al-Nadir. Abu Lubabah pointed to his throat, meaning: the Messenger has nothing but slaughter. This was his betrayal, in a long story. Jabir said: it was about a man among the hypocrites who wrote to Abu Sufyan with some news of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah said: it was about the killing of 'Uthman. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is likely that the verse applies to his killing, for his killing was a betrayal of Allah, His Messenger, and the trusts. End of quote. It was also said: it was about Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah when he wrote to the people of Makkah informing them of the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ departure toward them. It was also said: it was about people who used to hear the speech of the Messenger and spread it until it reached the polytheists. Their betrayal of Allah is in not carrying out His commands and doing what He forbade in secret. The betrayal of the Messenger is in what was entrusted to them. The betrayal of trusts is neglecting them and not regarding them. It was also said: "and betray those in charge of your trusts" (wa-takhunu dhawi amanatikum). "While you know" (wa-antum ta'lamun) is a circumstantial clause (jumlah hāliyyah), meaning: while you know the consequence and the harm of that. So that would be further from you falling into betrayal, because one who knows what follows from sin is the farthest of people from it. It was also said: "while you know" means you know that betrayal is committed by you deliberately, not by mistake. It was also said: "while you are knowing" means you know the ugliness of the ugly and the goodness of the good.

They permitted "wa-takhunu" to be jussive (majzūm, in the jussive mood), as a conjunction to "la takhunu" (do not betray), and to be accusative (mansūb, in the subjunctive mood) as an answer to the prohibition. Its being jussive is the more preferred, because the accusative implies prohibiting the combination, while the jussive implies prohibiting each one individually. Mujahid read "amanatakum" in the singular, and this is narrated from Abu 'Amr.

﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial, and that with Allah is a great reward﴾. That is: the cause of falling into trial, which is sin, or punishment, or a test, and an examination for you, and how you guard His limits regarding them. Therefore, in the fact that the great reward is with Him, there is an indication that a person should not be tempted by his wealth and children, so that he prefers his love for them over what is with Allah, and so he gathers wealth and loves children until he prefers that. This is just as Abu Lubabah did, because his wealth and children were with the Banu Quraydhah.

﴿O you who have believed, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion (furqan) and will remove from you your misdeeds and forgive you. And Allah is the possessor of great bounty﴾. Furqan: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Qutaybah, and Malik as narrated from Ibn Wahb, Ibn al-Qasim, and Ashhab said: it means a way out (makhraj). Malik recited: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Talaq: 2]. The meaning is a way out in religion from misguidance. Mizrad ibn Dirar said:

"He hastened to the horizon before it would set, but when the night grew dark, he did not find a furqan."

Another said:

"What is for you, from the length of grief, a furqan, after dwellers who departed and separated?"

Another said:

"How can I hope for eternity while death is seeking me, and for me from the cup of death there is no furqan?"

Ibn Zayd and Ibn Ishaq said: a separation between truth and falsehood. Qatadah and others said: deliverance. Al-Farra' said: victory and triumph. In the Hereafter it means He will admit you into Paradise and the disbelievers into the Fire. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: a distinction between your truth and the falsehood of those who dispute with you, meaning through victory and support over them. Furqan is a verbal noun from "faraqa bayna al-shay'ayn" (he separated between two things), meaning he came between them. Al-Zamakhshari said: victory, because truth is distinguished from falsehood, and disbelief is distinguished by humiliating its party and Islam by honoring its people, and from this is His saying: ﴿the Day of the Criterion (yawm al-furqan)﴾. Or it means clarity and manifestation, showing your matter and making your fame and traces known in all parts of the earth. You say: "I kept doing such-and-such until the furqan shone," meaning until dawn broke. Or it means a way out from doubts, success, and expansion of hearts. Or a differentiation between you and others among the adherents of religions, and superiority and excellence in this world and the Hereafter. End of quote. The word "furqanan" is unrestricted, so it is suitable for whatever creates a distinction between believers and disbelievers in the matters of this world and the Hereafter. If the piety here is from avoiding the major sins, then the misdeeds are the minor sins, so that the condition and the reward differ. Its expiation is in this world, and its forgiveness, meaning its removal, is on the Day of Resurrection. The two circumstances differ so that there is no repetition. The explanation of ﴿And Allah is the possessor of great bounty﴾ was given earlier, in al-Baqarah.

﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to confine you or kill you or expel you. They plot, and Allah plots, and Allah is the best of plotters.﴾ Lamma dhakkara al-mu'minin ni'amahu 'alayhim, dhakkarahu ﷺ ni'amahu 'alayhi fi khassati nafsihi. Quraysh had consulted in Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh) about what to do with him. Some said: he should be imprisoned, bound, and made to await the calamities of fate (rayb al-manun). Others said: he should be expelled from Mecca, so that you may be rid of him. Iblis appeared in the form of an old man from Najd. It was also said that these were the two opinions. Another said: a man from every tribe should gather and strike him with a single blow with their swords, so that his blood would be scattered among the tribes, and the Banu Hashim would not be able to fight all of Quraysh, and so they would accept the blood-money (diyah). Iblis endorsed this opinion. Allah the Exalted then revealed this to His Prophet ﷺ, and commanded him not to sleep in his bed, and permitted him to leave for Medina. He commanded 'Ali to sleep in his bed and wrap himself in his cloak. They spent the night watching, and when they rushed to the bed, they saw 'Ali and were bewildered. He left 'Ali behind to return the deposits that were with him, and went out to Medina.

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: li-yuthbitūka means li-yuqayyidūka (to bind you). 'Ata' and al-Suddi said: li-yuthkhinūka means with wounding and beating, from their saying: "they beat him until they made him (uthbitahu) unable to move, neither stirring nor departing," and "he shot the bird and uthbitahu," i.e., wounded it (athkhanahu). The poet said:

"I said: Woe to you, what is in your document?
He said: The caliph has become wounded (muthbitan) and in pain."

That is, wounded (muthkhanan).

Al-Nakha'i read li-yubayyitūka, from al-bayat (to attack by night). This plotting here, by the consensus of the exegetes, is what Quraysh agreed upon in Dar al-Nadwa, as we have indicated. This verse is Medinan, like the rest of the surah, and this is the correct view. From 'Ikrimah and Mujahid it is reported that it is Meccan. From Ibn Zayd: it was revealed following Allah's sufficiency for His Messenger against the mockers. The statement of 'Ikrimah and Mujahid may be interpreted as meaning that they both referred to the story of the verse up to the time of its revelation. The word yamkurūna is repeated to indicate the continuation and abundance of their plotting. The explanation of the rest of the verse has already been given in Al 'Imran.

﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, they say: "We have heard. If we willed, we would say the like of this."﴾ The one who said this was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and many followed him in saying it. He was one of the rebellious men of Quraysh. He traveled to Persia and al-Hirah, and heard the stories of the monks and the Gospels, and the tales of Rustam and Isfandiyar. He saw the Jews and Christians bowing and prostrating. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had him killed in cold blood at al-Safra', at al-Uthayl, on his return from Badr. In this construction there is permissibility of the present tense occurring after idha with the past tense as its response, which is eloquent usage, unlike the particles of condition, for which this is not permitted except in poetry, as in:

"Whoever harms me with anything, I was from him..."

The meaning of "we have heard" is: we have heard and we do not obey, or: we have heard this from you. Their saying "if we willed" means: if we willed the speech, we would say the like of this which you recite. The reference is to what is recited, in the sense of the recited matter. This statement of theirs is by way of slander and confrontation, and it was not within their capacity. They were challenged to produce a surah like it and they were unable. The hardest thing for them was to be defeated, especially in the domain of eloquence. They used to compete with one another and oppose one another, and judgment was made between them in this. They were the most eager of people to subdue the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. How then could they make the opposing (of the Qur'an) depend on will, and excuse themselves by saying that if they had wished they would have said the like of this speech?!

﴿This is nothing but the tales of the ancients.﴾ Its explanation has already been given in al-An'am.

﴿And when they said: "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."﴾ The one who said this was al-Nadr; it was also said Abu Jahl. Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated it. The majority said: the speakers were the disbelievers of Quraysh. The reference in His saying "if this" is to the Qur'an, or to what the Messenger ﷺ brought of monotheism and other things, or to the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ among all of Quraysh — these are opinions. The discussion of "Allahumma" has already been given. Al-Jumhur read hua al-haqqa with the accusative, treating hua as a separator (fasl). Al-A'mash and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with the nominative, which is permissible in Arabic. Then the sentence is the predicate of kana, and this is the dialect of Tamim, who use the nominative after hua, which in the dialect of others is a separator, as he said:

"And you were over it in the assembly, you were more capable."

The discussion of the separator and its benefit has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqarah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is permissible in Arabic to read al-haqq in the nominative, as a predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of kana. Al-Zajjaj said: I do not know of anyone who read it with this permissible form, and the reading of the people is only with the accusative of al-haqq, end. Yet the one who read with the nominative has been mentioned. This conditional sentence contains great exaggeration in denying the truth, meaning: if it is truly the truth, then punish us for denying it by raining stones upon us or with another punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: their intent is to deny that it is the truth. When its being the truth is negated, the denier does not deserve punishment. So linking the punishment to its being the truth, while believing it is not the truth, is like linking it to the impossible, as in his saying: "if falsehood were the truth", while believing it is not the truth. His saying "it is the truth" is a mockery of one who says, in a specifying and definitive manner, "this is the truth." It is said: amtarat, like anjamat and asbalat; and matarat, like hatafat. The word for rain (amtar) is used in the sense of punishment. [Question]: What is the benefit of His saying "from the sky," since rain only comes from there? [Answer]: It is as if he meant to say: "rain down upon us sijjil (baked clay stones)", which are stones marked for punishment; the place of "stones from the sky" is the place of sijjil, just as one says: "he poured upon him a coat of mail of iron", meaning a breastplate, end. The meaning of his answer is that His saying "from the sky" came by way of emphasis, just as His saying "of iron" means emphasis, since a coat of mail is only of iron, just as rain is only from the sky.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: their saying "from the sky" is exaggeration and hyperbole, end. What appears to me is that the wisdom in their saying "from the sky" is that it corresponds to the rains coming from the direction from which it is said revelation comes to him. That is: you mention that revelation comes to you from the sky, so bring us a punishment from the direction from which revelation comes to you; for it would be fitting to express the sending of stones upon them from a direction other than the sky with their saying "rain down stones upon us." They said that by way of disdain and the belief that what he brought is not the truth. It was also said: by way of envy and obstinacy, while knowing that it is the truth. Ibn Furak rejected this second view, saying: no rational person says this out of obstinacy, end. It seems he did not read: "And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them" [al-Naml: 14]. And the story of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, and the rabbis of the Jews about whom Allah the Exalted said: "So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it" [al-Baqarah: 89]. And the saying of the Messenger ﷺ to them: "By Allah, you know that I am the Messenger of Allah," or words close to it. Their demanding these two kinds is in line with what the earlier nations demanded. A Jew asked Ibn 'Abbas: "Who are you from?" He said: "From Quraysh." He said: "You are from those who said: 'If this is indeed the truth from You...' (the verse)." Why did they not say: "Guide us to it?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "And you, O Israelite, are from those whose feet had not dried from the moisture of the sea in which Pharaoh and his people were drowned, and Moses and his people were saved, until they said: 'Make for us a god as they have gods' [al-A'raf: 138], and Moses said to them: 'Indeed you are a people who are ignorant' [al-A'raf: 138]." Then the Jew lowered his head, silenced. From Mu'awiyah it is reported that he said to a man from Saba': "How ignorant is your people, when they made a woman their king over them!" He said: "More ignorant than my people are your people, when they said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he called them to the truth: 'If this is indeed the truth' (the verse), and they did not say: 'Guide us to it.'"

﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them.﴾ This verse, up to "they know," was revealed in Mecca. It was also said: after the battle of Badr, narrating what occurred in it. Ibn Abza said: the first clause was in Mecca following His saying "with a painful punishment"; the second was when he left Mecca on his way to Medina, while believers remained in Mecca seeking forgiveness; and the third was after Badr, when the punishment became manifest upon them. When they linked the raining of stones or the coming of a painful punishment to the condition that what the Messenger ﷺ brought is the truth, Allah the Exalted informed that they deserve the punishment, but He would not punish them while you are among them, as an honor to him and in accordance with Allah's habit with those who deny their prophets, that He does not punish them while their prophets remain among them with a punishment that uproots them. Ibn 'Abbas said: no nation was ever punished while its prophet was among it. This is the view of the majority of the interpreters. So the meaning is: "Your nation would not be punished while you are among them. Rather your honor with your Lord is greater." Allah the Exalted said: "And We sent you not except as a mercy to the worlds" [al-Anbiya': 107], and of His mercy, the Exalted, is that He does not punish them while the Messenger ﷺ is among them. Since raining stones upon them falls within punishment, the negation applied to the punishment of which the raining of stones is a kind. Thus He said: "And Allah would not punish them," and the construction did not come as: "Allah would not rain down or bring a punishment." The restriction of the negation of punishment to the presence of the Messenger among them is an indication that if he were not among them and left them, He would punish them; but He did not punish them out of honor to him, while they were in the position of those who would be punished for their denial. Ibn 'Atiyyah said, from Abu Zayd: "I heard from the Arabs one who says: 'wa-ma kana Allahu liyu'adhdhibahum,' with a fatha on the lam," which is an unknown dialect, not used in the Qur'an, end. With a fatha on the lam in liyu'adhdhibahum, Abu al-Sammal read it. 'Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, read with a fatha on the lam of command in His saying: "let man look at his food" [Abasa: 24]. Ibn Mujahid narrated from Abu Zayd that some Arabs put a fatha on every lam except in such as "al-hamdu lillah," end, meaning the lam of genitive when it enters a noun or the first-person suffix. The usage of "fihim" (among them) as a container is metaphorical, and the meaning is: while you are residing among them, not departing from them.

[p. 488]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verse 30–34 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And Allah would not punish them while you were among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness.﴾ Observe the fine arrangement of these two clauses. Since His presence among them was the reason for the negation of their punishment, He emphasized the predicate of kana (was) with the lam (of emphasis) according to the view of the Kufans; or He made the predicate of kana the negated desire (irada) according to the view of the Basrans. The negation of the desire to punish is more emphatic than the negation of punishment itself. As for their seeking forgiveness, since it falls short of that noble presence, it was not emphasized with the lam; rather, the predicate of kana is His saying "punishing them" (mu'adhdhibahum). Thus, there is a great difference between their seeking forgiveness and his ﷺ presence among them.

Apparently, all these pronouns in the clauses refer to the disbelievers. This is the view of Qatadah. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abza, Abu Malik and al-Dahhak said something whose implication is that the pronoun in His saying "punishing them" refers to the disbelievers of Makkah, and the pronoun in His saying "while they" refers to the believers who remained after the Messenger ﷺ in Makkah. That is: "Allah would not punish the disbelievers while believers are among them, seeking forgiveness." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "What defeats the beginning of this view is that the believers to whom the pronoun refers have not been mentioned beforehand."

Ibn 'Abbas also said something whose implication is that both pronouns refer to the disbelievers, and that they used to say in their supplications: "Forgive us (ghufranaka)," and say: "Here I am, You have no partner (labbayka la sharika laka)," and similar things which are supplication and seeking forgiveness. So Allah made this a security from the punishment of this world. Upon this, the statement of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Ibn 'Abbas is composed: Allah made two securities from the punishment of this world: the presence of the Messenger ﷺ among the people, and seeking forgiveness. The first was removed, and seeking forgiveness remained until the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Zajjaj and what was reported from Ibn 'Abbas said: "while they seek forgiveness" refers to the disbelievers, and what is meant by it is those for whom it was already decreed in Allah's knowledge that they would embrace Islam and seek forgiveness. So the meaning is: Allah would not punish the disbelievers, and among them are those who seek forgiveness and believe in a second state.

Mujahid said: "while they seek forgiveness," that is: "and their offspring seek forgiveness and believe," so it is attributed to them because their offspring are from them. Istighfar is the seeking of forgiveness (talab al-ghufran).

Al-Dahhak and Mujahid said: the meaning of yastaghfirun is "they pray" (yusallun). 'Ikrimah and Mujahid also said: "they submit (to Islam)" (yuslimun).

The apparent meaning of His saying "while they seek forgiveness" is that they are engaged in seeking forgiveness, that is: they seek forgiveness and so are not punished, just as the Messenger is among them and so they are not punished. Both states exist: the presence of the Messenger among them and their seeking forgiveness.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "while they seek forgiveness" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and its meaning is the negation of seeking forgiveness from them, that is: even if they were among those who believe and seek forgiveness from disbelief, He would not punish them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers﴾ [Hud: 117]. "But they do not seek forgiveness nor do they believe, and this is not expected of them." End of quote. What he said had been preceded to it by others, who said: the meaning is: "while they are in a state of repentance and seeking forgiveness from their disbelief, had that occurred from them." Al-Tabari chose this, and it is narrated from Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

﴿And what is wrong with them that Allah should not punish them, while they bar (people) from the Sacred Mosque, and they were not its guardians? Its guardians are only the God-fearing, but most of them do not know.﴾ Apparently, "ma" is interrogative, meaning: "What is it for them regarding the negation of punishment?" It is an interrogative whose meaning is affirmation (taqrir), that is: how could they not be punished while they are characterized by this state which calls for punishment, namely their barring the believers from the Sacred Mosque, while they are not its custodians, nor qualified for its guardianship. Among their barring is what they did to the Messenger ﷺ in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, and his expulsion along with the believers falls within the barring. They used to say: "We are the custodians of the House; we bar whom we wish and admit whom we wish." "An" is a verbal particle (masdariyyah). Al-Akhfash said: it is extra (za'idah). Al-Nahhas said: "If it were as he said, it would have raised their punishment," end of quote, so the verb would be in the position of a circumstantial clause, like His saying: ﴿And what is it with us that we do not believe in Allah?﴾ The position of "an" is accusative, or genitive according to the disagreement, since "fi" has been omitted from it; it is connected to what is connected to "lahum," that is: "What thing exists or is established for them regarding Allah not punishing them?" The meaning is: they have no share in the negation of punishment, and when that is negated, they will certainly be punished. Al-Tabari's estimate, "what prevents them from being punished," is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of grammatical analysis. Similarly, the statement of Ibn 'Atiyyah should be interpreted as: "What is their power," and similar verbs necessitate that it be in the accusative position.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in "its guardians" (awliyahu) is to the Sacred Mosque, due to its proximity and the soundness of the meaning. It was also said: "ma" is for negation, and then it is informative, that is: "and they do not have that Allah should not punish them," that is: punishment is not negated from them while they are characterized by this state. It was also said: the pronoun in "awliyahu" refers to Allah, the Exalted; this was narrated from al-Hasan. The apparent meaning of His saying "and they were not its guardians" is a resumptive informative statement, that is: they did not deserve to be its guardians. ﴿Its guardians are only the God-fearing﴾, that is: those who are God-fearing with respect to shirk. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its guardians are only the God-fearing" among the Muslims; not every Muslim is also among those fit to be in charge of it; only one who is righteous and pious deserves its guardianship, so how about idol-worshippers? End of quote. It is permissible that "and they were not its guardians" be conjoined to "while they bar," making it a circumstantial clause, and the meaning is: how could Allah not punish them while they are characterized by these two attributes: their barring from the Sacred Mosque and the negation of their being its guardians, that is, guardians of the Mosque, meaning they are not its custodians, so they should not bar from it; or the guardians of Allah, in which case they are disbelievers, and thus it ascends from one state to a greater one, namely that they are not believers. Whoever bars from the Mosque while being a disbeliever in Allah is deserving of punishment. The pronoun in "its guardians" (in awliyahu) is consequent upon what it refers to in His saying "and they were not its guardians."

They differed regarding this punishment. Some people said: it is the first, except that it had been prevented by two things: the presence of the Prophet among them and the seeking of forgiveness by those among them who were believers. When distinction took place through the Hijrah, the punishment fell upon the rest at the Day of Badr. It was also said: rather it occurred with the conquest of Makkah. Others said: this punishment is other than that. The first is the complete annihilation of all of them, which did not happen because of the knowledge of the Islam of some of them and the Islam of some of their descendants. The second is the killing of some of them on the Day of Badr. Ibn 'Abbas said: the first is the punishment of this world, and the second is the punishment of the Hereafter. So the meaning: Allah would not be the punisher of the polytheists, because of their seeking forgiveness in this world, and it is not for them that Allah should not punish them in the Hereafter.

The object of "la ya'lamun" (they do not know) is omitted; its estimate: they do not know that they are not its guardians, but rather they think that they are its guardians. The apparent sense is the exception of "most" in the negation of knowledge, since among them, and within their midst, there were those who inclined toward faith, so he would know that those barring are not the guardians of the House or the guardians of Allah. So it is as if it was said: "But most of them," that is: most of those residing in Makkah "do not know," in order to exclude from them al-'Abbas, Umm al-Fadl and others who had knowledge; or because among them were those who knew it but obstinately opposed it seeking leadership. Or "most" is intended to mean all, figuratively, as if it was said: "but they do not know," just as it is said: "Hardly any man says that," in the sense of pure negation. Keeping "most" on its apparent meaning is more appropriate, and that "most" is intended to mean all is the interpretation of al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah.

﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to confine you or kill you or expel you. They plot, and Allah plots, and Allah is the best of plotters.﴾ Lamma dhakkara al-mu'minin ni'amahu 'alayhim, dhakkarahu ﷺ ni'amahu 'alayhi fi khassati nafsihi. Quraysh had consulted in Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh) about what to do with him. Some said: he should be imprisoned, bound, and made to await the calamities of fate (rayb al-manun). Others said: he should be expelled from Mecca, so that you may be rid of him. Iblis appeared in the form of an old man from Najd. It was also said that these were the two opinions. Another said: a man from every tribe should gather and strike him with a single blow with their swords, so that his blood would be scattered among the tribes, and the Banu Hashim would not be able to fight all of Quraysh, and so they would accept the blood-money (diyah). Iblis endorsed this opinion. Allah the Exalted then revealed this to His Prophet ﷺ, and commanded him not to sleep in his bed, and permitted him to leave for Medina. He commanded 'Ali to sleep in his bed and wrap himself in his cloak. They spent the night watching, and when they rushed to the bed, they saw 'Ali and were bewildered. He left 'Ali behind to return the deposits that were with him, and went out to Medina.

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: li-yuthbitūka means li-yuqayyidūka (to bind you). 'Ata' and al-Suddi said: li-yuthkhinūka means with wounding and beating, from their saying: "they beat him until they made him (uthbitahu) unable to move, neither stirring nor departing," and "he shot the bird and uthbitahu," i.e., wounded it (athkhanahu). The poet said:

"I said: Woe to you, what is in your document?
He said: The caliph has become wounded (muthbitan) and in pain."

That is, wounded (muthkhanan).

Al-Nakha'i read li-yubayyitūka, from al-bayat (to attack by night). This plotting here, by the consensus of the exegetes, is what Quraysh agreed upon in Dar al-Nadwa, as we have indicated. This verse is Medinan, like the rest of the surah, and this is the correct view. From 'Ikrimah and Mujahid it is reported that it is Meccan. From Ibn Zayd: it was revealed following Allah's sufficiency for His Messenger against the mockers. The statement of 'Ikrimah and Mujahid may be interpreted as meaning that they both referred to the story of the verse up to the time of its revelation. The word yamkurūna is repeated to indicate the continuation and abundance of their plotting. The explanation of the rest of the verse has already been given in Al 'Imran.

﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, they say: "We have heard. If we willed, we would say the like of this."﴾ The one who said this was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and many followed him in saying it. He was one of the rebellious men of Quraysh. He traveled to Persia and al-Hirah, and heard the stories of the monks and the Gospels, and the tales of Rustam and Isfandiyar. He saw the Jews and Christians bowing and prostrating. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had him killed in cold blood at al-Safra', at al-Uthayl, on his return from Badr. In this construction there is permissibility of the present tense occurring after idha with the past tense as its response, which is eloquent usage, unlike the particles of condition, for which this is not permitted except in poetry, as in:

"Whoever harms me with anything, I was from him..."

The meaning of "we have heard" is: we have heard and we do not obey, or: we have heard this from you. Their saying "if we willed" means: if we willed the speech, we would say the like of this which you recite. The reference is to what is recited, in the sense of the recited matter. This statement of theirs is by way of slander and confrontation, and it was not within their capacity. They were challenged to produce a surah like it and they were unable. The hardest thing for them was to be defeated, especially in the domain of eloquence. They used to compete with one another and oppose one another, and judgment was made between them in this. They were the most eager of people to subdue the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. How then could they make the opposing (of the Qur'an) depend on will, and excuse themselves by saying that if they had wished they would have said the like of this speech?!

﴿This is nothing but the tales of the ancients.﴾ Its explanation has already been given in al-An'am.

﴿And when they said: "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."﴾ The one who said this was al-Nadr; it was also said Abu Jahl. Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated it. The majority said: the speakers were the disbelievers of Quraysh. The reference in His saying "if this" is to the Qur'an, or to what the Messenger ﷺ brought of monotheism and other things, or to the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ among all of Quraysh — these are opinions. The discussion of "Allahumma" has already been given. Al-Jumhur read hua al-haqqa with the accusative, treating hua as a separator (fasl). Al-A'mash and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with the nominative, which is permissible in Arabic. Then the sentence is the predicate of kana, and this is the dialect of Tamim, who use the nominative after hua, which in the dialect of others is a separator, as he said:

"And you were over it in the assembly, you were more capable."

The discussion of the separator and its benefit has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqarah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is permissible in Arabic to read al-haqq in the nominative, as a predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of kana. Al-Zajjaj said: I do not know of anyone who read it with this permissible form, and the reading of the people is only with the accusative of al-haqq, end. Yet the one who read with the nominative has been mentioned. This conditional sentence contains great exaggeration in denying the truth, meaning: if it is truly the truth, then punish us for denying it by raining stones upon us or with another punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: their intent is to deny that it is the truth. When its being the truth is negated, the denier does not deserve punishment. So linking the punishment to its being the truth, while believing it is not the truth, is like linking it to the impossible, as in his saying: "if falsehood were the truth", while believing it is not the truth. His saying "it is the truth" is a mockery of one who says, in a specifying and definitive manner, "this is the truth." It is said: amtarat, like anjamat and asbalat; and matarat, like hatafat. The word for rain (amtar) is used in the sense of punishment. [Question]: What is the benefit of His saying "from the sky," since rain only comes from there? [Answer]: It is as if he meant to say: "rain down upon us sijjil (baked clay stones)", which are stones marked for punishment; the place of "stones from the sky" is the place of sijjil, just as one says: "he poured upon him a coat of mail of iron", meaning a breastplate, end. The meaning of his answer is that His saying "from the sky" came by way of emphasis, just as His saying "of iron" means emphasis, since a coat of mail is only of iron, just as rain is only from the sky.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: their saying "from the sky" is exaggeration and hyperbole, end. What appears to me is that the wisdom in their saying "from the sky" is that it corresponds to the rains coming from the direction from which it is said revelation comes to him. That is: you mention that revelation comes to you from the sky, so bring us a punishment from the direction from which revelation comes to you; for it would be fitting to express the sending of stones upon them from a direction other than the sky with their saying "rain down stones upon us." They said that by way of disdain and the belief that what he brought is not the truth. It was also said: by way of envy and obstinacy, while knowing that it is the truth. Ibn Furak rejected this second view, saying: no rational person says this out of obstinacy, end. It seems he did not read: "And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them" [al-Naml: 14]. And the story of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, and the rabbis of the Jews about whom Allah the Exalted said: "So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it" [al-Baqarah: 89]. And the saying of the Messenger ﷺ to them: "By Allah, you know that I am the Messenger of Allah," or words close to it. Their demanding these two kinds is in line with what the earlier nations demanded. A Jew asked Ibn 'Abbas: "Who are you from?" He said: "From Quraysh." He said: "You are from those who said: 'If this is indeed the truth from You...' (the verse)." Why did they not say: "Guide us to it?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "And you, O Israelite, are from those whose feet had not dried from the moisture of the sea in which Pharaoh and his people were drowned, and Moses and his people were saved, until they said: 'Make for us a god as they have gods' [al-A'raf: 138], and Moses said to them: 'Indeed you are a people who are ignorant' [al-A'raf: 138]." Then the Jew lowered his head, silenced. From Mu'awiyah it is reported that he said to a man from Saba': "How ignorant is your people, when they made a woman their king over them!" He said: "More ignorant than my people are your people, when they said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he called them to the truth: 'If this is indeed the truth' (the verse), and they did not say: 'Guide us to it.'"

﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them.﴾ This verse, up to "they know," was revealed in Mecca. It was also said: after the battle of Badr, narrating what occurred in it. Ibn Abza said: the first clause was in Mecca following His saying "with a painful punishment"; the second was when he left Mecca on his way to Medina, while believers remained in Mecca seeking forgiveness; and the third was after Badr, when the punishment became manifest upon them. When they linked the raining of stones or the coming of a painful punishment to the condition that what the Messenger ﷺ brought is the truth, Allah the Exalted informed that they deserve the punishment, but He would not punish them while you are among them, as an honor to him and in accordance with Allah's habit with those who deny their prophets, that He does not punish them while their prophets remain among them with a punishment that uproots them. Ibn 'Abbas said: no nation was ever punished while its prophet was among it. This is the view of the majority of the interpreters. So the meaning is: "Your nation would not be punished while you are among them. Rather your honor with your Lord is greater." Allah the Exalted said: "And We sent you not except as a mercy to the worlds" [al-Anbiya': 107], and of His mercy, the Exalted, is that He does not punish them while the Messenger ﷺ is among them. Since raining stones upon them falls within punishment, the negation applied to the punishment of which the raining of stones is a kind. Thus He said: "And Allah would not punish them," and the construction did not come as: "Allah would not rain down or bring a punishment." The restriction of the negation of punishment to the presence of the Messenger among them is an indication that if he were not among them and left them, He would punish them; but He did not punish them out of honor to him, while they were in the position of those who would be punished for their denial. Ibn 'Atiyyah said, from Abu Zayd: "I heard from the Arabs one who says: 'wa-ma kana Allahu liyu'adhdhibahum,' with a fatha on the lam," which is an unknown dialect, not used in the Qur'an, end. With a fatha on the lam in liyu'adhdhibahum, Abu al-Sammal read it. 'Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, read with a fatha on the lam of command in His saying: "let man look at his food" [Abasa: 24]. Ibn Mujahid narrated from Abu Zayd that some Arabs put a fatha on every lam except in such as "al-hamdu lillah," end, meaning the lam of genitive when it enters a noun or the first-person suffix. The usage of "fihim" (among them) as a container is metaphorical, and the meaning is: while you are residing among them, not departing from them.

[p. 488]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verse 30–34 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And Allah would not punish them while you were among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness.﴾ Observe the fine arrangement of these two clauses. Since His presence among them was the reason for the negation of their punishment, He emphasized the predicate of kana (was) with the lam (of emphasis) according to the view of the Kufans; or He made the predicate of kana the negated desire (irada) according to the view of the Basrans. The negation of the desire to punish is more emphatic than the negation of punishment itself. As for their seeking forgiveness, since it falls short of that noble presence, it was not emphasized with the lam; rather, the predicate of kana is His saying "punishing them" (mu'adhdhibahum). Thus, there is a great difference between their seeking forgiveness and his ﷺ presence among them.

Apparently, all these pronouns in the clauses refer to the disbelievers. This is the view of Qatadah. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abza, Abu Malik and al-Dahhak said something whose implication is that the pronoun in His saying "punishing them" refers to the disbelievers of Makkah, and the pronoun in His saying "while they" refers to the believers who remained after the Messenger ﷺ in Makkah. That is: "Allah would not punish the disbelievers while believers are among them, seeking forgiveness." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "What defeats the beginning of this view is that the believers to whom the pronoun refers have not been mentioned beforehand."

Ibn 'Abbas also said something whose implication is that both pronouns refer to the disbelievers, and that they used to say in their supplications: "Forgive us (ghufranaka)," and say: "Here I am, You have no partner (labbayka la sharika laka)," and similar things which are supplication and seeking forgiveness. So Allah made this a security from the punishment of this world. Upon this, the statement of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Ibn 'Abbas is composed: Allah made two securities from the punishment of this world: the presence of the Messenger ﷺ among the people, and seeking forgiveness. The first was removed, and seeking forgiveness remained until the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Zajjaj and what was reported from Ibn 'Abbas said: "while they seek forgiveness" refers to the disbelievers, and what is meant by it is those for whom it was already decreed in Allah's knowledge that they would embrace Islam and seek forgiveness. So the meaning is: Allah would not punish the disbelievers, and among them are those who seek forgiveness and believe in a second state.

Mujahid said: "while they seek forgiveness," that is: "and their offspring seek forgiveness and believe," so it is attributed to them because their offspring are from them. Istighfar is the seeking of forgiveness (talab al-ghufran).

Al-Dahhak and Mujahid said: the meaning of yastaghfirun is "they pray" (yusallun). 'Ikrimah and Mujahid also said: "they submit (to Islam)" (yuslimun).

The apparent meaning of His saying "while they seek forgiveness" is that they are engaged in seeking forgiveness, that is: they seek forgiveness and so are not punished, just as the Messenger is among them and so they are not punished. Both states exist: the presence of the Messenger among them and their seeking forgiveness.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "while they seek forgiveness" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and its meaning is the negation of seeking forgiveness from them, that is: even if they were among those who believe and seek forgiveness from disbelief, He would not punish them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers﴾ [Hud: 117]. "But they do not seek forgiveness nor do they believe, and this is not expected of them." End of quote. What he said had been preceded to it by others, who said: the meaning is: "while they are in a state of repentance and seeking forgiveness from their disbelief, had that occurred from them." Al-Tabari chose this, and it is narrated from Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

﴿And what is wrong with them that Allah should not punish them, while they bar (people) from the Sacred Mosque, and they were not its guardians? Its guardians are only the God-fearing, but most of them do not know.﴾ Apparently, "ma" is interrogative, meaning: "What is it for them regarding the negation of punishment?" It is an interrogative whose meaning is affirmation (taqrir), that is: how could they not be punished while they are characterized by this state which calls for punishment, namely their barring the believers from the Sacred Mosque, while they are not its custodians, nor qualified for its guardianship. Among their barring is what they did to the Messenger ﷺ in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, and his expulsion along with the believers falls within the barring. They used to say: "We are the custodians of the House; we bar whom we wish and admit whom we wish." "An" is a verbal particle (masdariyyah). Al-Akhfash said: it is extra (za'idah). Al-Nahhas said: "If it were as he said, it would have raised their punishment," end of quote, so the verb would be in the position of a circumstantial clause, like His saying: ﴿And what is it with us that we do not believe in Allah?﴾ The position of "an" is accusative, or genitive according to the disagreement, since "fi" has been omitted from it; it is connected to what is connected to "lahum," that is: "What thing exists or is established for them regarding Allah not punishing them?" The meaning is: they have no share in the negation of punishment, and when that is negated, they will certainly be punished. Al-Tabari's estimate, "what prevents them from being punished," is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of grammatical analysis. Similarly, the statement of Ibn 'Atiyyah should be interpreted as: "What is their power," and similar verbs necessitate that it be in the accusative position.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in "its guardians" (awliyahu) is to the Sacred Mosque, due to its proximity and the soundness of the meaning. It was also said: "ma" is for negation, and then it is informative, that is: "and they do not have that Allah should not punish them," that is: punishment is not negated from them while they are characterized by this state. It was also said: the pronoun in "awliyahu" refers to Allah, the Exalted; this was narrated from al-Hasan. The apparent meaning of His saying "and they were not its guardians" is a resumptive informative statement, that is: they did not deserve to be its guardians. ﴿Its guardians are only the God-fearing﴾, that is: those who are God-fearing with respect to shirk. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its guardians are only the God-fearing" among the Muslims; not every Muslim is also among those fit to be in charge of it; only one who is righteous and pious deserves its guardianship, so how about idol-worshippers? End of quote. It is permissible that "and they were not its guardians" be conjoined to "while they bar," making it a circumstantial clause, and the meaning is: how could Allah not punish them while they are characterized by these two attributes: their barring from the Sacred Mosque and the negation of their being its guardians, that is, guardians of the Mosque, meaning they are not its custodians, so they should not bar from it; or the guardians of Allah, in which case they are disbelievers, and thus it ascends from one state to a greater one, namely that they are not believers. Whoever bars from the Mosque while being a disbeliever in Allah is deserving of punishment. The pronoun in "its guardians" (in awliyahu) is consequent upon what it refers to in His saying "and they were not its guardians."

They differed regarding this punishment. Some people said: it is the first, except that it had been prevented by two things: the presence of the Prophet among them and the seeking of forgiveness by those among them who were believers. When distinction took place through the Hijrah, the punishment fell upon the rest at the Day of Badr. It was also said: rather it occurred with the conquest of Makkah. Others said: this punishment is other than that. The first is the complete annihilation of all of them, which did not happen because of the knowledge of the Islam of some of them and the Islam of some of their descendants. The second is the killing of some of them on the Day of Badr. Ibn 'Abbas said: the first is the punishment of this world, and the second is the punishment of the Hereafter. So the meaning: Allah would not be the punisher of the polytheists, because of their seeking forgiveness in this world, and it is not for them that Allah should not punish them in the Hereafter.

The object of "la ya'lamun" (they do not know) is omitted; its estimate: they do not know that they are not its guardians, but rather they think that they are its guardians. The apparent sense is the exception of "most" in the negation of knowledge, since among them, and within their midst, there were those who inclined toward faith, so he would know that those barring are not the guardians of the House or the guardians of Allah. So it is as if it was said: "But most of them," that is: most of those residing in Makkah "do not know," in order to exclude from them al-'Abbas, Umm al-Fadl and others who had knowledge; or because among them were those who knew it but obstinately opposed it seeking leadership. Or "most" is intended to mean all, figuratively, as if it was said: "but they do not know," just as it is said: "Hardly any man says that," in the sense of pure negation. Keeping "most" on its apparent meaning is more appropriate, and that "most" is intended to mean all is the interpretation of al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah.

﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to confine you or kill you or expel you. They plot, and Allah plots, and Allah is the best of plotters.﴾ Lamma dhakkara al-mu'minin ni'amahu 'alayhim, dhakkarahu ﷺ ni'amahu 'alayhi fi khassati nafsihi. He said: "You are from those who said: 'If this is indeed the truth from You...' (the verse)." Why did they not say: "Guide us to it?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "And you, O Israelite, are from those whose feet had not dried from the moisture of the sea in which Pharaoh and his people were drowned, and Moses and his people were saved, until they said: 'Make for us a god as they have gods' [al-A'raf: 138], and Moses said to them: 'Indeed you are a people who are ignorant' [al-A'raf: 138]." Then the Jew lowered his head, silenced. From Mu'awiyah it is reported that he said to a man from Saba': "How ignorant is your people, when they made a woman their king over them!" He said: "More ignorant than my people are your people, when they said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he called them to the truth: 'If this is indeed the truth' (the verse), and they did not say: 'Guide us to it.'"

﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them.﴾ This verse, up to "they know," was revealed in Mecca. It was also said: after the battle of Badr, narrating what occurred in it. Ibn Abza said: the first clause was in Mecca following His saying "with a painful punishment"; the second was when he left Mecca on his way to Medina, while believers remained in Mecca seeking forgiveness; and the third was after Badr, when the punishment became manifest upon them. When they linked the raining of stones or the coming of a painful punishment to the condition that what the Messenger ﷺ brought is the truth, Allah the Exalted informed that they deserve the punishment, but He would not punish them while you are among them, as an honor to him and in accordance with Allah's habit with those who deny their prophets, that He does not punish them while their prophets remain among them with a punishment that uproots them. Ibn 'Abbas said: no nation was ever punished while its prophet was among it. This is the view of the majority of the interpreters. So the meaning is: "Your nation would not be punished while you are among them. Rather your honor with your Lord is greater." Allah the Exalted said: "And We sent you not except as a mercy to the worlds" [al-Anbiya': 107], and of His mercy, the Exalted, is that He does not punish them while the Messenger ﷺ is among them. Since raining stones upon them falls within punishment, the negation applied to the punishment of which the raining of stones is a kind. Thus He said: "And Allah would not punish them," and the construction did not come as: "Allah would not rain down or bring a punishment." The restriction of the negation of punishment to the presence of the Messenger among them is an indication that if he were not among them and left them, He would punish them; but He did not punish them out of honor to him, while they were in the position of those who would be punished for their denial. Ibn 'Atiyyah said, from Abu Zayd: "I heard from the Arabs one who says: 'wa-ma kana Allahu liyu'adhdhibahum,' with a fatha on the lam," which is an unknown dialect, not used in the Qur'an, end. With a fatha on the lam in liyu'adhdhibahum, Abu al-Sammal read it. 'Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, read with a fatha on the lam of command in His saying: "let man look at his food" [Abasa: 24]. Ibn Mujahid narrated from Abu Zayd that some Arabs put a fatha on every lam except in such as "al-hamdu lillah," end, meaning the lam of genitive when it enters a noun or the first-person suffix. The usage of "fihim" (among them) as a container is metaphorical, and the meaning is: while you are residing among them, not departing from them.

[p. 488]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verse 30–34 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And Allah would not punish them while you were among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness.﴾ Observe the fine arrangement of these two clauses. Since His presence among them was the reason for the negation of their punishment, He emphasized the predicate of kana (was) with the lam (of emphasis) according to the view of the Kufans; or He made the predicate of kana the negated desire (irada) according to the view of the Basrans. The negation of the desire to punish is more emphatic than the negation of punishment itself. As for their seeking forgiveness, since it falls short of that noble presence, it was not emphasized with the lam; rather, the predicate of kana is His saying "punishing them" (mu'adhdhibahum). Thus, there is a great difference between their seeking forgiveness and his ﷺ presence among them.

Apparently, all these pronouns in the clauses refer to the disbelievers. This is the view of Qatadah. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abza, Abu Malik and al-Dahhak said something whose implication is that the pronoun in His saying "punishing them" refers to the disbelievers of Makkah, and the pronoun in His saying "while they" refers to the believers who remained after the Messenger ﷺ in Makkah. That is: "Allah would not punish the disbelievers while believers are among them, seeking forgiveness." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "What defeats the beginning of this view is that the believers to whom the pronoun refers have not been mentioned beforehand."

Ibn 'Abbas also said something whose implication is that both pronouns refer to the disbelievers, and that they used to say in their supplications: "Forgive us (ghufranaka)," and say: "Here I am, You have no partner (labbayka la sharika laka)," and similar things which are supplication and seeking forgiveness. So Allah made this a security from the punishment of this world. Upon this, the statement of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Ibn 'Abbas is composed: Allah made two securities from the punishment of this world: the presence of the Messenger ﷺ among the people, and seeking forgiveness. The first was removed, and seeking forgiveness remained until the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Zajjaj and what was reported from Ibn 'Abbas said: "while they seek forgiveness" refers to the disbelievers, and what is meant by it is those for whom it was already decreed in Allah's knowledge that they would embrace Islam and seek forgiveness. So the meaning is: Allah would not punish the disbelievers, and among them are those who seek forgiveness and believe in a second state.

Mujahid said: "while they seek forgiveness," that is: "and their offspring seek forgiveness and believe," so it is attributed to them because their offspring are from them. Istighfar is the seeking of forgiveness (talab al-ghufran).

Al-Dahhak and Mujahid said: the meaning of yastaghfirun is "they pray" (yusallun). 'Ikrimah and Mujahid also said: "they submit (to Islam)" (yuslimun).

The apparent meaning of His saying "while they seek forgiveness" is that they are engaged in seeking forgiveness, that is: they seek forgiveness and so are not punished, just as the Messenger is among them and so they are not punished. Both states exist: the presence of the Messenger among them and their seeking forgiveness.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "while they seek forgiveness" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and its meaning is the negation of seeking forgiveness from them, that is: even if they were among those who believe and seek forgiveness from disbelief, He would not punish them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers﴾ [Hud: 117]. "But they do not seek forgiveness nor do they believe, and this is not expected of them." End of quote. What he said had been preceded to it by others, who said: the meaning is: "while they are in a state of repentance and seeking forgiveness from their disbelief, had that occurred from them." Al-Tabari chose this, and it is narrated from Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

﴿And what is wrong with them that Allah should not punish them, while they bar (people) from the Sacred Mosque, and they were not its guardians? Its guardians are only the God-fearing, but most of them do not know.﴾ Apparently, "ma" is interrogative, meaning: "What is it for them regarding the negation of punishment?" It is an interrogative whose meaning is affirmation (taqrir), that is: how could they not be punished while they are characterized by this state which calls for punishment, namely their barring the believers from the Sacred Mosque, while they are not its custodians, nor qualified for its guardianship. Among their barring is what they did to the Messenger ﷺ in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, and his expulsion along with the believers falls within the barring. They used to say: "We are the custodians of the House; we bar whom we wish and admit whom we wish." "An" is a verbal particle (masdariyyah). Al-Akhfash said: it is extra (za'idah). Al-Nahhas said: "If it were as he said, it would have raised their punishment," end of quote, so the verb would be in the position of a circumstantial clause, like His saying: ﴿And what is it with us that we do not believe in Allah?﴾ The position of "an" is accusative, or genitive according to the disagreement, since "fi" has been omitted from it; it is connected to what is connected to "lahum," that is: "What thing exists or is established for them regarding Allah not punishing them?" The meaning is: they have no share in the negation of punishment, and when that is negated, they will certainly be punished. Al-Tabari's estimate, "what prevents them from being punished," is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of grammatical analysis. Similarly, the statement of Ibn 'Atiyyah should be interpreted as: "What is their power," and similar verbs necessitate that it be in the accusative position.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in "its guardians" (awliyahu) is to the Sacred Mosque, due to its proximity and the soundness of the meaning. It was also said: "ma" is for negation, and then it is informative, that is: "and they do not have that Allah should not punish them," that is: punishment is not negated from them while they are characterized by this state. It was also said: the pronoun in "awliyahu" refers to Allah, the Exalted; this was narrated from al-Hasan. The apparent meaning of His saying "and they were not its guardians" is a resumptive informative statement, that is: they did not deserve to be its guardians. ﴿Its guardians are only the God-fearing﴾, that is: those who are God-fearing with respect to shirk. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its guardians are only the God-fearing" among the Muslims; not every Muslim is also among those fit to be in charge of it; only one who is righteous and pious deserves its guardianship, so how about idol-worshippers? End of quote. It is permissible that "and they were not its guardians" be conjoined to "while they bar," making it a circumstantial clause, and the meaning is: how could Allah not punish them while they are characterized by these two attributes: their barring from the Sacred Mosque and the negation of their being its guardians, that is, guardians of the Mosque, meaning they are not its custodians, so they should not bar from it; or the guardians of Allah, in which case they are disbelievers, and thus it ascends from one state to a greater one, namely that they are not believers. Whoever bars from the Mosque while being a disbeliever in Allah is deserving of punishment. The pronoun in "its guardians" (in awliyahu) is consequent upon what it refers to in His saying "and they were not its guardians."

They differed regarding this punishment. Some people said: it is the first, except that it had been prevented by two things: the presence of the Prophet among them and the seeking of forgiveness by those among them who were believers. When distinction took place through the Hijrah, the punishment fell upon the rest at the Day of Badr. It was also said: rather it occurred with the conquest of Makkah. Others said: this punishment is other than that. The first is the complete annihilation of all of them, which did not happen because of the knowledge of the Islam of some of them and the Islam of some of their descendants. The second is the killing of some of them on the Day of Badr. Ibn 'Abbas said: the first is the punishment of this world, and the second is the punishment of the Hereafter. So the meaning: Allah would not be the punisher of the polytheists, because of their seeking forgiveness in this world, and it is not for them that Allah should not punish them in the Hereafter.

The object of "la ya'lamun" (they do not know) is omitted; its estimate: they do not know that they are not its guardians, but rather they think that they are its guardians. The apparent sense is the exception of "most" in the negation of knowledge, since among them, and within their midst, there were those who inclined toward faith, so he would know that those barring are not the guardians of the House or the guardians of Allah. So it is as if it was said: "But most of them," that is: most of those residing in Makkah "do not know," in order to exclude from them al-'Abbas, Umm al-Fadl and others who had knowledge; or because among them were those who knew it but obstinately opposed it seeking leadership. Or "most" is intended to mean all, figuratively, as if it was said: "but they do not know," just as it is said: "Hardly any man says that," in the sense of pure negation. Keeping "most" on its apparent meaning is more appropriate, and that "most" is intended to mean all is the interpretation of al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah.

﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to confine you or kill you or expel you. They plot, and Allah plots, and Allah is the best of plotters.﴾ Lamma dhakkara al-mu'minin ni'amahu 'alayhim, dhakkarahu ﷺ ni'amahu 'alayhi fi khassati nafsihi. Quraysh had consulted in Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh) about what to do with him. Some said: he should be imprisoned, bound, and made to await the calamities of fate (rayb al-manun). Others said: he should be expelled from Mecca, so that you may be rid of him. Iblis appeared in the form of an old man from Najd. It was also said that these were the two opinions. Another said: a man from every tribe should gather and strike him with a single blow with their swords, so that his blood would be scattered among the tribes, and the Banu Hashim would not be able to fight all of Quraysh, and so they would accept the blood-money (diyah). Iblis endorsed this opinion. Allah the Exalted then revealed this to His Prophet ﷺ, and commanded him not to sleep in his bed, and permitted him to leave for Medina. He commanded 'Ali to sleep in his bed and wrap himself in his cloak. They spent the night watching, and when they rushed to the bed, they saw 'Ali and were bewildered. He left 'Ali behind to return the deposits that were with him, and went out to Medina.

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: li-yuthbitūka means li-yuqayyidūka (to bind you). 'Ata' and al-Suddi said: li-yuthkhinūka means with wounding and beating, from their saying: "they beat him until they made him (uthbitahu) unable to move, neither stirring nor departing," and "he shot the bird and uthbitahu," i.e., wounded it (athkhanahu). The poet said:

"I said: Woe to you, what is in your document?
He said: The caliph has become wounded (muthbitan) and in pain."

That is, wounded (muthkhanan).

Al-Nakha'i read li-yubayyitūka, from al-bayat (to attack by night). This plotting here, by the consensus of the exegetes, is what Quraysh agreed upon in Dar al-Nadwa, as we have indicated. This verse is Medinan, like the rest of the surah, and this is the correct view. From 'Ikrimah and Mujahid it is reported that it is Meccan. From Ibn Zayd: it was revealed following Allah's sufficiency for His Messenger against the mockers. The statement of 'Ikrimah and Mujahid may be interpreted as meaning that they both referred to the story of the verse up to the time of its revelation. The word yamkurūna is repeated to indicate the continuation and abundance of their plotting. The explanation of the rest of the verse has already been given in Al 'Imran.

﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, they say: "We have heard. If we willed, we would say the like of this."﴾ The one who said this was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and many followed him in saying it. He was one of the rebellious men of Quraysh. He traveled to Persia and al-Hirah, and heard the stories of the monks and the Gospels, and the tales of Rustam and Isfandiyar. He saw the Jews and Christians bowing and prostrating. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had him killed in cold blood at al-Safra', at al-Uthayl, on his return from Badr. In this construction there is permissibility of the present tense occurring after idha with the past tense as its response, which is eloquent usage, unlike the particles of condition, for which this is not permitted except in poetry, as in:

"Whoever harms me with anything, I was from him..."

The meaning of "we have heard" is: we have heard and we do not obey, or: we have heard this from you. Their saying "if we willed" means: if we willed the speech, we would say the like of this which you recite. The reference is to what is recited, in the sense of the recited matter. This statement of theirs is by way of slander and confrontation, and it was not within their capacity. They were challenged to produce a surah like it and they were unable. The hardest thing for them was to be defeated, especially in the domain of eloquence. They used to compete with one another and oppose one another, and judgment was made between them in this. They were the most eager of people to subdue the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. How then could they make the opposing (of the Qur'an) depend on will, and excuse themselves by saying that if they had wished they would have said the like of this speech?!

﴿This is nothing but the tales of the ancients.﴾ Its explanation has already been given in al-An'am.

﴿And when they said: "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."﴾ The one who said this was al-Nadr; it was also said Abu Jahl. Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated it. The majority said: the speakers were the disbelievers of Quraysh. The reference in His saying "if this" is to the Qur'an, or to what the Messenger ﷺ brought of monotheism and other things, or to the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ among all of Quraysh — these are opinions. The discussion of "Allahumma" has already been given. Al-Jumhur read hua al-haqqa with the accusative, treating hua as a separator (fasl). Al-A'mash and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with the nominative, which is permissible in Arabic. Then the sentence is the predicate of kana, and this is the dialect of Tamim, who use the nominative after hua, which in the dialect of others is a separator, as he said:

"And you were over it in the assembly, you were more capable."

The discussion of the separator and its benefit has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqarah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is permissible in Arabic to read al-haqq in the nominative, as a predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of kana. Al-Zajjaj said: I do not know of anyone who read it with this permissible form, and the reading of the people is only with the accusative of al-haqq, end. Yet the one who read with the nominative has been mentioned. This conditional sentence contains great exaggeration in denying the truth, meaning: if it is truly the truth, then punish us for denying it by raining stones upon us or with another punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: their intent is to deny that it is the truth. When its being the truth is negated, the denier does not deserve punishment. So linking the punishment to its being the truth, while believing it is not the truth, is like linking it to the impossible, as in his saying: "if falsehood were the truth", while believing it is not the truth. His saying "it is the truth" is a mockery of one who says, in a specifying and definitive manner, "this is the truth." It is said: amtarat, like anjamat and asbalat; and matarat, like hatafat. The word for rain (amtar) is used in the sense of punishment. [Question]: What is the benefit of His saying "from the sky," since rain only comes from there? [Answer]: It is as if he meant to say: "rain down upon us sijjil (baked clay stones)", which are stones marked for punishment; the place of "stones from the sky" is the place of sijjil, just as one says: "he poured upon him a coat of mail of iron", meaning a breastplate, end. The meaning of his answer is that His saying "from the sky" came by way of emphasis, just as His saying "of iron" means emphasis, since a coat of mail is only of iron, just as rain is only from the sky.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: their saying "from the sky" is exaggeration and hyperbole, end. What appears to me is that the wisdom in their saying "from the sky" is that it corresponds to the rains coming from the direction from which it is said revelation comes to him. That is: you mention that revelation comes to you from the sky, so bring us a punishment from the direction from which revelation comes to you; for it would be fitting to express the sending of stones upon them from a direction other than the sky with their saying "rain down stones upon us." They said that by way of disdain and the belief that what he brought is not the truth. It was also said: by way of envy and obstinacy, while knowing that it is the truth. Ibn Furak rejected this second view, saying: no rational person says this out of obstinacy, end. It seems he did not read: "And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them" [al-Naml: 14]. And the story of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, and the rabbis of the Jews about whom Allah the Exalted said: "So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it" [al-Baqarah: 89]. And the saying of the Messenger ﷺ to them: "By Allah, you know that I am the Messenger of Allah," or words close to it. Their demanding these two kinds is in line with what the earlier nations demanded. A Jew asked Ibn 'Abbas: "Who are you from?" He said: "From Quraysh." He said: "You are from those who said: 'If this is indeed the truth from You...' (the verse)." Why did they not say: "Guide us to it?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "And you, O Israelite, are from those whose feet had not dried from the moisture of the sea in which Pharaoh and his people were drowned, and Moses and his people were saved, until they said: 'Make for us a god as they have gods' [al-A'raf: 138], and Moses said to them: 'Indeed you are a people who are ignorant' [al-A'raf: 138]." Then the Jew lowered his head, silenced. From Mu'awiyah it is reported that he said to a man from Saba': "How ignorant is your people, when they made a woman their king over them!" He said: "More ignorant than my people are your people, when they said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he called them to the truth: 'If this is indeed the truth' (the verse), and they did not say: 'Guide us to it.'"

﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them.﴾ This verse, up to "they know," was revealed in Mecca. It was also said: after the battle of Badr, narrating what occurred in it. Ibn Abza said: the first clause was in Mecca following His saying "with a painful punishment"; the second was when he left Mecca on his way to Medina, while believers remained in Mecca seeking forgiveness; and the third was after Badr, when the punishment became manifest upon them. So the meaning is: "Your nation would not be punished while you are among them. Rather your honor with your Lord is greater."
