And from it the proverb: "Command *dūna* ʿUbaydah the *wazm*." He said: *wa-ākharīn*: the Banū Qurayẓah. Muqātil said: the Jews. al-Suddī said: the people of Persia. A group said: the disbelieving jinn, and al-Ṭabarī preferred this, relying on what is reported: that the neighing of horses makes the jinn flee from it, and that devils do not enter a house in which there is a horse for jihad, and similar to this. A group said: they are every enemy of the Muslims other than the group the Prophet (ﷺ) was ordered to scatter, along with those behind them. Ibn Zayd said: they are the hypocrites. This is more apparent, because He said: *lā taʿlamūnahum Allāh yaʿlamuhum* (you do not know them; Allah knows them), meaning: you do not know their persons and identities, since they conceal themselves from you by Islam. So the knowledge here is like recognition, transitive to one object, and it relates to the essences, not to a relation. Whoever made it relate to a relation and supposed a second object omitted, and estimated it as *muḥāribīn* (combatants), has gone too far, because omitting such a thing without prior mention is prohibited according to some grammarians and very rare according to others. So the Qur'an is not to be interpreted by it when it is possible to interpret the wording otherwise and the meaning remains firm. Some estimated: *lā taʿlamūnahum fāziʿīn rāhibīn* (you do not know them as fearful and terrified), Allah knows them in that state.

The apparent meaning is that it is a reference to the hypocrites, as we have said, by way of censure of them and alerting to the evil of their condition, and so that everyone who knows hypocrisy in himself may doubt himself when he hears the verse. And in their fear and terror there is great sufficiency for the manifestation and elevation of Islam.

al-Qurṭubī said, in meaning: It is not appropriate to specify *wa-ākharīn*, because He, exalted is He, said: *lā taʿlamūnahum Allāh yaʿlamuhum*, so how can anyone claim knowledge of them, unless a hadith from the Messenger (ﷺ) is authentically reported about them. End of quote.

Then Allah, exalted is He, urged spending in the way of Allah, whether for jihad or otherwise. The Companions used to equip a group with horses and camels, and ʿUthmān equipped the army of al-ʿUsrah (the Tabuk expedition) with a thousand dinars.

*Yuwaffa ilaykum* (it will be repaid to you): its reward and recompense in full, without any deficiency. It was also said: this repayment is in this world, according to what they spent, along with what He has prepared for them in the Hereafter as reward.

﴿So if you gain the upper hand over them in war, then scatter those behind them, that perhaps they may take heed.﴾ That is: if you prevail over them in war and gain power over them, then scatter those behind them. Ibn 'Abbas said: "then make an example of those behind them." Ibn Jubayr said: "warn those behind them against killing and mutilating whoever is captured." The meaning is: if you gain the upper hand over them, then kill them with a devastating slaughter until those behind them flee from you and disperse. Since al-tashrid (scattering, which is driving away and banishing) arises from killing those captured in war among the treaty-breakers, it was made the answer to the condition, since it is caused by the answer. A group said: "then make them hear (fasammi' bihim)," and al-Zahrawi related this from Abu 'Ubayda. Al-Zamakhshari said: "[scatter] those behind them of the disbelievers, so that none will dare to attack you after them, taking them as a lesson and heeding their fate." Al-Kirmani said: "It has been said that al-tashrid is the fear that leaves no sense of security," meaning: do not accept from them anything but faith or the sword. Al-A'mash, in one reading transmitted from him, recited (fasharridh) with a dhal (ذ), and so it is in the Mushaf of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud). They said: this root is not attested in the Arabic language. It has been said that the dhal is a substitution for the dal, as they said: laḥm kharadil and kharadhil (shredded meat). Al-Zamakhshari said: "(fasharridh) with the marked dhal means fafarriq (disperse), and it seems to be a metathesis of shadhara, from their saying: dhahabu shadharan (they went off scattered), and from it comes al-shadhar, the gems gathered from a mine because they are scattered." End of quote. The poet said:

"Dainty women, in protection, comfort and luxury, adorned with rubies and scattered, broken pearls."

Qatrub said: with the marked dhal it means making an example (al-tankil), and with the unmarked dal it means dispersing (al-tafriq). Abu Haywa and al-A'mash, in one reading transmitted from him, recited (min khalfihim) as a prepositional phrase, and the object of (fasharrid) is elided, meaning: people from behind them. The pronoun in (la'allahum) appears to refer to (man khalfahum), who are those scattered, meaning: perhaps they will be admonished by what happened to us, the covenant having ended; or they will remember your promise to them. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to those captured, but this is remote, since one who has been killed does not remember.

﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms. Indeed, Allah does not love the treacherous.﴾ The apparent sense is that this is a fresh statement, in which Allah informs of what he will do in the future with one from whom treachery is feared, until the end of time. Mujahid said: it refers to the Banu Qurayzah, but what he said does not hold, because the Banu Qurayzah were not within the category of those from whom treachery was feared, since their treachery was manifest and well known. Also, His saying "from a people" would not fit; had it been about the Banu Qurayzah, it would have said "and if you fear from them." Yahya ibn Sallam said: (takhafanna) means (ta'lamu), "you know," and some have related that this is the view of the majority. It has also been said that fear retains its ordinary meaning, so the sense is that signs of evil appear from them and sayings that indicate treachery are reported from them. The signs are known, while the treachery which is the end of these signs is feared, not certain. The word "treachery" indicates a prior covenant, since one who has no covenant between you and him, fighting him is not treachery. So Allah commanded His Prophet, when he perceives from the people of a covenant what we have mentioned and fears their treachery, to cast their covenant back to them, which is al-nabdh (throwing back). The object of (fanbidh) is elided, the implied meaning being: fanbidh ilayhim 'ahdahum, "throw their covenant back to them," that is, cast it off and discard it. In His saying (fanbidh) there is an indication of not caring about it, like His saying ﴿so they threw it behind their backs﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187] and ﴿so We threw them into the sea﴾ [al-Qasas: 40], as the poet said: "like the throwing of a patched sandal." It is as if one only throws away and casts aside something trivial that one does not care about. The force of this expression implies waging war against them and fighting them openly, unless they are removed. The meaning of (ʿala sawa'in) is: on a straight, even path. That is, you must openly declare the abrogation of the covenant and inform them plainly and clearly that you have severed what is between you and them, and not engage them in battle while they still assume the covenant persists, for that would be treachery on your part. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the treacherous﴾, so there must be no concealment from you regarding the covenant. Al-Zamakhshari said this in these words, and others such as Ibn 'Abbas in its meaning. Al-Walid ibn Muslim said: (ʿala sawa'in) means "gradually" (ʿala mahal), as Allah says: ﴿A declaration of immunity from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made covenants among the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawba: 1], and so on. Al-Farra' said the meaning is: throw back to them with moderation and evenness of affair, that is, make it clear to them according to what appeared from them, neither exceeding nor surprising them with war, but treat them exactly as they treated you, meaning by reciprocity and equal measure. Zayd ibn 'Ali read (sawa'in) with a kasra on the sin (سِوَاءٍ). The apparent sense of (inna Allah) is that it is an explanation of His saying (fanbidh): throw back to them on equal terms, keeping aloof from treachery, ﴿indeed Allah does not love the treacherous﴾. It may also be a rebuke of the treacherous people with whom the Messenger made a covenant. The phrase (ʿala sawa'in) may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the agent in (fanbidh), meaning: being on a straight path; or from the agent and the prepositional phrase, meaning: being equal in knowledge or in enmity.

﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose that they have outstripped [Us]. Indeed, they cannot escape.﴾ Al-Zuhri said: it was revealed concerning those of the disbelievers who escaped at Badr. The meaning is: do not think they are saved and escaped, for they cannot elude the one pursuing them; rather, they must be seized. It has been said: this refers to this world, and they will not escape but Allah will give you victory over them. It has also been said: it refers to the Hereafter, as al-Hasan said. It has been said that (alladhina kafaru) is general, as Ibn 'Abbas said. (A'jaza) means: to overcome and to escape. Suwayd said:

"Abu Layla Tufayl, healthy of skin, despite the marks of weapons, has outmaneuvered us."

Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and Hafs read (wa-la yahsabanna) with the ya' (يَحْسَبَنَّ), meaning: and let not the Messenger suppose, or let not a supposer, or let not the believer suppose; or there is a pronoun referring to those behind them, so that it is the object: (yahsabanna alladhina kafaru), and (sabaqu) (they outstripped). The rest of the Seven read it with the ta' (تَحْسَبَنَّ), addressing the Messenger or the listener. They permitted that in the reading with the ya', the agent of (la yahsabanna) is (alladhina kafaru). This is explained by eliding the first object for the sake of the meaning, its estimated form being: anfusahum sabaqu, "themselves they outstripped." It is also explained by assuming (anna) before (sabaqu), which is elided but intended, and it fills the place of the two objects of (yahsabanna). This is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah: (annahum sabaqu). It has also been said that the estimate is: wa-la tahsabannahumu alladhina kafaru, the pronoun being elided as it is understood. We have already refuted this view at the end of Al 'Imran. On the view that the agent is (alladhina kafaru), al-Zamakhshari explained the reading with the ya', and mentioned that the transmitted explanation of it is by eliding the object, either the pronoun, or themselves, or the (anna), or that the verb falls on (annahum la yu'jizun), with (anna) not being a complement, and (sabaqu) being in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: outstripping, or escaping in flight. And [the explanation] is: and let not the slain of the believers, those who disbelieve, be supposed to have outstripped. Then he said: all these explanations are strained, and this reading which Hamzah alone transmitted is not clear. Hamzah did not transmit it alone, as he claimed; rather Ibn 'Amir also read it, and he was one of the Arabs who were early in correct speech. 'Ali, 'Uthman, Hafs from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa', Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Ibn Muhaysin, 'Isa and al-A'mash also read it with the ta'. The explanation of it was given earlier in other terms that are good Arabic, so there is no need to heed his claim that it is unclear. The difference over the fath and kasr of the sin in His saying ﴿the ignorant man supposes them to be rich﴾ [al-Baqara: 273] was mentioned earlier. As for his saying: "it is said that it falls on (annahum la yu'jizun) with (anna) not being a complement," this cannot apply to the reading of Hamzah, because he reads with a kasra on the hamza, and if it fell on it, he would have read with a fatha on anna. Only Ibn 'Amir among the Seven read with the fatha, and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim considered Ibn 'Amir's reading improbable, though there is nothing improbable in it, because it is a causal explanation of the prohibition, meaning: do not suppose them escaped, because they cannot be overcome, meaning: no supposition of their escape should occur from you, because they cannot be overcome, meaning: they cannot elude. Al-A'mash read (wa-la yahsabu) with fatha on the sin, ya' from below, and the elision of the nun, and it should be explained as the elision of the light nun before a sakin, so it is like the poet's:

"Do not humiliate the poor man, lest you bow down one day while fate has raised him."

Ibn Muhaysin read (la tu'jizunni) with a kasra on the nun and a ya' after it. Al-Zajjaj said: the preferred form is the fatha on the nun, but the kasra is permitted, meaning: they cannot overcome me; and the first nun is elided because of the meeting of two nuns, as the poet said:

"You see him like the white plant, scented with musk, displeasing to the enemies when they press him."

The line belongs to 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib. Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash said regarding the verse of Mutammim ibn Nuwayra:

"Indeed I know, without doubt, that I am for calamities, so do you see me flinch?"

This is permitted under necessity. Some said: the first nun was elided, and its elision is not permitted, because it is the nun of inflection (nun al-i'rab), which marks grammatical case. Al-Mubarrad said: in cases like this I see the elision of the second nun, and so he said regarding the verse of 'Amr. Talha read with a kasra on the nun without shadda and without ya'. Ibn Muhaysin also transmitted the reading with shadda on the nun and a kasra, assimilating the nun of inflection into the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya). He also transmitted a reading with a fatha on the nun, shadda on the jim and a kasra on the nun. Al-Nahhas said: this is an error on two counts. One: the meaning of its ('ajz) is weakness and the weakness of its affair. The other: it should have been with two nuns. End of quote. As for it being with one nun, this is permitted, not obligatory, and it was read thus among the Seven. As for (ʿajjazani) with shadda, Sahib al-Lawami' (the author of al-Lawami') mentioned that its meaning is to delay and hinder. He said: it may also mean to attribute to me weakness; and the shadda in this reading has this meaning, so the reading is not an error, as al-Nahhas mentioned.

﴿And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of steeds of war, by which you may strike terror into the enemy of Allah and your enemy, and others besides them whom you do not know, [but] Allah knows them. And whatever you spend in the way of Allah will be fully repaid to you, and you will not be wronged.﴾ When it happened in the story of Badr that they set out against the disbelievers without complete equipment or preparation, and Allah commanded him to scatter and to throw back the covenant to those who broke it, this became a path to taking up combat and to rallying against them. So His command to the believers to prepare whatever power they could for jihad was given. Al-i'dad (preparation) is al-irsad (readying and watching). Allah made it conditional upon ability, as a kindness from Him. The addressees are the believers. The pronoun in (lahum) refers to the disbelievers mentioned earlier, who were the ones commanded to be fought at that time, and it includes those who come after them. It has been said that it refers to those to whom the covenant is thrown back. The apparent meaning is general to everything by which one guards against fighting the enemy, of what the exegetes mentioned as specific instances, which is intended as an illustration: such as shooting, male horses, strength of hearts, unity of word, fortified castles, instruments of war and their quantities, provisions, and fine equipment. So much so that Mujahid was seen preparing for jihad with a sack, and he said: this is part of strength. As for what is in Sahih Muslim from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was on the pulpit, saying: ﴿And prepare against them whatever you are able of power﴾. Indeed, power is archery; indeed, power is archery," its meaning, Allah knows best, is that the greatest part of power, and the most effective against the enemy, is archery, just as it was said: "Hajj is 'Arafa" (the Hajj is the standing at 'Arafa). Traditions about the virtue of archery have also come. According to what we have chosen, the generality of power, the words ﴿and of steeds of war﴾ are an explicit mention of the virtue of keeping horses ready, since horses are the basis of wars, and goodness is tied to their forelocks, and they are the mounts of brave horsemen. Abu Zayd said: "a string of horses" (ribat) is five or more, and a group of them is rubt, and those which are kept tethered (yartabit) are so called; it is said from this: rabata, rabṭan, and irtabata. End of quote. He said:

"She blames me for tethering the horses and holding them back, and Allah has enjoined them upon the Prophet Muhammad."

(p-٥١٢) Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: *Ribāṭ al-khayl* is the plural of *rabṭ*, like *kalb* and *kilāb*, and *rabṭuhā* (the tying of them) is not multiplied except when they are numerous. It is also permissible that *ribāṭ* be a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) of *rabaṭa*, like *ṣāḥa ṣiyāḥan*, because the *maṣādir* (verbal nouns) of the unaugmented triliteral verb (*al-thulāthī ghayr al-mazīd*) are not regular. If we take it as a verbal noun of *rābaṭa*, and the tying of horses and their keeping is something each person does for the action of another, so the believers bind themselves (*yuribāṭu*) to one another, then when each one of them ties a horse for the sake of his companion, a bond (*ribāṭ*) comes about among them, and that is what is urged in the verse. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever ties a horse in the way of Allah, it is as one who extends his hand with charity and does not withdraw it." The reports with this meaning are numerous. End of quote.

So he permitted that *ribāṭ* be a plural of *rabṭ*, or a verbal noun of *al-rabṭ* and *al-rābiṭ*. His statement, "because the *maṣādir* of the unaugmented triliteral verb are not regular," is not correct; rather, it has regular *maṣādir* which the grammarians have mentioned.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: *al-Ribāṭ* is a name for the horses that are tied in the way of Allah. It is permissible that they be called *ribāṭ*, which means *al-murābaṭah* (standing guard and being stationed at the frontier). It is also permissible that it be the plural of *rabīṭ*, like *faṣīl* and *fiṣāl*.

Al-Ḥasan, Abū Ḥaywah and ʿAmr ibn Dīnār recited *(wa-min rubuṭi)* with a *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ* and the *bāʾ*. And from Abū Ḥaywah and al-Ḥasan also: *(rubṭin)*, with a *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ* and a sukūn on the *bāʾ*, like *kitāb*, *kutub* and *kutb*. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "Regarding its plural, while it is a verbal noun, there is no disagreement; there is an issue (*naẓar*)." End of quote.

It is not necessary that it be a verbal noun. Do you not see the statement of Abū Zayd: that it is from horses, five or more, and that their collective is *rubuṭ*, and they are the ones that are tied? The apparent meaning is the generality of horses, males and females. ʿIkrimah said: *ribāṭ al-khayl* means its females, and he interpreted *al-quwwah* (strength) as its males. Some scholars recommended tying the females because of the offspring they produce, as it is said: "Their bellies are a treasure." It was also said: *ribāṭ al-khayl* means the males among them, because of the strength and endurance they have for fighting, confrontation, attack, retreat and running.

The pronoun in *bihi* refers to what is in the phrase *mā istaṭaʿtum* (what you can). It was also said that it refers to *al-iʿdād* (the preparation), or to *al-quwwah* (strength), or to *ribāṭ*. As for *turhibūna* (you terrify), they said it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in *aʿiddū*, or from the pronoun in *lahum*. Through this binding and terrifying, several benefits are achieved: among them, that they will not intend to enter the abode of Islam; and with the intensification of fear, they may commit to paying the *jizyah* (poll tax) or submit, or not assist the rest of the disbelievers.

Al-Ḥasan, Yaʿqūb, and Ibn ʿAqīl (transmitting from Abū ʿAmr) recited *turhibūna* with a shadda, which makes it transitive by doubling, as it is made transitive by the *hamzah*. Abū Ḥātim said: "ʿAmr claimed that al-Ḥasan recited *(yurhibūna)* with a *yāʾ* at the beginning and without a shadda." End of quote.

The pronoun in *yurhibūna* refers to what it referred to in *lahum*, and they are the disbelievers. The meaning is: when the disbelievers know what you have prepared for war, of strength and the tying of horses, they frighten those among the disbelievers near them and terrify them, since they inform them of your preparation for war, so they fear you. And if they have frightened those near you, then their fear of you is even greater.

Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah and Mujāhid recited *tukhzūna bihi* in place of *turhibūna bihi*. al-Ṭabarī mentioned it as an explanation (*tafsīr*), not as a recitation (*qirāʾah*), and this is what is proper, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the *muṣḥaf* (the written Qur'an).

al-Sulamī recited *(ʿaduwwan lillāh)* with tanwīn and the *lām* of *jarr*. The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* said: It was said he meant by it the generic noun (*ism al-jins*), and its meaning is: enemies of Allah. He made it indefinite in the sense of the general, because it is also indefinite, not made definite by an *idāfah* to a definite noun, since it is an active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*), whose meaning is the present and future, and this does not become definite even if it is put in construction with definite nouns. As for *ʿaduwwakum*, it is permissible that it is indefinite like this, and it is permissible that it has become definite by repetition of its mention. Similar to it: "I saw a companion of yours, so my companion said to me..." And Allah knows best. End of quote.

He mentioned first *ʿaduww Allāh* to magnify what they are upon of disbelief, to strengthen the condemnation of them, and because for the sake of their enmity toward Allah they must be fought and hated. Then he said *ʿaduwwakum* as an encouragement to fight them, since by nature a person is hostile to whoever is hostile to him and seeks to harm him. What is meant by these two attributes are those among the disbelievers near the abodes of Islam, from the people of Makkah and the polytheists of the Arabs. It is said that it is also permissible that all disbelievers be meant.

*Wa-ākharīna min dūnihim* (and others besides them). The root of *dūn* is that it be a spatial adverb (*ẓarf makān*) in its literal sense, or a metaphorical one. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "*Min dūnihim* is equivalent to your saying: *dūna an takūna hāʾulāʾ*. So *dūn* in the speech of the Arabs, and *min dūn*, requires the absence of what comes after it of the event in which the speech takes place." And from it the proverb: "Command *dūna* ʿUbaydah the *wazm*." He said: *wa-ākharīn*: the Banū Qurayẓah. Muqātil said: the Jews. al-Suddī said: the people of Persia. A group said: the disbelieving jinn, and al-Ṭabarī preferred this, relying on what is reported: that the neighing of horses makes the jinn flee from it, and that devils do not enter a house in which there is a horse for jihad, and similar to this. A group said: they are every enemy of the Muslims other than the group the Prophet (ﷺ) was ordered to scatter, along with those behind them. Ibn Zayd said: they are the hypocrites. This is more apparent, because He said: *lā taʿlamūnahum Allāh yaʿlamuhum* (you do not know them; Allah knows them), meaning: you do not know their persons and identities, since they conceal themselves from you by Islam. So the knowledge here is like recognition, transitive to one object, and it relates to the essences, not to a relation. Whoever made it relate to a relation and supposed a second object omitted, and estimated it as *muḥāribīn* (combatants), has gone too far, because omitting such a thing without prior mention is prohibited according to some grammarians and very rare according to others. So the Qur'an is not to be interpreted by it when it is possible to interpret the wording otherwise and the meaning remains firm. Some estimated: *lā taʿlamūnahum fāziʿīn rāhibīn* (you do not know them as fearful and terrified), Allah knows them in that state.

The apparent meaning is that it is a reference to the hypocrites, as we have said, by way of censure of them and alerting to the evil of their condition, and so that everyone who knows hypocrisy in himself may doubt himself when he hears the verse. And in their fear and terror there is great sufficiency for the manifestation and elevation of Islam.

al-Qurṭubī said, in meaning: It is not appropriate to specify *wa-ākharīn*, because He, exalted is He, said: *lā taʿlamūnahum Allāh yaʿlamuhum*, so how can anyone claim knowledge of them, unless a hadith from the Messenger (ﷺ) is authentically reported about them. End of quote.

Then Allah, exalted is He, urged spending in the way of Allah, whether for jihad or otherwise. The Companions used to equip a group with horses and camels, and ʿUthmān equipped the army of al-ʿUsrah (the Tabuk expedition) with a thousand dinars.

*Yuwaffa ilaykum* (it will be repaid to you): its reward and recompense in full, without any deficiency. It was also said: this repayment is in this world, according to what they spent, along with what He has prepared for them in the Hereafter as reward.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verse 61:

﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it, and put your trust in Allah. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

Janaha (to incline) al-rajulu ila al-akhar: he inclined toward the other. And janahat al-ibil: the camels inclined their necks while walking. Dhu al-Rumma said:

"When he dies upon the saddle, I revive his spirit with your remembrance, while the loosely-led camels are inclining (junnah)."

And janaha al-layl: the night approached and let its ropes (atnab) incline toward the earth. Al-Nabigha said, describing birds that follow the army:

"Birds that have certainly known that their portion, when the two armies meet, is the first to prevail."

From this comes the term jawanih for the ribs, because they incline over the belly cavity. From the same root comes al-janah (the wing), because of its inclination. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: janaha al-rajulu ila fulan and janaha lahu means he followed him and submitted to him.

The pronoun in janahu refers to those with whom you made a covenant on equal terms (ala sawa'), namely the Banu Qurayza and the Banu al-Nadir. It is also said that it refers to the polytheists of Quraysh and the Arabs. It is also said that it refers to a people who asked the Messenger ﷺ to accept the jizya from them. Janaha is transitive with both ila and al-lam.

Al-silm (peace) may be masculine or feminine. It is said that the feminine usage is a dialect. It is also said that it is according to the meaning of al-musalama (peacemaking). It is also said that it is by analogy to its opposite, which is war. The poet said:

"I have exhausted its implements in war, and I have counted its burdens for peace."

The difference in reading the sin and its vowelling has already been mentioned. Al-silm, in linguistic usage, means reconciliation (al-sulh). Qatada said: it is the truce and armistice with the polytheists. This relates to the opinion of the Imam: if he sees it as beneficial he does it, otherwise he does not. It is also said: it was revealed concerning the people of Ma'tib, who asked for a truce, so Allah commanded His Prophet to accept it. Then it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Fight those who do not believe﴾ [al-Tawba: 29]. It is also said: it means paying the jizya. Al-Hasan said: al-silm is Islam. From Ibn Abbas: it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Fight those who do not believe﴾ [al-Tawba: 29]. From Mujahid: it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5]. Al-Zamakhshari said: the correct view is that the matter is left to what the Imam sees as beneficial for Islam and its people, whether war or peace. It is not obligatory that they must always be fought, nor that they must always be granted a truce.

Al-Ashhab al-Uqayli read: fa-jnu'h, with a damma on the nun, which is the dialect of Qays. The majority read it with a fatha, which is the dialect of Tamim. Ibn Jinni said: the analogical form for an intransitive verb is to vowel the middle radical of the imperfect with a damma, and it is more analogical than yafil with kasra. Allah commanded him to put his trust in Him and not care about them. Even if they conceal deceit within their inclination toward peace, Allah is sufficient for whoever trusts in Him. He is the All-Hearing of their words and the All-Knowing of their intentions.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 8, verses 62–63:**

﴿And if they intend to deceive you, then indeed Allah is sufficient for you. It is He who strengthened you with His help and with the believers, and who joined their hearts together. Even if you had spent everything on earth, you could not have joined their hearts, but Allah joined them. Indeed, He is All-Mighty, All-Wise.﴾

That is: "And if those inclined to peace intend to deceive you, by showing peace while concealing treachery and betrayal, then incline to it. Do not concern yourself with their corrupt intentions, for indeed Allah is sufficient for you and your protector. Whoever has Allah as his sufficiency does not care about one who intends evil. Then He reminded him of what He had done for him earlier: strengthening him with victory and with the joining together of the believers in aiding him and supporting him against his enemies. Just as He was gentle with you at first, He will be gentle with you at the end. The believers here are the Aws and the Khazraj. Between the two groups there was such enmity, because of the wars that had taken place between them, that it would never have ended had it not been for Islam. But Allah, exalted is He, bestowed upon them the favour of Islam, so He replaced their enmity with love and their estrangement with closeness. The meaning of ﴿Even if you had spent everything on earth﴾ is: in joining their hearts and uniting them in love for one another. That this refers to the Aws and the Khazraj is supported by the sayings of the commentators. Ibn Mas'ud said: it was revealed concerning those who love one another for the sake of Allah. Ibn 'Atiyya said: If someone were to take the view that it refers to all the believers, among the Muhajirun (emigrants) and the Ansar (helpers), and considered the joining together to be what occurred among their whole community, then each of them would be joined to the others for the sake of Allah.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The joining together of the hearts of those to whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent occurred because of the clear signs they saw. The Arabs, because of their zeal, tribal partisanship, and harbouring of resentment over even the smallest matter, and their keeping it before their eyes until they took revenge, hardly ever had two hearts joined together among them. Then their hearts were joined in following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they became united. This was due to the bond Allah arranged among them, the unity of their word He gathered, the mutual love and affection He created between them, the removal of hatred from among them, and the obligation He placed upon them to love for the sake of Allah and to hate for the sake of Allah. None has the power to do this except One who possesses the hearts; He turns them as He wills and does in them what He intends. End of quotation.

His final statement is close to the words of the Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah, the Sunni orthodox school), because they said: this verse is evidence that beliefs, desires, and aversions are created by Allah, since what resulted in this affection was caused by faith and following the Messenger (ﷺ). If faith were an act of the servant, then the love that follows from it would be an act of the servant, and that contradicts the plain meaning of the verse. Al-Qadi (al-Baydawi) said: Had it not been for the subtle kindnesses of Allah, moment by moment, these states would not have come about, so they are attributed to Allah on this interpretation. An analogy is that the knowledge and good manners of a child are attributed to his father, because he attained them only through the father's help and upbringing. So it is here as well. End of quotation. This is the position of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school that held that human beings create their own acts).

**[p-515]** ﴿O Prophet, God is sufficient for you, and so are the believers who follow you.﴾ It was revealed at al-Bayda' during the Battle of Badr, before the fighting began. Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar and Anas said that it was revealed concerning the conversion of ʿUmar (ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him). Ibn Jubayr said: "Thirty-three men and six women had embraced Islam, then ʿUmar embraced Islam, and it was revealed."

The apparent reading is to put *wa-man* (and whoever) in the nominative, as a coordination with what precedes it, and on this al-Hasan and a group of scholars interpreted it, meaning: "God is sufficient for you, and so are the believers." Al-Sha'bi and Ibn Zayd said the meaning of the verse is: "God is sufficient for you, and so is whoever follows you." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "*Man* in this interpretation is in the accusative position, coordinated with the position of the *kaf* (the pronoun 'you'), because its position is accusative in the sense of 'what suffices you' which has taken the place of *hasbuka* (sufficient for you)," end of quote. This is not sound, because *hasbuka* is not one of those words in which the *kaf* occupies an accusative position. Rather, this is a correct genitive construction (idafa), not an accusative one. *Hasbuka* is a subject (mubtada') with a pronoun as its genitive complement, and it is neither a verbal noun (masdar) nor an active participle (ism fa'il). The only way to make it accusative would be to say that it is coordinated by *ʿatf al-tawahhum* (coordination on an assumed form), as if one imagined that it had been said: "God suffices you" or "God has sufficed you." But coordination on an assumed form is not a productive rule, so the Qur'an should not be read according to it when there is an alternative. What should be taken as the meaning of the words of al-Sha'bi and Ibn Zayd is that *wa-man* is in the genitive, with the word *wa-hasb* (and sufficiency for) elided, since *hasbuka* indicates it. This is like the line of verse:

*Do you reckon every man a man, and a fire kindled at night a fire?*

That is: "and every fire." So it is not coordination on a genitive pronoun. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "This form of eliding the noun (*hadhf al-mudaf*) is disliked, as it is a necessity of poetry," end of quote. But it is neither disliked nor a necessity. Sibawayh permitted it in ordinary speech, and the line of verse and other eloquent speech are explained by it.

al-Zamakhshari said: "*Wa-man ittaba'aka*: the *wa* is in the sense of *ma'a* (with), and what follows it is in the accusative. You say: '*wa-hasbuka wa-Zaydan dirham*' (sufficient for you and Zayd is a dirham), and it is not put in the genitive, because coordinating an apparent noun in the genitive on a pronoun is impermissible." He said:

*So sufficient for you, and al-Dahhak, is a sword of Indian steel.*

The meaning is: "God has sufficed you and those who follow you among the believers, as a helper," end of quote. What al-Zamakhshari said contradicts the words of Sibawayh. Sibawayh said: "They say *hasbuka wa-Zaydan dirham*, because it contains the meaning of *kafaka* (has sufficed you)." He disliked that they should treat it as a pronoun of the verb implied (the verb being implied), as if he said: "*hasbuka* and *yahsubu akhaka dirham*." For that reason he said: "*kafika* (it suffices you)," end of quote. *Kafika* is from *kafahu yakfihi*. Similarly *qatuka* (enough for you), and you say: "*kafika wa-Zaydan dirham*" and "*qatuka wa-Zaydan dirham*." This is not an example of the object of accompaniment (*maf'ul ma'ahu*). Sibawayh only brought it as evidence for taking the verb as implied, since *hasbuka* indicates *kafaka*. *Yahsibuni* is the present tense of *ahsabani fulan* when someone gives me, so that I say *hasbi* (enough for me). Thus the governing element in this is a verb that the meaning indicates. In *kafika wa-Zaydan dirham* it is clearer, because it is a verbal noun of the implied verb, meaning "and it suffices Zayd." In *qatuka wa-Zaydan dirham* the supposition is more remote, because there is nothing from the wording of the implied verb in *qatuka*; it only explains the meaning. In that implied verb there is a subject which refers back to the dirham, and the intention regarding the dirham is that it is placed first, so it becomes coordination of sentences. It cannot be a case of *al-a'mal* (the rule of two governing elements competing for one word), because the subject's demand for the predicate and its governing of it is not of the kind of a verb's demand or what is like it, nor its governing, so this should not be suspected.

al-Zajjaj said: "*Hasb* is a verbal noun (ism fi'l), the *kaf* is in the accusative, and the *wa* is in the sense of *ma'a* (with)." According to this, God is the subject of *hasbuka*, and according to this reading *wa-man* may be coordinated on the *kaf*, because it is the object of the verbal noun and not in the genitive, since a verbal noun cannot take an *idafa*. However, al-Zajjaj's view is wrong because governing elements enter upon *hasbuka*. You say: *bi-hasbika dirham* (with what suffices you, a dirham), and God says: ﴿Indeed, God is sufficient for you﴾ [al-Anfal: 62]. It has not been established that *hasb* is a verbal noun in any place, so that it should be thought to be a verbal noun in one place and a non-verbal noun in another, like *ruwayda* (let be).

Abu al-Baqa' permitted the nominative reading of *wa-man* in two ways: as the predicate of an elided subject, meaning *wa-hasbuka man ittaba'aka* (and sufficient for you are those who follow you); and as a subject whose predicate is elided, meaning *wa-man ittaba'aka min al-mu'minin* (and whoever follows you among the believers) is likewise, that is, *hasbuhum Allah* (God is sufficient for them).

al-Sha'bi read: *wa-man atba'aka* (with the *nun* of *man* silent), and *atba'a* is in the pattern of *akrama*.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verses 65–66:

﴿O Prophet, urge the believers to fight. If there are twenty among you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are a hundred among you, they will overcome a thousand of those who disbelieve, because they are a people who do not understand. Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you, and He knows that there is weakness in you. So if there are a hundred among you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are a thousand among you, they will overcome two thousand, by the permission of Allah. And Allah is with the steadfast.﴾

These two sentences are conditional. Within them is the command for twenty to stand firm against two hundred, and for a hundred to stand firm against a thousand. For this reason abrogation (naskh) entered them; for if it were a purely informative statement, there would be no abrogation in it. However, when the conditional carries the sense of a religious obligation (taklif), abrogation may apply to it, and this is one of those cases. For this reason it was abrogated by His words: ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you﴾. The restriction "with steadfastness" at the beginning of each conditional is verbally omitted from the second, because its mention in the first indicates it. The restriction of the second conditional by the words "from those who disbelieved" (min alladhina kafaru) is verbally omitted from the first conditional in His words ﴿they will overcome two hundred﴾. Consider the eloquence of this speech: a restriction from the first sentence is stated and its counterpart is omitted from the second, while a restriction is stated in the second and omitted from the first. Since steadfastness is highly required, it is stated in the first of the two sentences of lightening and omitted from the second, because the preceding one indicates it. Then the verse is concluded with His words: ﴿Allah is with the steadfast﴾ [al-Anfal: 46], as an intensification of the high requirement. The restriction of disbelief was not included in the two sentences of lightening, being satisfied with what came before them.

Reports from Ibn Abbas and others among the Companions are widely transmitted that the steadfastness of one against ten was an obligation; when it became burdensome for them, it shifted to the steadfastness of one against two, also as a means of drawing near [to Allah]. Whether it was an obligation or a recommendation, it is abrogation. The view of those who said it is a lightening and not abrogation, such as Makki ibn Abi Talib, is weak. Makki said: it is only like the lightening of fasting during travel; if one fasts, he does not sin and it suffices him. The correspondence of these numbers is that the obligation or recommendation of steadfastness was at first, at the beginning of Islam; so twenty represented a small expedition (sariyyah) and a hundred represented an army. When the scope of Islam expanded, after a time, a hundred represented small expeditions and a thousand represented an army.

The command of the Most High to His Prophet to urge the believers to fight is not evidence for the beginning of the obligation of fighting; rather, fighting was already obligatory before this verse, and this verse came only to urge them toward a matter that had already become incumbent upon them. The Most High stated the cause of victory: that the disbelievers are a people who do not understand. The meaning is that they are ignorant people who fight without seeking reward or hoping for recompense, like cattle, so their intentions are weakened, and due to their ignorance of Allah they lose His support; so He forsakes them. This is in contrast to one who fights with insight, who is promised by Allah victory and triumph.

It is related from Ibn Jurayj: it was incumbent upon them not to flee, and one must stand firm against ten. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had sent Hamzah with thirty riders, and he met Abu Jahl with three hundred riders. It was said: then this became burdensome for them and they complained of it, and that was after a long period; so it was abrogated and lightened for them by the resistance of one against two. Some scholars said: The ruling of obligation established by the implication of this verse is that every adult Muslim who confronts the polytheists, whether slave or free, is forbidden to flee as long as he has his weapon with which to fight. If he has no weapon, he may retreat, and even if three face him, retreat is permitted for him, though steadfastness is better.

Al-Bayhaqi and others narrated that the army of Mu'tah, who were three thousand Muslims, stood against two hundred thousand: a hundred thousand from the Romans and a hundred thousand from the Nabateans. It is also narrated that they stood against four hundred thousand, but the first is the correct one. In the history of the conquest of al-Andalus it is recorded that Tariq, the freedman of Musa ibn Nusayr, marched with one thousand and seven hundred men to al-Andalus, in Rajab of the year ninety-three after the Hijrah. He met the king of al-Andalus, Ludhriq, who had seventy thousand cavalrymen; Tariq advanced toward him and stood firm against him, so Allah defeated the tyrant Ludhriq, and the conquest came about. End of quotation. The island of al-Andalus has continually seen a small band of them meet a large number of Christians, and they overcome them. We were informed by one who witnessed the battle that took place at Dayumus al-Saghir, twelve miles from the city of Granada, in the year seven hundred and nineteen, when the Muslims numbered one thousand seven hundred horsemen from the Andalusians and Berbers, while the Christians numbered one hundred thousand foot soldiers, sixty thousand archers, and fifteen thousand horsemen between archers and armored troops. They stood firm against them, captured their chieftains, and killed the king of Castile, Don Juan; his brother Don Pedro escaped wounded. The kings of the Christians—the aforementioned king of Castile, the king of France, the king of Portugal, the king of Galicia, and the king of the fortress of Rabah—had all come out determined to uproot the Muslims from the island, but Allah defeated them. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): Why did he repeat the same meaning, which is the resistance of a group against a larger one, twice, before the lightening and after it? (I say): To indicate that the situation with few and with many is one; they do not differ, for the situation may differ between twenty resisting two hundred and a hundred resisting a thousand, so likewise between a hundred resisting two hundred and a thousand resisting two thousand. End of quotation. The meaning of "by the permission of Allah" is by His will and His enablement. In His words ﴿And Allah is with the steadfast﴾ is encouragement toward steadfastness in facing the enemy, and good tidings of victory and triumph, because whoever Allah is with is the victor.

Al-A'mash read "ḥarriṣ" with the unpointed ṣād, from ḥirṣ (eagerness), which is close to the reading of the majority with ḍād. The Kufans read ﴿yakun minkum mi'atun﴾ with the masculine in both places; Kharijah narrated it from Nafi'. The two Haramis (Makkan and Madinan) and Ibn 'Amir read with the feminine. Abu 'Amr read with the masculine in the first, observing "yaghlibu," and with the feminine in the second, observing "ṣābiratun." Al-A'raj read everything with the feminine except His words ﴿wa-in yakun minkum alfun﴾, which is with the masculine without dispute. Al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read "'ulima" in the passive voice. The two Haramis, the two Iraqi readers, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Ibn al-Qa'qa', Qatadah, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "ḍa'fan" [with a fatha on the ḍād], and in al-Rum [with a ḍamma on the ḍād and sukun on the 'ayn], Isa ibn 'Umar read both with ḍamma, Hamzah and 'Asim read with fatha on the ḍād and sukun on the 'ayn; all of these are verbal nouns (maṣādir). It is related from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' that a ḍamma on the ḍād is the dialect of the Hijaz and a fatha is the dialect of Tamim. Ibn al-Qa'qa' read "ḍu'afa," the plural of ḍa'if, like ẓarif and ẓurafa'; al-Naqqash related it from Ibn 'Abbas. It is said: weakness (ḍa'f) is in the bodies; it is also said: in insight and steadfastness in religion, and they varied in this. Al-Tha'alibi said: ḍa'f with a fatha on the ḍād is in the intellect and judgment, and ḍu'f is in the body. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is a view that the reading rejects. End of quotation.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verses 67–69:

﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he has inflicted a massacre upon the land. You desire the goods of this world, but Allah desires the Hereafter. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿Had there not been a decree from Allah that preceded, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took.﴾ ﴿So eat of what you have taken as lawful and good, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

It was revealed concerning the captives of Badr. The Messenger (ﷺ) had consulted Abu Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿAli. Abu Bakr advised taking ransom (istihya'), while ʿUmar advised killing them, in a lengthy hadith that is related in Sahih Muslim. Abu al-Darda' and Abu Haywa recited: ﴿ma kana li-nnabiyyi mu'arrafan﴾ (It is not for the Prophet to be made known). The intended meaning, in both the indefinite and definite forms, is the Messenger (ﷺ). However, indefiniteness carries a sense of vagueness as to whom the negation is not directed at specifically. A similar construction and the manner of this negation have been discussed before. Here it is by omission of a noun: the meaning is "It is not for the companions of a Prophet, or the followers of a Prophet," and this is omitted for brevity. For this reason the plural appears in His words ﴿You desire the goods of this world﴾, and the construction "you desire" (singular) was not used, because he did not order the sparing of men at the time of war, nor did he ever desire the goods of this world; rather, it was done by the majority of those who engaged in the fighting. The exegetes have elaborated at length on the story of these captives, and this is mentioned in the biographies (siyar), but we have omitted it because some of it is not fitting to mention with regard to the station of the Messengers. Abu ʿAmr read ﴿an takuna﴾ with the feminine, in agreement with the feminine form of the collective noun, while the rest of the seven and the majority read it in the masculine according to the meaning. The majority and the seven read ﴿asra﴾ on the pattern fa'la; this is the analogical form of fa'il in the sense of maf'ul when it denotes an affliction, like jarih and jarha (wounded). Yazid ibn al-Qaqaʿ and al-Mufaddal from ʿAsim read ﴿ʾusara﴾, and fa'il was likened to fa'lan, as in kaslan and kusala (lazy), just as they likened kaslan to asir, saying kasla as its plural; this was stated by Sibawayh. Both of these are anomalous. Al-Zajjaj claimed that ʾusara is the plural of asra, so it is a plural of a plural. The earlier discussion of whether fu'ala is a plural or a collective noun has been mentioned, and Sibawayh's view is that it is among the patterns of plurals. The referent of asra and usara is one and the same. Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla read: al-asra are those not bound when they are taken, and al-usara are those bound with ropes. Abu Hatim reported that he heard this from the Arabs, and Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash also mentioned it, saying: "The Arabs do not recognize this; both are the same to them." Abu Jaʿfar, Yahya ibn Yaʿmar and Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿hatta yuthakhkhina﴾ with shadda, treating it as transitive by doubling; the majority read it with the light form and made it transitive by the hamza, since before transitivity it was thakhana. The meaning of ﴿ʿaradh al-dunya﴾ is what you took in ransom for the captives. The ransom for each man was twenty ounces, the ransom of al-ʿAbbas was forty ounces, and from Ibn Sirin it is reported to be a hundred ounces. An ounce (uqiyya) is forty dirhams and six dinars. They had inclined toward ransom in order to strengthen themselves for jihad, out of preference for kinship and hope for Islam's acceptance. Inflicting massacre and killing was more awe-inspiring to the unbelievers and more exalting for the banner of Islam. This was at a time when the Muslims were few. When the sphere of Islam widened and its people became mighty, there was revealed: ﴿then either a favour afterwards or ransom﴾ (Q 47:4). It is also read ﴿yuridun﴾ with the yaʾ from below. It is called "ʿaradh" because it is an event of short duration. The majority read ﴿al-akhirah﴾ in the accusative, while Sulayman ibn Jammaz al-Madani read it in the genitive. They differed over the omitted noun being supplied. Some supplied it as ʿaradh al-akhirah, and said that ʿaradh was omitted because of the indication of ʿaradh al-dunya. Some said: the ʿaradh is omitted in the reading of the majority, and the genitive noun was put in its place in case, so it was put in the accusative. Among those who supplied ʿaradh al-akhirah was al-Zamakhshari, who said: "by way of contrast," meaning its reward, end quote. What we mean is that since the ransom was called "the goods of this world," the reward of the Hereafter was called "goods" by way of contrast, not that the reward of the Hereafter is perishable and transient like the goods of this world; it was called "goods" by way of contrast, though without the contrast it would not be so called. Some supplied it as the deed of the Hereafter, meaning what leads to reward in the Hereafter. All of them treated it like the verse:

"And a fire kindled by night, a fire"

and they meant only the omission of the noun, while keeping the genitive on the noun that follows, because the genitive of such as "wa-nārin" is permissible and eloquent, when there is no separation between the genitive word and the conjunction, or it is separated by "la," as in: "mithlu Zaydin wa-la akhihi yaqulani dhalik" (the likeness of Zayd and not his brother say that). The omitted noun was mentioned before in its like both in wording and meaning. As for when they are separated by other than "la," as in this reading, it is anomalous and rare. Allah is Almighty: He helps His friends, makes victory theirs, and empowers them over their enemies, in killing and in taking captives. All-Wise: He places things in their proper places. Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil said: Had Allah not written in the Mother of the Book that He would make the spoils lawful to you, a punishment would have touched you for what you hastened to take of them and of the ransom on the day of Badr before you were commanded to do so. A great punishment. Ibn ʿAbbas also said, and Mujahid: Had it not been predetermined that whoever commits a sin in ignorance is punished, you would have been punished. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn al-Husayn and Ibn Ishaq said: It was predetermined that no one is punished except after a prohibition, and he had not prohibited them. Al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Abi Najih reporting from Mujahid said: Had it not been that what had preceded for the people of Badr, that Allah would not punish them, He would have punished them. Al-Mawardi said: Had the Qur'an not required the forgiveness of minor sins, He would have punished them. Some people said: the preceding Book is His pardon of them in this specific sin. It was said: it is that He would not punish them while the Messenger was among them. It was said: it is what He prescribed for Himself of mercy. It was said: it had preceded that He would not lead a people astray after He had guided them. It was said: it had preceded that He would make the spoils and the ransom lawful to them, said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Hurayrah and al-Hasan. It was said: it had preceded that He would forgive minor sins for those who avoid major sins; had He not, He would have punished you by taking the spoils, and al-Nahhas preferred this. Some people said: the preceding Book is the Qur'an, and the meaning: Had it not been the Book that preceded, so that you believed in it and affirmed it, the punishment would have touched you for your taking this ransom. Al-Zamakhshari said: Had it not been a judgment from Him, exalted, whose affirmation preceded in the Preserved Tablet, which is that He does not punish anyone for an error, and this was an error in judgment, for they considered that sparing them might be a cause of their Islam and repentance, and that their ransom could strengthen them for jihad in the way of Allah, and it was hidden from them that killing them was more honourable for Islam, more awe-inspiring to those behind them, and more weakening to their strength, end quote. It is related: "Had a punishment descended in this matter, Umar would have escaped it," and in another hadith, "and Saʿd ibn Muʿadh," because their opinion was that the captives be killed. What I say is: they were first commanded to kill the unbelievers in several verses, such as His words: ﴿And kill them wherever you find them﴾ (Q 4:89), and ﴿And kill them wherever you encounter them﴾ (Q 2:191). When the battle of Badr occurred and they took a group of the polytheists captive, they differed over taking ransom from them and over killing them. Those who favoured ransom were rebuked, since the command to kill had already been given, and they had not carried out the command but inclined toward ransom and were eager to obtain wealth. Do you not see the saying of al-Miqdad when the Messenger (ﷺ) ordered the killing of ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt; he said: "My captive, O Messenger of Allah!" And the saying of Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr to one who had captured his brother: "Tighten your grip on him, for he has a wealthy mother." Then, after this rebuke, the Messenger ordered the killing of some, release with favour for some, and ransom for some. That was an abrogation of the obligation to kill. Then Allah, exalted, said: ﴿Had there not been a decree from Allah that preceded﴾, concerning His support, your victory, and your subjugation of your enemies, until you prevailed over them in killing, capture and plunder, despite your small number and equipment, a great punishment from them would have touched you for what you took of their spoils and their ransom, because they were greater in number and equipment than you. But Allah, exalted, made it easy for you, and no punishment from them touched you, neither by killing, nor capture, nor plunder. That was by the preceding judgment in His decree that He would empower you over them and not empower them over you. So the meaning is not that it touched you from Allah, but that it would have touched you from your enemies, as He said: ﴿If a wound touches you, a similar wound has touched the people﴾ (Q 3:140), and He said: ﴿If you suffer pain, they suffer pain as you suffer﴾ (Q 4:104). Then Allah, exalted, said: ﴿So eat of what you have taken as lawful and good﴾, that is, of what you have taken, and among it is what was obtained by the ransom which the Messenger (ﷺ) approved. He said: "None of them shall escape except with a ransom or the striking of a neck." This command is not the origin of the permissibility of spoils, since their lawfulness had already preceded the day of Badr, but it is a command conveying emphasis and including the wealth of ransom within the generality of what you have taken, since the rebuke had occurred concerning the inclination to ransom, and then the Messenger approved it. ﴿Lawful﴾ is in the accusative as a state of ﴿mā﴾ if it is a relative pronoun, or of its omitted pronoun, or as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: eating lawful eating. They permitted "mā" to be a verbal particle as well. It is reported that they refrained from the spoils and did not stretch out their hands toward them, so this was revealed. Al-Zamakhshari made His words "so eat" a consequence of an omitted clause which is the cause, and the particle fa' indicated this, and he supplied it as: "I have made the spoils lawful to you, so eat." Al-Zajjaj said: the fa' is for the apodosis, and the meaning: "I have made the ransom lawful to you, so eat." Allah, exalted, commanded them to fear Him, because fear of Him leads to obeying Allah's command and refraining from undertaking what has not been preceded by permission. So it contains an exhortation to piety for those who inclined toward ransom. Then the two attributes came, indicating the forgiveness and mercy of Allah toward those who inclined toward ransom before permission was given. Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is that if you fear Him after what has passed from you of seizing the ransom before you were permitted it, He will forgive you, have mercy on you, and turn to you in forgiveness. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: His words "and fear Allah" came as an eloquent parenthetical interjection in the midst of the speech, because His words "Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" are connected to His words: ﴿So eat of what you have taken as lawful and good﴾. It was also said: Forgiving of what you did, Merciful in making lawful what you took.

Abu Hatim reported that he heard this from the Arabs, and Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash also mentioned it, saying: "The Arabs do not recognize this; both are the same to them." Abu Jaʿfar, Yahya ibn Yaʿmar and Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿hatta yuthakhkhina﴾ with shadda, treating it as transitive by doubling; the majority read it with the light form and made it transitive by the hamza, since before transitivity it was thakhana. The meaning of ﴿ʿaradh al-dunya﴾ is what you took in ransom for the captives. The ransom for each man was twenty ounces, the ransom of al-ʿAbbas was forty ounces, and from Ibn Sirin it is reported to be a hundred ounces. An ounce (uqiyya) is forty dirhams and six dinars. They had inclined toward ransom in order to strengthen themselves for jihad, out of preference for kinship and hope for Islam's acceptance. Inflicting massacre and killing was more awe-inspiring to the unbelievers and more exalting for the banner of Islam. This was at a time when the Muslims were few. When the sphere of Islam widened and its people became mighty, there was revealed: ﴿then either a favour afterwards or ransom﴾ (Q 47:4). It is also read ﴿yuridun﴾ with the yaʾ from below. It is called "ʿaradh" because it is an event of short duration. The majority read ﴿al-akhirah﴾ in the accusative, while Sulayman ibn Jammaz al-Madani read it in the genitive. They differed over the omitted noun being supplied. Some supplied it as ʿaradh al-akhirah, and said that ʿaradh was omitted because of the indication of ʿaradh al-dunya. Some said: the ʿaradh is omitted in the reading of the majority, and the genitive noun was put in its place in case, so it was put in the accusative. Among those who supplied ʿaradh al-akhirah was al-Zamakhshari, who said: "by way of contrast," meaning its reward, end quote. What we mean is that since the ransom was called "the goods of this world," the reward of the Hereafter was called "goods" by way of contrast, not that the reward of the Hereafter is perishable and transient like the goods of this world; it was called "goods" by way of contrast, though without the contrast it would not be so called. Some supplied it as the deed of the Hereafter, meaning what leads to reward in the Hereafter. All of them treated it like the verse:

"And a fire kindled by night, a fire"

and they meant only the omission of the noun, while keeping the genitive on the noun that follows, because the genitive of such as "wa-nārin" is permissible and eloquent, when there is no separation between the genitive word and the conjunction, or it is separated by "la," as in: "mithlu Zaydin wa-la akhihi yaqulani dhalik" (the likeness of Zayd and not his brother say that). The omitted noun was mentioned before in its like both in wording and meaning. As for when they are separated by other than "la," as in this reading, it is anomalous and rare. Allah is Almighty: He helps His friends, makes victory theirs, and empowers them over their enemies, in killing and in taking captives. All-Wise: He places things in their proper places. Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil said: Had Allah not written in the Mother of the Book that He would make the spoils lawful to you, a punishment would have touched you for what you hastened to take of them and of the ransom on the day of Badr before you were commanded to do so. A great punishment. Ibn ʿAbbas also said, and Mujahid: Had it not been predetermined that whoever commits a sin in ignorance is punished, you would have been punished. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn al-Husayn and Ibn Ishaq said: It was predetermined that no one is punished except after a prohibition, and he had not prohibited them. Al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Abi Najih reporting from Mujahid said: Had it not been that what had preceded for the people of Badr, that Allah would not punish them, He would have punished them. Al-Mawardi said: Had the Qur'an not required the forgiveness of minor sins, He would have punished them. Some people said: the preceding Book is His pardon of them in this specific sin. It was said: it is that He would not punish them while the Messenger was among them. It was said: it is what He prescribed for Himself of mercy. It was said: it had preceded that He would not lead a people astray after He had guided them. It was said: it had preceded that He would make the spoils and the ransom lawful to them, said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Hurayrah and al-Hasan. It was said: it had preceded that He would forgive minor sins for those who avoid major sins; had He not, He would have punished you by taking the spoils, and al-Nahhas preferred this. Some people said: the preceding Book is the Qur'an, and the meaning: Had it not been the Book that preceded, so that you believed in it and affirmed it, the punishment would have touched you for your taking this ransom. Al-Zamakhshari said: Had it not been a judgment from Him, exalted, whose affirmation preceded in the Preserved Tablet, which is that He does not punish anyone for an error, and this was an error in judgment, for they considered that sparing them might be a cause of their Islam and repentance, and that their ransom could strengthen them for jihad in the way of Allah, and it was hidden from them that killing them was more honourable for Islam, more awe-inspiring to those behind them, and more weakening to their strength, end quote. It is related: "Had a punishment descended in this matter, Umar would have escaped it," and in another hadith, "and Saʿd ibn Muʿadh," because their opinion was that the captives be killed. What I say is: they were first commanded to kill the unbelievers in several verses, such as His words: ﴿And kill them wherever you find them﴾ (Q 4:89), and ﴿And kill them wherever you encounter them﴾ (Q 2:191). When the battle of Badr occurred and they took a group of the polytheists captive, they differed over taking ransom from them and over killing them. Those who favoured ransom were rebuked, since the command to kill had already been given, and they had not carried out the command but inclined toward ransom and were eager to obtain wealth. Do you not see the saying of al-Miqdad when the Messenger (ﷺ) ordered the killing of ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt; he said: "My captive, O Messenger of Allah!" And the saying of Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr to one who had captured his brother: "Tighten your grip on him, for he has a wealthy mother." Then, after this rebuke, the Messenger ordered the killing of some, release with favour for some, and ransom for some. That was an abrogation of the obligation to kill. Then Allah, exalted, said: ﴿Had there not been a decree from Allah that preceded﴾, concerning His support, your victory, and your subjugation of your enemies, until you prevailed over them in killing, capture and plunder, despite your small number and equipment, a great punishment from them would have touched you for what you took of their spoils and their ransom, because they were greater in number and equipment than you. But Allah, exalted, made it easy for you, and no punishment from them touched you, neither by killing, nor capture, nor plunder. That was by the preceding judgment in His decree that He would empower you over them and not empower them over you. So the meaning is not that it touched you from Allah, but that it would have touched you from your enemies, as He said: ﴿If a wound touches you, a similar wound has touched the people﴾ (Q 3:140), and He said: ﴿If you suffer pain, they suffer pain as you suffer﴾ (Q 4:104). Then Allah, exalted, said: ﴿So eat of what you have taken as lawful and good﴾, that is, of what you have taken, and among it is what was obtained by the ransom which the Messenger (ﷺ) approved. He said: "None of them shall escape except with a ransom or the striking of a neck." This command is not the origin of the permissibility of spoils, since their lawfulness had already preceded the day of Badr, but it is a command conveying emphasis and including the wealth of ransom within the generality of what you have taken, since the rebuke had occurred concerning the inclination to ransom, and then the Messenger approved it. ﴿Lawful﴾ is in the accusative as a state of ﴿mā﴾ if it is a relative pronoun, or of its omitted pronoun, or as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: eating lawful eating. They permitted "mā" to be a verbal particle as well. It is reported that they refrained from the spoils and did not stretch out their hands toward them, so this was revealed. Al-Zamakhshari made His words "so eat" a consequence of an omitted clause which is the cause, and the particle fa' indicated this, and he supplied it as: "I have made the spoils lawful to you, so eat." Al-Zajjaj said: the fa' is for the apodosis, and the meaning: "I have made the ransom lawful to you, so eat." Allah, exalted, commanded them to fear Him, because fear of Him leads to obeying Allah's command and refraining from undertaking what has not been preceded by permission. So it contains an exhortation to piety for those who inclined toward ransom. Then the two attributes came, indicating the forgiveness and mercy of Allah toward those who inclined toward ransom before permission was given. Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is that if you fear Him after what has passed from you of seizing the ransom before you were permitted it, He will forgive you, have mercy on you, and turn to you in forgiveness. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: His words "and fear Allah" came as an eloquent parenthetical interjection in the midst of the speech, because His words "Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" are connected to His words: ﴿So eat of what you have taken as lawful and good﴾. It was also said: Forgiving of what you did, Merciful in making lawful what you took.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 8, verses 70–71:

﴿O Prophet, say to those prisoners who are in your hands: If Allah knows any good in your hearts, He will give you better than what was taken from you, and He will forgive you. Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿But if they intend treachery against you, they have already betrayed Allah before, so He gave you power over them. Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾

This verse was revealed after Badr, concerning the prisoners of Badr. They were informed that Allah knew they had an inclination toward Islam and hoped for it, if they were ransomed and returned to their people. It was also said that it was revealed concerning al-Abbas and his companions, who said to the Messenger: "We believe in what you have brought, and we testify that you are the Messenger of Allah. We will surely advise you against our people." The phrase ﴿في أيديكم﴾ (in your hands) means "I have given you authority over them," as if the hands were grasping them. The correct view is that the prisoners numbered seventy and the slain numbered seventy, as established in Sahih Muslim. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Musayyab and Abu Amr ibn al-Ala. When they were brought to Madinah, Shuqran, the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), was in charge of them. Malik said: they were polytheists. Among them was al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, who was captured by Abu al-Yusr Ka'b ibn Amr, a brother of Banu Salama. Abu al-Yusr was short, while al-Abbas was large and tall. When he brought him, the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "A angel helped you against him." And it is reported from al-Abbas: "I was a Muslim, but they forced me." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If what you say is true, then Allah will reward you. But as for the outward of your affair, you were against us." He was one of those who had guaranteed the feeding of the people of Badr, and he came out with gold for that purpose.

It is also reported that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to al-Abbas: "Ransom your two nephews," meaning Aqil ibn Abi Talib and Nawfal ibn al-Harith. He said: "O Muhammad, you have left me to beg from the Quraysh for as long as I live." He (ﷺ) said to him: "Where is the money that you gave to Umm al-Fadl when you left Makkah, and you said to her: 'I do not know what will befall me in this journey; if something happens to me, then it is for you, for Abd Allah, Ubayd Allah and al-Fadl'?" Al-Abbas said: "How do you know that?" He said: "My Lord informed me of it." Al-Abbas said: "I testify that you are truthful, and that there is no god but Allah, and that you are His servant and Messenger. By Allah, no one had known of it except Allah. I gave it to her in the dark of the night. I had been in doubt about your affair, but now that you have informed me of this, there is no doubt." Al-Abbas said: "Allah then replaced it for me with something better than that. I now have twenty slaves, the least of whom trades for twenty thousand, and He gave me Zamzam, which I would not want to exchange for all the wealth of Makkah, and I await forgiveness from my Lord."

It is also reported that the wealth of Bahrain, eighty thousand, came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He performed ablution for the noon prayer and did not pray until he had distributed it. He ordered al-Abbas to take from it, and he took as much as he could carry. He used to say: "This is better than what was taken from me, and I hope for forgiveness."

The meaning of ﴿إن يعلم الله﴾ (If Allah knows) is: if it becomes clear to people that Allah's knowledge of good in your hearts, that is Islam, as you claimed, by showing Islam, then He will give you better than what was taken from you as ransom, and He will forgive you what you have committed, for Islam erases what came before it.

Al-Jumhur recite ﴿من الأسرى﴾ (from the prisoners). Ibn Muhaysin recites ﴿من أسرى﴾ (from prisoners) in the indefinite form. Qatadah, Abu Ja'far, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Nasr ibn Asim and Abu Amr, among the seven, recite ﴿من الأُسارى﴾ (from the captives). There is disagreement about the reading attributed to al-Hasan and al-Jahdari. Al-A'mash recites ﴿يُثِبكم خيرًا﴾ (will reward you with good), from ﴿الثواب﴾ (reward). Al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, Shayba and Humayd recite ﴿مما أخَذ﴾ (what was taken), in the active voice.

As for the giving of this good, it is said it is in this world, it is said in the Hereafter, and it is said it is in both.

The apparent view is that the pronoun in ﴿وإن يريدوا﴾ (But if they intend) refers to the prisoners, since they are the nearest mentioned. The treachery (khiyanah) here is that some of them showed Islam, then were returned to their religion, and so they betrayed Allah by going out with the polytheists. Al-Kirmani said: ﴿وإن يريدوا﴾ means the prisoners ﴿خيانتك﴾ (your betrayal), meaning breaking what they pledged with you. ﴿فقد خانوا الله﴾ (they have betrayed Allah) through disbelief and ingratitude before the covenant. It was said: before Badr. ﴿فأمكن منهم﴾ (so He gave you power over them), or: ﴿فأمكنك منهم﴾ (so He gave you power over them), and you defeated them and took them captive.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿خيانتك﴾ means they break what they pledged to you of Islam, and they turn to apostasy and prefer the religion of their fathers. ﴿فقد خانوا الله من قبل﴾ means in their disbelief and breaking of what was taken from every sensible person of its obligations. ﴿فأمكن منهم﴾ means as you saw on the day of Badr; so He will give you power over them if they return to treachery.

It was also said that the intended treachery is withholding what they guaranteed of the ransom.

Ibn Atiyyah said: if they are sincere, then such and such is done to them; but if they conceal treachery, and they desire to betray the covenant entrusted to them, then that does not please them, and they do not feel at ease with it, for Allah is ever watchful. They are the ones who betrayed Him by their disbelief and their neglect of reflecting on His signs. He has made those signs clear to them and given them the faculty by which to grasp them, so this became like a firm covenant. Therefore their recompense for their betrayal of Him was that He gave the believers power over them and made them captives in their hands. Allah is All-Knowing of what they conceal, whether sincerity or treachery, and Wise in what He requites them. End of quotation.

It was also said: the pronoun in ﴿وإن يريدوا﴾ refers to those about whom it was said ﴿وإن جنحوا للسلم﴾ (And if they incline to peace), meaning: and if they intend your betrayal by displaying peace.

The majority hold that the pronoun in ﴿وإن يريدوا﴾ refers to the prisoners. It is reported from Qatadah that this verse concerns the story of Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh. If he said that by way of illustration, it is possible; but if it is meant that the verse was revealed about that, then no, because the matter of Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh was clarified at the conquest of Makkah, whereas this verse was revealed after Badr. (p-521)
