Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verse 72:

﴿Indeed, those who believed and emigrated and strove with their wealth and their lives in the way of Allah, and those who gave shelter and helped—those are allies of one another. And those who believed but did not emigrate, you have no obligation of protection toward them until they emigrate. And if they seek your help in matters of religion, then it is incumbent upon you to help, except against a people between you and whom there is a covenant. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ Allah divided the believers into: the Emigrants (muhajirun), the Helpers (ansar), and those who did not emigrate. He began with the Emigrants, because they are the foundation of Islam and the first to respond to Allah. Some of them emigrated to Medina, some to Abyssinia, and some to Ibn Dhi Yazan, and then they emigrated to Medina. They were an example for others in faith and a cause of strengthening the religion. "Whoever establishes a good practice, he will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection." He mentioned the Helpers second, because they equaled them in faith and in striving with their persons and wealth. However, he placed emigration in parallel with sheltering and helping, and the Emigrants alone had precedence. He mentioned a third group: those who believed but did not emigrate and did not help. They missed these two virtues and were deprived of wilaya until they emigrate. The meaning of "allies of one another" (awliya' ba'd) is in support, cooperation and mutual assistance, as in other verses, such as: ﴿And the believing men and believing women are allies of one another﴾ [al-Tawba: 71]. (p-522) Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada said: this refers to inheritance. The Messenger (ﷺ) established brotherhood between the Emigrants and the Helpers, so an Emigrant would inherit from his Helper brother if he had no Emigrant wali in Medina, and there was no inheritance between him and his Muslim relative who was not an Emigrant. Ibn Zayd said: this continued until the conquest of Mecca; then they inherited again after that, since there was no more emigration. So the meaning of ﴿you have no obligation of protection toward them﴾ is the negation of allegiance in inheritance. The statement ﴿And those of blood relationship are closer to one another﴾ [al-Anfal: 75] was an abrogation of that. On the first view, the negation of wilaya is taken as a description of the state, since their protection and support are impossible due to the distance between the Emigrants and them, and in this is an exhortation to the Bedouins to emigrate. It was said: wilaya cannot be the meaning, because it is joined to it by ﴿And if they seek your help in matters of religion, then it is incumbent upon you to help﴾, and the conjoined element differs from the element it is joined to, so the negated wilaya must be other than support. End. When the verse "you have no obligation of protection toward them until they emigrate" was revealed, al-Zubayr said: Shall we help them in a matter if they seek help from us? Then ﴿And if they seek your help﴾ was revealed. The meaning of "covenant" (mithaq) is a pact, because your helping them would breach the pact, so you do not fight; the covenant prevents that. He restricted seeking help to religion, because seeking help through zeal and tribalism in other than religion is forbidden. The particle ʿalā (incumbent) indicates obligation, and for this al-Zamakhshari estimated it with his words: "then it is obligatory upon you to help them." Zuhayr said:

"For their wealthy ones is the provision of whoever seeks them, and among the poor is generosity and giving."

Al-A'mash, Ibn Thabbat and Hamza read ﴿wilayatihim﴾ with a kasra, while the rest of the seven and the majority read it with a fatha. Both are dialects, as said by al-Akhfash. Al-Asma'i considered al-Akhfash's kasra reading a solecism and erred in that, because it is a mutawatir reading. Abu Ubayda said: with a kasra it is from wilayat al-sultan (rule of authority), and with a fatha from al-mawla (the protector), it is said: mawla, and between wilaya with a fatha of the waw. Al-Zajjaj said: with a fatha it is from support and kinship, and with a kasra it is like the office of command. He said: the kasra is permissible, because in one group taking charge of another there is a kind of craft and work, and whatever is of the type of craft takes a kasra, like qisara (fulling) and khiyata (sewing). Al-Zamakhshari followed al-Zajjaj, saying: it was read as ﴿wilayatihim﴾ with fatha and kasra, i.e., from their taking charge in inheritance. The kasra was justified because one group's taking charge of another is likened to work and craft, as if by taking charge of his companion he is undertaking a matter and engaging in a task. Abu Ubayd said: what we hold is the adoption of the fatha in these two places, meaning here and in al-Kahf, because their meaning is from muwalat (allegiance), since it is in religion. Al-Farra' said: he means from their inheritances, and the kasra of the waw is more beloved to me than its fatha, since it is only fathed when it is support. Al-Kisa'i went with the fatha as support. The fatha and kasra have both been mentioned in both meanings. Al-Sulami and al-A'raj read ﴿bima ya'malun﴾ with the ya' (third person, the absent).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verse 73:

﴿And those who disbelieve, some of them are allies of others.﴾ A group read: awliya' bi-ba'd (with the preposition bi). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this plural refers to inheritance, mutual aid and support. Al-Zamakhshari said: its apparent meaning is the affirmation of friendship among them, like His saying, exalted is He, concerning the Muslims (﴿Those, some of them are allies of others﴾ [al-Anfal: 72]), and its meaning is: a prohibition for the Muslims from befriending those who disbelieve and from inheriting from them, and an obligation to keep away from them and sever ties with them even if they are relatives, and that they should leave them to inherit from one another. Another scholar said: when He mentioned the three categories of believers, and that they are allies, one supporting another and one inheriting from another, He made clear that the group of disbelievers is likewise, since before the mission of the Messenger (ﷺ) the People of the Book among them would call upon the Quraysh and would wait for misfortunes to befall them; then, after his mission, they became allies of one another and a single body against the Messenger, to protect their leaderships and to form a faction against the believers.

﴿If you do not do it, there will be turmoil on earth and great corruption.﴾ The pronoun in taf'aluhu (you do it) refers to the covenant, i.e., to observing it, or to the support, or to the inheritance, or to the whole of what preceded; these are four opinions. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, if you do not do what I commanded you of, namely the connection among the Muslims and the allegiance of some of them to others, even in inheritance, giving precedence to the bond of Islam over the bond of kinship, and you do not sever the ties between you and the disbelievers, and you do not treat their kinship as if it were no kinship at all, there will occur turmoil on earth and a great evil; for as long as the Muslims do not become one hand against polytheism, polytheism remains manifest and corruption increases. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "fitnah" is trial by war and what accompanies it of raids, expulsion and captivity, and "great corruption" is the manifestation of polytheism. Al-Baghawi said: "fitnah on earth" is the strength of disbelief, and "great corruption" is the weakness of Islam. Abu Musa al-Hijazi read from al-Kisa'i: kathir, with the three-dotted tha' (ث), and it is narrated that the Messenger (ﷺ) recited: wa-fasadun 'arid (and a wide corruption).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 8, verse 74:

﴿Those who believed, migrated, and struggled in the way of Allah, and those who sheltered and helped, those are the true believers. For them is forgiveness and a generous provision.﴾ This verse exalts the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun) and the Helpers (al-Ansar). It is abridged, for what has been omitted from it is "with their wealth and their lives." It is not a repetition, because the preceding verses included the guardianship of some of them over others, the division of the believers into three categories, and the ruling on their guardianship and support. This verse includes praise, honour, and distinction, and what their condition led to: forgiveness and a generous provision. The interpretation of the last of the verses similar to this one was already given at the beginning of this surah.

﴿Those who believed afterwards, migrated, and struggled alongside you, they are of you﴾ [al-Anfal: 75]. This means those who joined the migration after those who had preceded them in it. Allah, the Exalted, judged that they are among the believers who came first in reward and recompense, although the early ones (al-Sabiqun) have a distinct superiority of precedence, and of advancing in faith, migration, and struggle. The meaning of "afterwards" (min ba'du) is: after the first migration. That was after al-Hudaybiyah, as said by Ibn Abbas. Ibn Atiyyah added: and the Pledge of Rid'wan (Bay'at al-Ridwan). This is because the migration after that was of a lower rank than the migration before it, and it was called the Second Migration, since the war laid down its burdens for about two years, and then came the Conquest of Makkah. The Prophet, peace be upon him, also said: "There is no migration after the Conquest." Al-Tabari said: "After what I have explained of the ruling on guardianship," so the barrier between the two migrations was the revelation of this verse. Thus Allah, the Exalted, informs in this verse that they are among the first in mutual support and the rest of the rulings of Islam. It was also said: after the Day of Badr. Al-Asamm said: after the Conquest. In His saying "alongside you" (ma'akum) there is an indication that they are followers, not the principal ones, as He said: ﴿So those are with the believers﴾ [al-Nisa': 146], and likewise: ﴿then they are of you﴾ [al-Anfal: 75], just as a client (mawla) of a people is considered one of them, and a sister's son of a people is considered one of them.

And those related by blood (ulu al-arham) are more entitled to one another in the Book of God. Indeed God has knowledge of everything. That is, [the verse refers to] the possessors of kinship ties. Others have said: his words concerning the emigrants (muhajirun) and the helpers (ansar), "some of them are allies of others", refer to inheritance by the brotherhood that existed between them. He said: this [verse] concerns inheritance, and it abrogates (naskh) inheritance by that brotherhood, and makes it obligatory that a person inherit from his believing relative even if he was not a emigrant. The companions of Abu Hanifa (ashab Abi Hanifa) used it as evidence for granting inheritance to dhawu al-arham (distant blood relatives who are not sharers or residuaries). A group among them, including Malik, said: it does not concern inheritance, and this is an escape from granting inheritance to the maternal uncle, the paternal aunt and the like. Another group said: it does concern inheritance, but it was abrogated by the explicit verse of inheritance. The apparent meaning is that the Book of God is the Qur'an that was sent down, and that is in the verse of inheritance. It has been said: "the Book of God" means the preserved tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) that precedes [revelation]. It has also been said: "the Book of God" means in this revealed verse. Al-Zajjaj said: "in His ruling (hukm)", and al-Zamakhshari followed him, saying: "in His ruling and His apportionment (qismah)". Ending the surah with the words "Indeed God has knowledge of everything" is at the peak of eloquence (bara'ah), since it contains many rulings on the essential matters of the religion and its foundations and a detailed explanation of its conditions. The attribute of knowledge encompasses all of that and comprehends its beginnings and its ends.
